The blue camp finally has its champion back." } }, { "model": "campaign_trail.answer_feedback", "pk": 196032, "fields": { "answer": 196031, "candidate": 68, "answer_feedback": "Framing the DPP as a creeping authoritarian regime hits a nerve with anti-establishment voters and civil libertarians alarmed by independent media pressure. For an aging political broker whose influence relies entirely on mutual patronage, Wang’s lukewarm speeches fail to generate enthusiasm or sway undecided voters in the south." } }, { "model": "campaign_trail.answer_feedback", "pk": 197132, "fields": { "answer": 197131, "candidate": 68, "answer_feedback": "Wang Jin-pyng abruptly announces a bout of severe exhaustion and completely boycotts your campaign tour across Kaohsiung, Pingtung, and Tainan. While purists applaud your unyielding moral stance, southern local organizers quietly throw up their hands in frustration, leaving your ground operations severely starved for resources and manpower." } }, { "model": "campaign_trail.answer_feedback", "pk": 197232, "fields": { "answer": 197231, "candidate": 68, "answer_feedback": "Unabashed political transactionalism carries the day, immediately sending shockwaves through the news cycle as Wang Jin-pyng is officially named to the top of the KMT party list. Photos of you and Wang smiling broadly and raising joined hands on stage draw scathing criticism from green commentators, who mock the scene as a return to old-school patronage and backroom spoils-sharing. Yet, behind the scenes, the payoff is immediate and immense: southern faction bosses, irrigation association directors, and local kingmakers unleash their get-out-the-vote machinery across the south. Should the KMT secure a legislative majority, the master bargainer will once again wield the Speaker's gavel." } }, { "model": "campaign_trail.answer_feedback", "pk": 128352, "fields": { "answer": 28352, "candidate": 68, "answer_feedback": "Reuniting the executive team of 2012 locks down the KMT's organizational machinery overnight. In his home stronghold of Nantou County, your support numbers are expected to surge significantly as local mobilization kicks into high gear. However, the national political cost remains severe. You have secured the party machine and Nantou's base at the expense of any claim to reform." } }, { "model": "campaign_trail.answer_feedback", "pk": 198132, "fields": { "answer": 286199, "candidate": 68, "answer_feedback": "Invoking your Hong Kong roots and legal precision fails to insulate you from a ferocious political backlash. Soong's face reddens as he tries to interject past the moderator's timer, dragging the broadcast into an embarrassing brawl over twenty-year-old party feuds. While green partisans remain hostile, you successfully reframe the debate from a red-smearing ambush into a sharp critique of partisan opportunism." } }, { "model": "campaign_trail.answer_feedback", "pk": 199232, "fields": { "answer": 199231, "candidate": 68, "answer_feedback": "Delivering a rare moment of personal humility draws mixed reactions in a hyper-polarized political climate. Post-debate pollsters and business owners hail this sharp, data-backed confrontation as your single most effective performance of the campaign." } }, { "model": "campaign_trail.answer_feedback", "pk": 200032, "fields": { "answer": 200031, "candidate": 68, "answer_feedback": "Floodlights illuminate Ketagalan Boulevard into a blinding sea of blue, with the Presidential Office looming in the background like a silent prize. In the crowd, the human spectrum of the capital unfolds: a retired 80-year-old general in an impeccably pressed suit weeps quietly while clutching an ROC flag, a young office worker in high heels shivers in the winter drizzle while holding a fluorescent stick, and sausage truck owners spin their grills at high speed, the sizzle of fat mixing with the roar of the speakers. The sheer density of the Taipei crowd creates an electric, nostalgic surge that reverberates across every television screen on the island." } }, { "model": "campaign_trail.answer_feedback", "pk": 200132, "fields": { "answer": 200131, "candidate": 68, "answer_feedback": "Rain glimmers under the massive floodlights at Banqiao Station Square, casting an amber glow over a dense sea of wet umbrellas that stretches all the way to the department store towers. Standing beside Eric Chu on the stage, you see the quiet exhaustion and genuine hope written on thousands of ordinary faces. A factory worker from Sanchong, his fingers still stained with machine grease, grips a damp flag with raw, wind-chapped hands. Beside him, a young mother who just stepped off the MRT holds her three-year-old daughter tight against her shoulder, the toddler sound asleep under a plastic rain poncho despite the booming loudspeakers. These are the suburban families who power the island—commuters, tech workers in soggy windbreakers, and small shop owners who braved the freezing drizzle after a twelve-hour workday. When Eric Chu takes the microphone, his usual technocratic polish melts into a surprisingly raw, emotional plea for working households. As his voice echoes off the concrete plaza, thousands of flags wave in unison, the steam rising from wet winter coats like a collective, silent sigh of hope." } }, { "model": "campaign_trail.answer_feedback", "pk": 200232, "fields": { "answer": 200231, "candidate": 68, "answer_feedback": "Hakka floral banners flutter in the chilly evening breeze as thousands pack the square near Zhongli Night Market. The atmosphere is warm and deeply grounded: an elderly Hakka grandmother in a traditional floral headscarf shouts words of encouragement in her native dialect, young semiconductor engineers in hoodies take selfies with your passing motorcade, and night market stallholders pass steaming bowls of hot grass jelly to shivering supporters in the front rows. Tapping into the Hakka community’s deep cultural pride and the industrial workers’ desire for economic stability creates a powerful, authentic wave of momentum." } }, { "model": "campaign_trail.answer_feedback", "pk": 200332, "fields": { "answer": 200331, "candidate": 68, "answer_feedback": "Ditching the Taipei megacity spotlight for the salty sea mist of Keelung Harbor and the howling winds of Hsinchu delivers a refreshing, raw energy to the campaign’s final hour. Dockworkers in rubber boots and calloused hands rub shoulders with young Hsinchu chip designers shivering in windbreakers, all united under flickering port lights. Fishwives leave their midnight market stalls to hand you fresh tea, shouting that small cities matter too. By honoring these neglected working harbors and high-tech parks, you ignite a fierce, localized pride that big-city campaigns could never match." } }, { "model": "campaign_trail.answer_feedback", "pk": 114515, "fields": { "answer": 114514, "candidate": 68, "answer_feedback": "Sensation and disbelief ripple across the electorate as news of the spy allegations dominates every headline. With the news cycle consumed by paranoia and conspiracy theories, all you can do is pray that reasonable voters see through the hysteria when they step into the polling booth. It is a chilling reminder of how fragile democratic norms can be." } }, { "model": "campaign_trail.answer_feedback", "pk": 40001, "fields": { "answer": 40000, "candidate": 68, "answer_feedback": "Rallying the base under the banner of Orthodox Blue triggers a wave of strategic voting across pan-blue strongholds. Remembering how close the contest was in 2012, many moderate conservatives who were considering Soong quietly decide to abandon the PFP and coalesce around your ticket to prevent a DPP victory. However, the stubborn core of Soong diehards refuses to budge, and their lingering presence on the ballot could easily tip the scales against you if the margin on election day proves razor-thin." } } Hailing from Nantou County, Wu Den-yih is the ultimate local-born Taiwanese political heavyweight within the Kuomintang establishment. Unlike the traditional Taipei Mainlander princelings, Wu forged his career from the grassroots up—starting as a Taipei City Councilor before serving as Nantou Magistrate and later a two-term Mayor of Kaohsiung. His deep-rooted connections to local factions across central and southern Taiwan make him an irreplaceable organizational pillar within the party apparatus.

Wu reached the apex of executive power during Ma Ying-jeou's presidency, serving as Premier of the Executive Yuan from 2009 to 2012 before being elevated to Vice President from 2012 to 2016. Recognized for his sharp, encyclopedic memory, fierce parliamentary debate skills, and formidable administrative grasp, he steered the government through the aftermath of the 2008 global financial crisis and Typhoon Morakot. To his supporters, he represents the consummate party strategist and executive powerhouse who knows every gear of the state machine.

Reuniting with Ma Ying-jeou on the 2020 ticket creates an unprecedented reunion of the executive team that governed for four years. As the KMT Party Chairman, Wu commands the party's ground machinery, grassroots branches, and factional alliances across the island. His presence on the ticket ensures that the KMT's organizational engine will operate with synchronized efficiency across central and southern battlegrounds.

However, Wu Den-yih also carries some of the highest negative ratings in modern Taiwanese political history. Fiercely targeted by green opponents and online youth as a slick, untrustworthy political strategist, he suffers from profound unpopularity among swing voters and young people. By reuniting Ma and Wu, the campaign doubles down on the exact leadership pairing that voters turned away from four years ago, placing a high-stakes bet that proven party experience will outweigh the public's appetite for fresh faces.

`; if (typeof window.changeVPAndShowOverlay === 'function') { window.changeVPAndShowOverlay( 'Wu Den-yih', 'Wu', 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/wuwuwu.jpg?v=1786555400454', wu_desc, wu_scores ); } } // 郝龙斌获选 if(ans === 2756){ let hau_scores = [0.80, 0.90, 0.50, 0.85, -0.60]; currentMateName = 'Hau Lung-pin'; currentMateTitle = 'Vice President Candidate'; // 郝龙斌的史诗级长篇传记 let hau_desc = `

He began his political career as a firebrand in the New Party before pragmatically returning to the KMT fold, eventually serving two full terms as the Mayor of Taipei—the traditional springboard to higher national office.

To his supporters, he represents the educated, dignified, and administratively competent face of the traditional Kuomintang, a stark contrast to the chaotic populism that has increasingly defined recent electoral cycles.

Eric Chu is highly educated, relentlessly pragmatic, and completely unoffensive, representing the rational core of the establishment.'; let chu_bio = `

Born into a meticulously calculated political union, Eric Chu’s very existence seems designed for high office. His father was a local politician in Taoyuan with deep ties to the military veterans, while his mother hailed from a prominent native Taiwanese family in Daxi. This perfect synthesis of Waishengren and Benshengren heritage provided him with an immaculate, bulletproof pedigree. Armed with a Ph.D. in Accounting from New York University, Chu was handpicked by the Kuomintang in the late 1990s as the shining face of their new, highly educated generation. He did not fight his way out of the mud; he took an elevator straight to the executive floor.

His ascent was characterized by clinical, spreadsheet-like efficiency. From a young legislator to the Magistrate of Taoyuan, and eventually ascending to Vice Premier, Chu rarely made mistakes. His crowning achievement arrived in 2010, when he narrowly defeated Tsai Ing-wen to become the Mayor of New Taipei City, securing the nation’s most populous municipality for the KMT. He governed not through fiery populist sermons, but through data analytics, urban renewal projects, and a polite, permanently affixed smile. He was the golden prince in waiting, the inevitable successor to Ma Ying-jeou.

But destiny has a cruel sense of irony. His immaculate trajectory was violently derailed in the catastrophic election cycle of 2016. Amidst a collapsing party and terrible poll numbers, Chu orchestrated the infamous 'Change Hung' maneuver, forcefully replacing Hung Hsiu-chu as the presidential nominee at the eleventh hour. The gamble backfired spectacularly. He was crushed by Tsai Ing-wen in a historic landslide, bearing the cross of the party’s darkest hour. The golden boy was suddenly deeply scarred, heavily mocked by the internet youth, and bitterly resented by the deep-blue ideological purists.

Now, emerging from years of quiet rehabilitation, Chu claims the 2020 nomination seeking his ultimate vindication. He promises to surgically remove the chaotic populism infecting the party and return the Republic to a path of rational, moderate technocracy. However, he faces an excruciating dilemma. He is a perfectly calibrated accountant in an era that demands street fighters. To survive, he must somehow convince the radicalized base that he is not a cowardly traitor, while simultaneously persuading the disillusioned progressive youth that he is not just another boring, obsolete bureaucrat. It is the safest bet the KMT could make, but safety rarely wins a holy war.

`; if (typeof window.changePresidentAndShowOverlay === 'function') { window.changePresidentAndShowOverlay('Eric Chu', 'Former Mayor of New Taipei', 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/20190715_news_zhu_li_lun_.jpg', chu_short, chu_bio); } } // 2. 吴敦义 (Wu Den-yih) if (ans === 2583) { let wu_short = 'The architect of the 2018 sweeping triumph has claimed the ultimate prize. Wu Den-yih relies entirely on cold, calculated political machinery to grind out a victory.'; let wu_bio = `

Before he became the grandmaster of the Kuomintang’s backroom mechanics, Wu Den-yih was a child who learned the terrifying fragility of power the hard way. Born in rural Nantou, his father was a victim of the White Terror, unjustly imprisoned by the very authoritarian regime Wu would later serve. Growing up in the shadow of political persecution, Wu realized early on that survival required absolute cunning, ruthless pragmatism, and a flawless mastery of the system. He studied history at National Taiwan University, writing sharp, calculating editorials that eventually caught the eye of Chiang Ching-kuo himself.

Wu became the ultimate ‘Benshengren’ prodigy of the martial law era. At twenty-five, he was a Taipei City Councilor. At thirty-three, he was the Magistrate of Nantou. He eventually seized the mayoralty of Kaohsiung, where he meticulously constructed an intricate, subterranean empire of local factions, patronage networks, and temple alliances. But his ruthless ascent hit a brutal wall in 1998, when a highly controversial, fabricated audio tape scandal handed him a razor-thin, humiliating defeat in Kaohsiung. Exiled to the political wilderness, many assumed the cunning tactician was permanently finished.

Yet, Wu is the ultimate political survivor. He slowly, painfully clawed his way back as a regional legislator, waiting in the shadows until 2009. When the Ma Ying-jeou administration was collapsing under the disastrous response to Typhoon Morakot, Ma summoned Wu to be his Premier. Bringing a steady hand and a terrifyingly efficient bureaucratic mind, Wu stabilized the government and engineered an economic rebound, eventually being rewarded with the Vice Presidency. He had returned to the absolute summit.

Taking over the bankrupt, morally shattered KMT chairmanship in 2017, Wu orchestrated the stunning 2018 local election landslide. Now, stepping out of the shadows to claim the 2020 presidential nomination is his final, Machiavellian masterstroke. But his vulnerability is fatal: he possesses the public charisma of a dry financial audit. Widely perceived by the electorate as a scheming, archaic old man prone to disastrous public gaffes, Wu must win this election without inspiring a single soul. He intends to forcefully grind the DPP into dust using overwhelming organizational leverage, proving that the dark arts of institutional control still dictate the destiny of the Republic.

`; if (typeof window.changePresidentAndShowOverlay === 'function') { window.changePresidentAndShowOverlay('Wu Den-yih', 'KMT Chairman', 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/1076x768_20190430000021.jpg', wu_short, wu_bio); } } // 3. 郭台铭 (Terry Gou) if (ans === 2588) { let gou_short = 'The Kuomintang has undergone an absolute corporate acquisition. Terry Gou brings a massive financial war chest and a ruthless CEO persona to the political battlefield.'; let gou_bio = `

Terry Gou did not inherit an empire; he forged it in the suffocating heat of a tin-roofed shed. Born in Banqiao to a low-ranking police officer who fled the mainland, Gou grew up in cramped, impoverished quarters. In 1974, armed with a mere 100,000 NTD loaned from his aging mother, he founded Hon Hai Plastics, manufacturing cheap television knobs with a handful of exhausted laborers. He was relentless, driven by a violent, all-consuming hunger for wealth and supremacy.

He famously flew to the United States, crashing uninvited into the headquarters of major tech companies, refusing to leave the lobby until they gave him a contract. He slept on factory floors, out-worked his competitors, and eventually opened colossal mega-factories in Shenzhen. He transformed his sweaty plastic workshop into Foxconn—a transnational, terrifyingly efficient leviathan that dictates global supply chains and builds the world’s iPhones. He transitioned from a struggling salesman to a billionaire dictator who negotiates with Xi Jinping and Donald Trump as an absolute equal.

Disgusted by the paralyzing inefficiency of career politicians, Gou decided that the Republic of China was essentially an underperforming subsidiary desperately in need of aggressive restructuring. Watching Donald Trump conquer Washington, Gou realized that vast wealth and sheer outsider audacity could completely shatter traditional political structures. When the Kuomintang was bankrupt and unable to even make payroll, Gou tossed them a 45 million NTD loan, effectively executing a hostile financial takeover of a century-old political party.

Now, as the 2020 presidential nominee, he offers the electorate a ruthless, economic-first populism. To the struggling middle class and business elite, he represents the ultimate promise of wealth. But his candidacy carries apocalyptic geopolitical liabilities. His massive manufacturing empire in mainland China makes him the ultimate target for DPP smears, raising profound, terrifying doubts about his ability to protect Taiwanese sovereignty against Beijing’s leverage. Furthermore, his abrasive, tyrannical management style threatens to alienate the very democratic institutions he seeks to lead. Terry Gou intends to run Taiwan Incorporated, and he accepts no board of directors.

`; if (typeof window.changePresidentAndShowOverlay === 'function') { window.changePresidentAndShowOverlay('Terry Gou', 'Foxconn Founder', 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/guodong.jpg', gou_short, gou_bio); } } // 4. 洪秀柱 (Hung Hsiu-chu) if (ans === 2593 ) { let hung_short = 'The Little Pepper has returned for absolute vengeance. She leads a fiercely loyal, ultra-deep blue crusade, transforming the KMT into an ideologically pure fortress.'; let hung_bio = `

Hung Hsiu-chu is a woman forged in the fires of historical tragedy and ideological stubbornness. Her father was a manager at the Taiwan Sugar Corporation who was unjustly arrested during the White Terror, tortured, and sent to the notorious political prison on Green Island for over three years. This left her family in absolute, grinding poverty. Yet, in a profound psychological paradox, instead of harboring resentment toward the Kuomintang, Hung internalized a fierce, hyper-orthodox loyalty to the pure, uncorrupted ideals of the Republic of China that the party claimed to represent. She became a disciplinary director at a high school, cultivating a strict, uncompromising demeanor.

Entering the Legislative Yuan in 1990, she quickly earned the moniker 'The Little Pepper' (小辣椒). Unlike her colleagues, she never built a corrupt local faction or relied on dark money; her power lay entirely in her razor-sharp, devastating rhetoric and her absolute ideological purity, which won her the fanatical devotion of the Huang Fu-hsing military veterans. She was the unapologetic conscience of the deep-blue base.

In 2015, when the male heavyweights of the KMT cowered in fear of Tsai Ing-wen, Hung bravely stepped forward to claim the presidential nomination. Her reward was a brutal, humiliating betrayal. Deeming her 'One China, Same Interpretation' platform too extreme, the cowardly party establishment orchestrated the infamous 'Change Hung' maneuver, forcefully deposing her at the eleventh hour. The elites threw her away to save themselves, only to be massacred in the general election anyway.

Now, following the total collapse of the moderate wing, Hung has returned for absolute, righteous vengeance. Reclaiming the nomination, her rallies resemble religious crusades, filled with weeping veterans who crave an uncompromising defense of their Chinese heritage. However, her unapologetic unification rhetoric completely alienates the mainstream Taiwanese youth and the moderate middle class. She has turned the KMT into an ideologically pure fortress, but it is a fortress under heavy siege, entirely isolated from the shifting reality of the island.

`; if (typeof window.changePresidentAndShowOverlay === 'function') { window.changePresidentAndShowOverlay('Hung Hsiu-chu', 'Current KMT Chairwoman', 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/C1433840772304.jpg', hung_short, hung_bio); } } // 5. 韩国瑜 (Han Kuo-yu) if (ans === 2599) { let han_short = 'The party has strapped itself to a populist rocket. Han Kuo-yu commands a fanatic, almost cult-like grassroots movement, speaking the raw language of the working class.'; let han_bio = `

Han Kuo-yu’s life is a chaotic, turbulent narrative of violence, exile, and miraculous resurrection. Born in a cramped Juancun (military dependents' village) in Banqiao, he was a restless, rebellious youth who constantly found himself in street brawls. His parents sent him to the military academy to instill discipline, setting the foundation for his aggressive, martial worldview. Entering the Legislative Yuan in the chaotic 1990s, Han was a fiery, deeply polarizing figure, most famously remembered for violently flipping a table and striking Chen Shui-bian across the face during a heated debate.

But the fire burned out quickly. By the early 2000s, Han was effectively exiled from national politics. For nearly two decades, he wandered in the political wilderness, largely forgotten by the polished, Ivy-League elites who had taken over the KMT. He eventually secured a quiet, bureaucratic job managing the Taipei Agricultural Products Marketing Corporation. It was there, amidst the pre-dawn auctions, that he learned the raw, unvarnished language of the vegetable vendors, truck drivers, and working-class commoners. He drank with them, understood their economic suffocations, and absorbed their deep resentment toward the political aristocracy.

Sent to Kaohsiung as a sacrificial lamb in 2018, Han was expected to quietly lose. Instead, he triggered a political earthquake. The 'Han Wave' tore through the deep-green south, fueled by sheer economic desperation and a visceral disgust with the progressive establishment. He did not just win the mayoralty; he became a political deity to millions of forgotten citizens.

Now, abandoning his mayoral post after barely six months, he has hijacked the presidential nomination. His rallies are earth-shattering spectacles of raw, populist emotion. But the backlash is equally terrifying. The educated youth, the media establishment, and the progressive middle class view him with apocalyptic dread. Wang Jin-pyng is the eternal survivor of Taiwanese politics. Born into a wealthy farming family in Luzhu, Kaohsiung, Wang initially worked as a mild-mannered mathematics teacher. He quietly inherited his family's vast local influence and entered the Legislative Yuan in 1975, during the suffocating height of martial law. While others gave fiery speeches, Wang mastered the silent, invisible art of networking.

His true ascent began during the Lee Teng-hui era. As Lee ruthlessly purged the orthodox Mainlander old guard to localize the Kuomintang, Wang became his indispensable native Taiwanese enforcer in the legislature. Crowned President of the Legislative Yuan in 1999, Wang ruled the parliament for an unprecedented seventeen years. He rarely raised his voice and never engaged in toxic ideological crusades. Instead, he resolved impossible political deadlocks through masterful, closed-door backroom negotiations, earning the undisputed title of the 'King of Deals'.

His subterranean empire of local factions, temple directors, and cross-party alliances made him seemingly immortal. But no empire lasts forever. To the deep-blue purists and progressive youth alike, he is the walking embodiment of corrupt, old-school 'Black Gold' politics. He must now prove that his invisible empire of favors can withstand the bright, unforgiving lights of a national presidential election.

Born in Hong Kong to orthodox Kuomintang elites, Ma Ying-jeou is the quintessential golden boy of the Pan-Blue establishment. Educated at National Taiwan University, New York University, and Harvard Law School, Ma rose rapidly through party ranks, famously serving as late President Chiang Ching-kuo's English interpreter. As Minister of Justice in the 1990s, he built an unyielding reputation as a stern anti-corruption crusader before dethroning Chen Shui-bian in the 1998 Taipei mayoral race—establishing himself as the undisputed heir to the Republic of China's conservative mainstream.

His ascent culminated in the historic 2008 presidential election, where he swept into office with over 7.6 million votes on a platform of clean governance and cross-strait reconciliation. Over eight years in power, Ma anchored his administration in the 1992 Consensus, expanding economic ties through the landmark ECFA agreement and crowning his tenure with the historic 2015 Ma-Xi summit in Singapore. Yet his polished, rigidly legalistic demeanor and small-circle decision-making gradually alienated local faction bosses and created deep friction with a changing electorate.

The 2014 Sunflower Student Movement shattered his economic narrative, triggering a catastrophic 2016 electoral collapse that handed power to Tsai Ing-wen. For four long years out of office, Ma endured an unceasing barrage of prosecutor probes, court subpoenas, and media mockery, branded by green partisans as an out-of-touch, pro-Beijing relic. Yet while others crumbled under judicial warfare, the Teflon pan quietly survived, watching the DPP's domestic stumbles slowly revive public nostalgia for his sterile predictability.

Now, through a surreal alignment of party desperation and factional maneuverings, the former president has staged an unprecedented comeback to claim the 2020 nomination. To his loyal base, he is the last untainted guardian of constitutional order, rule of law, and cross-strait peace. To his detractors, his return is a shameless, power-hungry farce that threatens to reignite every trauma of 2016. He must now prove that his rigid legalism and tested governance can persuade a deeply polarized electorate that once discarded him.

curr : best; }); return w.candidate === candidateId; }); return !hasWin; // 如果没找到任何胜利的县市，返回 true } // ========================================== // 国民党大胜结局模块 (按候选人彻底独立打包版) // ========================================== if (!exclusive_action_executed && ach_winnerID == ach_ID_KMT) { exclusive_action_executed = true; let endText = ''; let pct = FINAL_VOTE_PERCENT; // 获取真实得票率 let endImage = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/kmt_defeat_bg.jpg'; // 默认兜底败选图 // 音乐与标题设置的初始空变量 let s_name = 'Victory Anthem'; let s_artist = 'KMT'; let s_cover = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/250px-Emblem_of_the_Kuomintang.svg.png'; let s_url = ''; let mainTitle = ''; let subTitle = ''; if (Number(campaignTrail_temp.mayingjiu) === 1) { if (pct < 50.0) { endText += `

On the night before the election, Ma Ying-jeou lay in bed staring at the ceiling. The traffic outside on Xinglong Road had thinned out. After he counted the engine roar of the thirty-seventh scooter, Chow Mei-ching turned over.

`; endText += `

“You’re still awake.”

`; endText += `

It wasn’t a question. Her tone was identical to the one she used twenty years ago when catching him stealing braised pork from the fridge in the middle of the night.

`; endText += `

Ma rested his hands behind his head, his knuckles touching the stack of polling reports on the nightstand. “I was thinking about Wang Jin-pyng’s rally in the south last week. He invited so many people—”

`; endText += `

“You’re voting tomorrow. What’s the point of thinking about Wang Jin-pyng now?” Chow Mei-ching didn't open her eyes. “Even if he hosted five hundred tables, they wouldn't vote for you.”

`; endText += `

“I know.”

`; endText += `

“Then what are you still thinking about?”

`; endText += `

Ma remained silent for a few seconds. “I was thinking about the polls. They’re all about the same, but the margin of error—”

`; endText += `

“Margin of error.” Chow Mei-ching repeated the four words, a flattened amusement in her voice. “You told me ‘margin of error’ when you ran for Taipei Mayor in 1998, and you told me ‘margin of error’ when you ran for President in 2012. You’ve been running for over thirty years, and every single time it’s 'margin of error.'”

`; endText += `

“This time is different.”

`; endText += `

“When did you ever say it was the same?”

`; endText += `

Ma choked on his words. He tried to decipher his wife’s expression in the dark, but Chow Mei-ching had already turned to the other side, leaving him only her back.

`; endText += `

“I’m serious,” he said. “Tsai Ing-wen is different this time. She brought all those young people back, the online momentum—”

`; endText += `

“Then have you ever wondered why you always discuss polls with me on Election Eve instead of your party secretary-general?” Chow Mei-ching finally turned back around. “Because your secretaries-general don't dare tell you the truth, and you don't dare tell them the truth either. So you come to me, because I’ll tell you: close your eyes and sleep.”

`; endText += `

Ma didn't respond.

`; endText += `

Chow Mei-ching sighed, reaching out to pat his shoulder—neither too hard nor too light, like dusting an old suit that needed brushing off. “You’re always like this. When you get pre-election anxiety, you talk to me—not because you want an answer, but because you want to voice your unease. Well, I’ve given you my answer: sleep. Tomorrow after you vote, no matter the outcome, you still have to finish the remaining work. If you don't sleep now, what will your face look like on camera tomorrow?”

`; endText += `

“Look like what?”

`; endText += `

“Like a seventy-year-old who hasn't retired yet.”

`; endText += `

Ma smiled. That was probably the first nice thing she had said all night.

`; endText += `

He still lay with his eyes open for nearly an hour, listening to Chow Mei-ching’s breathing gradually deepen into a long, relaxed rhythm. He recalled that night in 2008, lying there in the same way, but the apprehension back then was entirely different—that year’s anxiety was the excitement of finally stepping up after waiting eight years. What about tonight? Tonight’s tension was more a fear of humiliation. Since democratization, former presidents attempting a comeback were not unheard of, but none had ever succeeded. If he lost, he would become the latest stepping stone for that unwritten rule—when people mentioned Ma Ying-jeou, they would no longer merely recall those eight years, but add a phrase: “that guy who failed his comeback.” He could even imagine the phrasing commentators would use: a fallen veteran, the final disillusionment of an old era, avenged by the very same opponent.

`; endText += `

The thought made his stomach contract.

`; endText += `

He counted twelve more scooters and finally fell asleep at 2:17 a.m.

`; endText += `

On the morning of Election Day, as Ma Ying-jeou queued at the polling station near his old home in Muzha, the crowd of onlookers was at least half the size of four years ago. He noticed two young people pointing their phones at him to film. Behind the lenses, those faces bore no anger, merely a lazy, curious expression—like watching a seventy-year-old panda in a zoo rumored to still be eating bamboo.

`; endText += `

After casting his ballot, he walked out to find Chow Mei-ching waiting outside, holding two cups of soy milk.

`; endText += `

“Wait at home?” she asked.

`; endText += `

“Head to headquarters,” Ma took the soy milk. “Drink it on the way.”

`; endText += `

The count began at four in the afternoon. Ma sat in the war room at Campaign Headquarters, four televisions before him locked onto different news channels. He insisted on ignoring those flashy 3D animated vote bar charts, looking only at the Central Election Commission’s official figures—though the CEC website was either overwhelmed or lagging, refreshing at an excruciatingly slow pace.

`; endText += `

King Pu-tsung sat to his left, answering calls one after another—picking up, hanging up, picking up again—his expression maintaining a professional composure throughout, like an old captain remaining unflustered high in the sky.

`; endText += `

“Taipei City’s reports are coming in slow,” King murmured, pulling away for another call before Ma could respond.

`; endText += `

Ma stared at the blue and green bars representing Tsai Ing-wen and himself on screen. The bars moved, crawling upward millimeter by millimeter, but the gap between them remained locked in a suffocatingly narrow range. Sometimes he led her by a fraction of a percentage point; sometimes she edged past him by a fraction. The two numbers rolled back and forth on the television screen like two snakes biting each other’s tails.

`; endText += `

His palms began to sweat. It reminded him of the 2012 election—that time had also been a midnight deadlock from the start, but back then he had at least maintained a steady lead in several central counties. Though not as optimistic as the unreleased exit polling estimates, his bottom card had always been in hand.

`; endText += `

Today was different.

`; endText += `

Today’s Taiwan was no longer the Taiwan of eight years ago. Over the past few years, the Sunflower Movement, marriage equality, pension reform, cross-strait relations—every issue had acted like a blade, slicing blue and green voters into increasingly thin, sharp fragments. Swing voters had virtually vanished; all that remained were the iron bases biting tightly at both ends. The higher the turnout, the worse it was for him, because ninety percent of those mobilized young people would not vote for the Kuomintang.

`; endText += `

He could only gamble on one thing: fear.

`; endText += `

Fear of uncertainty in cross-strait relations would drag those silent, middle-aged and elderly voters out of their homes to vote. These people wouldn't post articles online or express themselves on social platforms where youth gathered; their sole way of expressing themselves was walking into the polling booth and quietly stamping their seals behind the curtain.

`; endText += `

“How about the People First Party?” Ma suddenly spoke, his voice dry like swallowing flour. “What’s James Soong at now?”

`; endText += `

An aide quickly pulled up the figures. “3.2 percent.”

`; endText += `

“Drop further,” Ma stared at the number like staring at a dam blocking the water flow. “Drop below two percent.”

`; endText += `

Nobody responded to his remark. Everyone in the war room was making calls, taking down figures, pulling data—but Ma knew they heard him. He felt he had spent too many years in this position, losing the patience for public pleasantries. In the final hours of an election, hoping the opponent’s spoiler vote share shrank further was something every politician thought, but only he would say it out loud in the war room.

`; endText += `

He didn't intend to change.

`; endText += `

Around eight o'clock, vote boxes in the central region began opening in large numbers. This was the most critical hour of the entire election. Ma watched figures from Taichung, Changhua, and Nantou flood in, those blue and green bars leaping frantically as if electrified. For a single moment, Tsai Ing-wen’s vote count suddenly surged upward by a massive jump, and the air in the war room nearly frozen solid.

`; endText += `

King Pu-tsung’s pen stopped on the paper, the ink blooming into a tiny round smudge.

`; endText += `

Then, the iron-clad deep-blue strongholds began reporting back.

`; endText += `

Specific districts in New Taipei, Hakka townships in Miaoli, Hualien and Taitung—the reporting speed in these places was as slow as ever, but every number they spat out was heavy, stacking steadily on his column like bricks.

`; endText += `

The bar began to move. Slowly, almost imperceptibly, but the direction was definite.

`; endText += `

His blue line climbed inch by inch, catching up to her, passing her by 0.3, 0.5, 0.7 percentage points.

`; endText += `

King Pu-tsung set down his phone and turned to look at Ma. There was no joy in that gaze, only a calm judgment derived after verifying all the data. “Held the line.”

`; endText += `

Ma didn't answer. He was still staring at the screen, his fingers tapping rhythmically on the desk.

`; endText += `

At 10:11 p.m., the CEC announced counting progress had surpassed ninety-five percent. The news anchors’ voices suddenly shifted from tense reporting to hesitant silence, and then that well-trained, evasive tone used in the face of uncertainty collapsed, replaced by a genuine awe at the fact itself.

`; endText += `

“Can we put it this way—according to current trends, Ma Ying-jeou is very likely to—”

`; endText += `

Ma didn't hear the second half of the sentence. Because the door to the war room was pushed open, and the noise from outside rolled in like a thunderclap.

`; endText += `

Someone shouted the first “Freeze-gar”!

`; endText += `

Then a second, a third, and then everyone was shouting. The sound bounced off the war room’s ceiling and walls, returning sharper and denser, as if the pressure of the entire island’s election had been unleashed into this single room in an instant.

`; endText += `

Ma felt people slapping his back, his shoulders, shaking his hand vigorously, shoving flags before his face. Surrounded by the crowd, he was pushed forward, his feet moving involuntarily toward the door, a slightly stiff smile plastered on his face.

`; endText += `

Through a gap in the crowd, he caught a glance at the television screen.

`; endText += `

That blue line had settled on a specific figure—${FINAL_VOTE_PERCENT.toFixed(1)}%—a number that barely crossed the winning threshold, a number achieved only after staking incumbency prestige, local factions, and all the political debts of old heavyweights. It didn't even exceed that psychological defense line, but it stopped above his opponent’s, steady as an old coin with worn edges finally landing on the ground, bouncing no more.

`; endText += `

He won. The margin was tiny, small enough that any election expert would call it a “victory within the margin of error”—but a win was a win.

`; endText += `

When Ma stood on the podium, the late-winter night wind made the hem of his suit jacket flutter. Winter in the Taipei basin wasn't cold this year, but standing beneath the spotlights, he suddenly felt his palms icy cold and his face burning hot.

`; endText += `

The crowd below was packed with supporters, many with red-rimmed eyes. He saw a seventy-something-year-old veteran holding an ROC flag with frayed edges, his lips trembling. He saw several middle-aged women crying in an embrace, tears washing two faint tracks through their makeup.

`; endText += `

He cleared his throat and stepped close to the microphone.

`; endText += `

When his voice came through the sound system, it cracked slightly, like the static hum of an old radio first turned on.

`; endText += `

“Dear fellow countrymen, elders, and all friends who support the Republic of China—we won.”

`; endText += `

The crowd erupted.

`; endText += `

“This is the choice of the Taiwanese people! This is the value of democracy! This is the unyielding spirit of the Republic of China!” His voice began to rise, adopting his signature rhythmic cadence, hammering every word into the air like driving nails. “Today, you told me with your ballots, and you told the entire world with the collective will of twenty-three million compatriots—the Taiwanese people will not back down under pressure, the Taiwanese people will not bow before threats, and the Taiwanese people choose peace, prosperity, and continuing along the right path!”

`; endText += `

He took a breath. The red tally lights on the news cameras were all lit, their black lenses reflecting his figure swaying in the wind.

`; endText += `

“I know that tonight, many feel encouraged, while many also feel disappointed. But I want to tell every fellow citizen—elections are temporary, but Taiwan is forever. No matter who you voted for, no matter which party you support, we all live on this land, and we are all one family.”

`; endText += `

He paused. The microphone caught his rapid breath adjustment, brief, less than half a second.

`; endText += `

“But I must also speak a truth.”

`; endText += `

The uproar below quieted slightly.

`; endText += `

“This campaign was the toughest I have ever fought in my political life,” his pace slowed. “Not merely because the opponent was formidable—yes, Madam Tsai Ing-wen is extremely formidable. She represents a different direction, and her supporters are passionate and resolute. I wish to express my respect to her here.”

`; endText += `

He stopped briefly. It was out of habituated political courtesy, but he immediately shifted his tone.

`; endText += `

“The reason it was tough is that we had to make choices constantly regarding the core values and position of our nation. Cross-strait relations are not a slogan or a debate tournament; they are a reality that countless families and businesses face every day. The reason I can stand here tonight is that the Taiwanese people saw this clearly.”

`; endText += `

Applause erupted below once more.

`; endText += `

“So tonight, I want to say to every supporter—this is not a moment of my personal victory; this is a moment of our collective choice!” His tone rose again, the edges of his vocal cords slightly raspy. “Since democratization, no president has ever received the people’s mandate for a third time. Tonight, you created history! This is not Ma Ying-jeou’s record; this is the record of Taiwan’s democracy! This is the record of the Republic of China!”

`; endText += `

He felt his eyes moisten slightly, but he held it back. The times Ma Ying-jeou had wept before the camera in his lifetime could be counted on one hand, and he didn't intend to break that rule tonight.

`; endText += `

“And I also know that regarding certain records of history,” he suddenly lowered his voice, almost as if speaking to himself—yet the microphone delivered every single word clearly to every corner of the plaza, “whether tonight is the final page or the first page depends on how we walk forward from here.”

`; endText += `

That sentence caused several senior aides in the front row to exchange glances. It wasn't in the speech text. King Pu-tsung stood at the side of the stage, expressionless, arms folded across his chest, his fingers tapping lightly against his sleeve.

`; endText += `

Ma didn't explain the line. He quickly pulled his voice back into that soaring closing rhythm, speaking of cross-strait peace, the future of the Republic of China, and the realization of the Three Principles of the People. His phrasing was as precise as a speech text he had memorized for twenty years—because he had indeed spoken these sentences for twenty years.

`; endText += `

Only this time, after all the shouts of “Long live the Republic of China” and “Long live Taiwan’s democracy” concluded, he did not immediately leave the stage. He stood there facing the barrage of flashbulbs, like a swimmer who had finally crossed the entire strait, standing on a reef gasping for air—there were more reefs below, but right now, at least he was still standing.

`; endText += `

Someone pushed ${currentMateName} onto the stage. He stood beside him, bowing slightly to the crowd below, his expression restrained. Ma turned his head to look at him, wanting to say something—perhaps a thank-you, perhaps a tease, perhaps a riddle only they understood—but in the end he said nothing, merely reaching out to shake his hand.

`; endText += `

That hand was dry and warm, identical to when it patted his shoulder last night.

`; endText += `

Below the stage, thousands of smartphone flashes lit up simultaneously, illuminating the entire plaza like a man-made galaxy. And beyond that galaxy, in another campaign headquarters a few kilometers away, a number was being written into history—the first president unable to secure re-election since democratization.

`; s_name = 'An He - Tarcy Su(2020)'; s_cover = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/anhe.jpg'; s_url = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/%E8%98%87%E6%85%A7%E5%80%AB%20Tarcy%20Su%20%5B%20%E5%AE%89%E5%92%8C%20AnHe%20%5D%20Official%20Music%20Video%20-%20%E7%9B%B8%E4%BF%A1%E9%9F%B3%E6%A8%82BinMusic%20(youtube).mp3'; endImage = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/majiong1.webp'; mainTitle = 'SURVIVING THE TEMPEST'; subTitle = 'A thinnest of margins seals an unprecedented comeback over a polarized island.'; } else if (pct >= 50.0) { endText += `

When Ma Ying-jeou popped his third mint candy into his mouth, the lozenge slipped across his tongue, nearly causing him to choke. He coughed twice, reached for the plastic water bottle on the table, unscrewed the cap, didn't drink, and screwed it back on.

`; endText += `

Vice President ${currentMateName} sat in the leather armchair across from him, a folded newspaper resting on his knees. The front-page headline read in bold characters: "Hong Kong Unrest Continues to Spread; Cross-Strait Relations Face New Variables." He stared at the headline for a few seconds before folding the paper and tossing it onto the lower rack of the coffee table. “When this paper went to print, they probably still thought those words could serve as an ATM for the election.”

`; endText += `

Ma glanced at the folded front page, saying nothing, his lip twitching faintly. The arc hovered somewhere between irony and exhaustion, like listening to a tired old song being requested yet again.

`; endText += `

“When trouble broke out in Hong Kong, the DPP were as thrilled as if it were New Year’s,” ${currentMateName} leaned back, his shoe scuffing the edge of the coffee table, leaving a faint gray streak. “Lai Ching-te in Tainan said ‘God bless Taiwan,’ and Chen Chu in Taipei said ‘history is on our side.’ They genuinely believed that once that card was played, the blue camp would collapse from north to south.”

`; endText += `

“And then?” Ma placed the water bottle on the table with a dull thud.

`; endText += `

“And then the Taiwanese people realized their own roofs were leaking,” ${currentMateName} gave a dry, impolite laugh. “The One Fixed Day Off labor law managed to offend both labor and business. Pension reform drove retired soldiers, teachers, and civil servants onto the streets. Same-sex marriage alienated both sides. And the cigarette smuggling scandal burnt right up to the doorstep of the Presidential Office. While they were busy picking up that gun in Hong Kong, they failed to notice their own backyard was on fire.”

`; endText += `

Ma didn't answer. He looked at the clock on the wall; less than ten minutes remained before the major cable networks officially began broadcasting the vote count. On screen, a weather anchor in a bright yellow jacket was casually delivering tomorrow’s precipitation probability, her lighthearted tone suggesting this Saturday night was no different from any other.

`; endText += `

When Xiao Chen, an aide, pushed open the door, he held no papers. Walking directly up to Ma, he whispered: “In the deep-blue strongholds, the lines at polling stations were far longer than four years ago. Several contacts report that turnout might break records.”

`; endText += `

Ma nodded, his lips moving silently, forming those same four words.

`; endText += `

“Stay calm, stay humble,” ${currentMateName} chimed in before Ma could utter them aloud, throwing up his hands. “You’ve said that nearly ten times in the last three hours. I’ve been counting for you.”

`; endText += `

Ma finally let out a soft smile—not his standardized campaign poster grin, but a gentler, sheepish smile at being exposed. “Habit. Back in Taipei in 1998, an aide calculated that I said those four words once every ten minutes on election night.”

`; endText += `

“Did it help?”

`; endText += `

“No. You still get nervous. But saying it out loud feels like sharing half the anxiety with someone else.” Ma reached into his pocket and produced another mint. He thought for a moment, left it unwrapped, and slipped it back into his pocket.

`; endText += `

The door opened again. Chow Mei-ching walked in holding a plastic shopping bag printed with a supermarket logo, a stalk of bright green spring onion sticking out from the top. Scanning the three men in the room, she set the bag in the corner and dusted her hands off.

`; endText += `

“The cashier downstairs asked me why I was still grocery shopping today,” Chow Mei-ching sat on the sofa, her crisp, practical demeanor clashing with the slow-fermenting political tension in the room. “I told her I’m not the candidate. If I don't buy groceries, am I supposed to eat cold wind?”

`; endText += `

Ma turned to look at her, a hint of warmth in his eyes. “You could wait until the results come out before going down. If it’s good news, maybe the cashier will give you a discount.”

`; endText += `

“I’d be lucky if she doesn't raise prices on me.” Chow Mei-ching pulled a pack of dry noodles from the bag, set it on the coffee table, and then extracted a plastic Tupperware container. “This is tomorrow’s lunch. No matter what happens tonight, we still have to eat tomorrow.”

`; endText += `

${currentMateName} watched the bag of noodles placed on the coffee table of the Kuomintang presidential candidate on election night—sitting alongside water bottles, remote controls, and mint wrappers—and burst out laughing.

`; endText += `

The weather broadcast finally concluded, and the screen cut back to the news studio. The anchor had changed into a darker suit, her face powdered heavier than before, glowing matte under the studio lights. In a voice calibrated for momentous occasions, she announced: “Ladies and gentlemen, we now begin our live broadcast of the 2020 Presidential Election results.”

`; endText += `

Rows of tally boxes appeared on screen entering standby, the figures inside still resting at zero.

`; endText += `

Ma’s right thumb began rubbing the watch strap on his left wrist again—a delicate, rhythmic motion, sliding repeatedly along the leather edge as if soothing an invisible pet.

`; endText += `

“In the 2008 election,” he spoke suddenly, his voice lower than before. “Before the count began, I sat in this exact building—same floor, different room. Vincent Siew sat to my left, asking every five minutes: ‘Have the northern numbers come in yet?’ I told him, ‘Vincent, don't rush, the north is ours.’ He said he knew, but he just wanted to confirm. When the numbers finally came out, he stopped asking and started wiping his glasses. He wiped them for nearly twenty minutes.”

`; endText += `

“You won by nearly seventeen percentage points that time,” ${currentMateName} said.

`; endText += `

“I didn't win that election,” Ma shook his head. “Chen Shui-bian won it for me.”

`; endText += `

It wasn't false modesty. The political tsunami of 2008 was indeed brewed by the DPP; the KMT had simply stood directly beneath the spillway of history. And now, twelve years later, sitting in the same building, watching the tally boxes flicker from zero, a familiar sensation was slowly condensing in the air—only this time, the ones standing beneath the spillway were on the other side.

`; endText += `

When the first hour’s numbers came out, the rhythm in the room began to shift.

`; endText += `

It wasn't a sudden explosion of wild joy, but a steady, tide-like confirmation. Reports from polling stations in several central Taiwanese townships showed the blue vote accumulating at a uniform pace—like someone tapping a drum on the table at an unyielding rhythm: thump, thump, thump. ${currentMateName} stared at a row of numbers on screen for a long time, then leaned back against his chair, exhaling a long, deep breath that fogged the side of an empty water bottle on the table.

`; endText += `

“Remember those anti-extradition protests last year?” he said, looking at no one in particular. “Back then, people on the internet claimed the KMT was finished, Ma Ying-jeou was finished, that the cross-strait brand was completely destroyed. A dozen pollsters wrote ten-thousand-word essays concluding the blue camp couldn't be saved.”

`; endText += `

“And then?” Ma asked. This “and then” carried a different tone from thirty minutes prior, underlaid with a faint, razor-sharp edge.

`; endText += `

“And then the Taiwanese people realized shouting slogans doesn't lower electricity bills,” ${currentMateName} picked up the remote and switched channels. On screen, turnout figures for the central region flashed, the blue bar graph steadily pressing above the green line. “After the labor law took effect, small business owners called Tsai ‘a second Empress Wu.’ When pension reform hit, retired soldiers and teachers sprayed ‘Shameful’ across the wall opposite the Presidential Office. When the cigarette scandal broke, green commentators themselves asked on television, ‘Are we electing the head of a smuggling ring?’ No matter how big the Hong Kong issue is, it doesn't outweigh the panic of realizing your salary next month can't cover your mortgage.”

`; endText += `

The broadcast cut to Tsai Ing-wen’s campaign headquarters. The venue was crowded, but the camera angles were curious—first focusing on cheering crowds, then slowly pulling back to reveal gaps along the periphery and staff gazing down at their smartphones. A subtle difference in density was emerging—not in raw numbers, but in temperature. The people over there were shouting, but pausing afterward to exchange glances, as if waiting for a reason to keep shouting. The people here were waiting, chatting casually about where to get late-night snacks after the count.

`; endText += `

Chow Mei-ching sat on the sofa, putting the pack of dry noodles back into the grocery bag. Her movements were entirely natural, showing none of the demeanor of someone watching her husband’s political destiny assembled number by number on television. She checked a Tupperware container, set it back, and finally extracted a container of strawberries, picking out the largest one and handing it to Ma.

`; endText += `

Ma took it, held it in his hand without eating. The chill of the strawberry seeped through his fingertips, meeting the warmth of his palm, the cold side gradually warming up.

`; endText += `

The numbers kept rising.

`; endText += `

In several traditionally impenetrable green strongholds in the south, the opening counts were unexpectedly tight. Not a complete flip, nothing so dramatic, but the margins they usually took for granted were dissolving like ice at room temperature, softening at the edges before shrinking. TV pundits used various buzzwords to explain the phenomenon—“the pendulum effect,” “the return of swing voters,” “the awakening of economic voters.” But everyone sitting in this room knew the true explanation was simple: over the past four years, too many people felt they were treated like clay to be reshaped at will, and today, they decided they had had enough.

`; endText += `

Ma suddenly remembered an incident. One day last year, visiting a traditional market in the central region to campaign, a middle-aged fishball vendor grabbed his hand. His palm was covered in fishy moisture, gripping so hard it felt less like a handshake and more like a plea for rescue. The man said: “President Ma, I don't care about Hong Kong or blue or green. All I know is my daughter rents a room in Taipei for twelve thousand a month, and out of a thirty-thousand salary, she’s left with eighteen thousand. Whoever can lower housing prices and raise wages, I’ll vote for them.” Accompanying reporters didn't capture the moment—it wasn't dramatic enough, just a raspy fishmonger and a display case of chilled fishballs. But Ma remembered the force of that grip—not a handshake, but the grip of a drowning man grasping a final floating log.

`; endText += `

And today, thousands upon thousands of hands like that were dropping ballots into boxes across the island.

`; endText += `

By the middle of the second hour, the numbers on screen were no longer a deadlock. On the blue side, the tally climbed with physical stability, every new figure larger than the last. It felt like watching tree rings expanding—not an explosion, but a growth, each ring consuming a few millimeters of the green side until a thick, undeniable outline formed.

`; endText += `

${currentMateName} stood up. He didn't shout or slam the table; he simply stood there watching the screen, hands behind his back, fingers clenching and unclenching. “Look at these places,” he gestured toward the screen. “Agricultural townships in the south, supposed to be iron-clad DPP strongholds, are now opening with margins within a few percentage points of us. Once cross-strait relations tensed up, export channels for farm produce were blocked. Their pineapples couldn't sell—not because Beijing didn't want them, but because their own government couldn't find a way out. Farmers don't care about abstract slogans; they care about whether trucks can come in and goods can go out.”

`; endText += `

When Xiao Chen entered again, his face had transformed completely. His previous tension was a tight, inward contraction; now it was relaxed, but incomplete, a stiff residual grin like holding back a volcano about to erupt.

`; endText += `

“Turnout in southern Taiwan is beyond expectations,” he said, his voice dropping low like sharing a secret. “In districts previously considered unbreakable, turnout is up nearly ten percent compared to four years ago. And according to internal tracking, the swing voter flow—”

`; endText += `

He didn't finish. The screen suddenly cut to Tsai Ing-wen’s campaign headquarters. As the camera panned across green banners, it caught a detail: a staff member was untying a large banner tied to a railing. Not a celebration cleanup, but an unconscious, premature gesture born of sensing the inevitable. The staff member moved slowly, as if giving himself something to do.

`; endText += `

Ma saw the frame. He didn't smile or gloat; he merely narrowed his eyes slightly, then popped the warm strawberry into his mouth. As he bit down, juice splattered onto his thumb. He glanced down, pulled a crumpled napkin from his pocket, and wiped it clean.

`; endText += `

The female news anchor began speaking in the volume reserved for historic moments, her pace twice as fast, every word squeezed from her throat. The figures behind her continued leaping, but anyone could see the outcome was no longer a matter of math, but of time.

`; endText += `

When the blue numbers crossed the fifty-percent line, a roar amplified by a microphone echoed through the television—the crowd downstairs, their voices penetrating floorboards and broadcast signals to resonate in the room. The true roar came directly through the window, deeper and thicker, like a heavy blanket shaken out in mid-air.

`; endText += `

${currentMateName} turned around to look at Ma. He reached out—not a formal handshake, but a crisp high-five. Snap. Their palms met, paused for two seconds, and released.

`; endText += `

“${FINAL_VOTE_PERCENT.toFixed(1)}%,” ${currentMateName} announced the newly updated number on screen, his voice slightly raspy. “Higher than 2012.”

`; endText += `

Ma didn't repeat the number. He sat there, his back straight as a ramrod—a posture ingrained into his body like a soldier accustomed to wearing a uniform. He looked at the screen, a fine light glinting in his eyes, not tears, but light reflecting off his pupils.

`; endText += `

“During the 2018 local elections, people called it the ‘Han Wave,’ an internet fad, a one-off consumption,” Ma crumpled the napkin into a small ball and tossed it into the trash. “It wasn't. That was the Taiwanese people saying through their ballots: we’ve endured for two years, and this is a warning. If you still don't listen, we’ll say it again in two years.”

`; endText += `

And this second time, the message was spoken far louder. Loud enough to flip central Taiwan upside down; loud enough for pineapple farmers, fish farmers, and B&B owners in the south to stack a falling house of dominoes. The first tile fell in 2018; the second and third followed, one by one, until tonight, the entire structure collapsed.

`; endText += `

The television cut to Tsai Ing-wen’s concession speech. She stood on a well-arranged stage, the banner behind her reading “Taiwan Must Win.” The lighting hit her face, powder concealing most expressions, leaving only a microscopic, nearly unnoticeable red tint at the corners of her eyes. She spoke with uncanny calm, as if reading a pre-written script—and perhaps it was; every candidate prepares two speeches, one for winning and one for losing. The only difference is how many times you rehearse the losing one in your heart before reading it aloud.

`; endText += `

Ma glanced at his watch. Chow Mei-ching noticed and asked if he was hungry. He said a little. She lifted the pack of noodles in her hand and said she’d cook a bowl at home. Ma nodded, stood up, and walked toward the door.

`; endText += `

The crowd downstairs continued to roar. The sound rose like waves and wind, surging through concrete, glass windows, photographs of past presidents on the wall, the unfinished container of strawberries, and a crumpled plastic wrap, finally reaching the door Ma pushed open.

`; endText += `

Before stepping out, he glanced back at the room—the room where he had spent nearly four hours, with strawberry tops on the coffee table, mint wrappers in the trash, and a faint warm impression left by ${currentMateName}’s palm on the chair armrest. The numbers on television were still leaping, but they no longer mattered. He nodded gently to the two people in the room—his campaign running mate and his wife of over thirty years.

`; endText += `

Then he pushed open the door and stepped out into that wall of sound.

`; endText += `

Chow Mei-ching followed two steps behind, holding the supermarket plastic bag. As she passed the doorframe, a green onion leaf slid out from the top, dangling at the edge of the bag. She didn't stuff it back in, merely switching hands and continuing forward.

`; s_name = 'Rhapsody - Jam Hsiao (2011)'; s_cover = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/xiaojt.jpg'; s_url = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/%E7%8B%82%E6%83%B3%E6%9B%B2%20%E8%90%A7%E6%95%AC%E8%85%BE%20(%E6%AD%8C%E8%AF%8D%E7%89%88)%20-%20GM%20Lyric%20(youtube).mp3'; endImage = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/majionghuosheng2.jpg'; mainTitle = 'RESETTING THE CLOCK'; subTitle = 'A decisive victory seals an historic comeback, closing an eight-year political cycle.'; } } // ====================================================================== // 🧩 模块一：【候选人专属区块】 (包含胜负幅度、专属战况、专属音乐) // ====================================================================== // 1. 韩国瑜 (Han Kuo-yu) if (Number(campaignTrail_temp.hanguoyu) === 1) { if (pct < 50.0) { endText += `

Three o'clock in the afternoon. The polls will not officially close for another hour, but inside the VIP holding room of the Kuomintang central headquarters, the air is already thick enough to choke on. The air conditioning is humming at its absolute maximum, yet the collar of your trademark blue shirt is damp with cold sweat. You sit heavily on a leather sofa, staring at the muted television screens displaying endless loops of voting lines. Beside you, Lee Chia-fen grips your hand. Her knuckles are white, her eyes carrying the heavy, exhausted trauma of a year spent walking through a ruthless political meat grinder. Outside the thick bulletproof glass of the building, the streets of Taipei reek of scooter exhaust, cheap betel nut, and the overwhelming scent of braised pork rice. Hundreds of thousands of fanatical supporters, waving a terrifying ocean of red-and-blue flags, are already blowing air horns with a primal, almost religious fury. They have been gathering since dawn.

`; endText += `

But inside this room, the atmosphere is toxic with unspoken animosity. The orthodox party elites—men in immaculate dark suits, the Ivy-League technocrats, the old-guard warlords—stand in hushed, terrified clusters. Chairman Wu Den-yih sits in an armchair opposite you, mechanically swirling a cup of lukewarm tea. He glances at his luxury watch, then offers a tight, thoroughly unconvincing smile. ‘We have done everything the party machine could possibly do, Mayor Han,’ Wu says, his voice smooth but laced with a subtle, patronizing edge. ‘The ground game is fully mobilized. Now, we leave it to the voters and to fate. Regardless of what happens tonight, the party remembers your... unique contribution.’ You nod slowly, your expression carefully neutral. ‘The grassroots will speak, Chairman,’ you reply simply. ‘They always do.’ You know exactly what Wu is doing. He is preemptively washing his hands. If the numbers crash tonight, these blue-blooded aristocrats will not hesitate for a single second to throw you to the wolves, blaming your vulgar populism for destroying their century-old institution. For eighteen months, they have treated you like a bizarre mutation, a bald, jobless outcast who somehow hijacked their dignified political machine. They despise you. But today, their entire political survival depends entirely on the sweat, blood, and rage of the unwashed masses chanting your name outside.

`; endText += `

Four o'clock. The heavy steel doors of the polling stations across the island slam shut, sealing the fate of the Republic of China inside millions of flimsy cardboard boxes. The news anchors on the LED screens suddenly snap to attention. The agonizing trickle of early returns begins.

`; endText += `

Miles away, across the city, the mood inside the Democratic Progressive Party headquarters on Beiping East Road is a stark, chilling contrast. President Tsai Ing-wen stands alone by the floor-to-ceiling window of her private office, staring out at the gray Taipei skyline. The room behind her is completely silent. Her top strategists and faction bosses, who just yesterday were arrogantly boasting about their impenetrable lead, are staring at their tablets in sheer, apocalyptic disbelief. The cruel, unforgiving mathematics of democracy are asserting their absolute dominance on the screens. The green firewall built upon the tear gas of Hong Kong is collapsing. The fabricated Wang Liqiang spy scandal, designed to paint you as a communist sleeper agent, has proven entirely useless against the raw, visceral wrath of taxi drivers, night market vendors, and forgotten laborers who simply want to put food on the table. Taichung, Changhua, and Yunlin are violently hemorrhaging green votes.

`; endText += `

Tsai watches the numbers from Kaohsiung and the deep south flash on the screen in glaring red. Her invincible fortress is crumbling to dust. She crosses her arms tightly, a profound, icy loneliness washing over her. She played the geopolitical game perfectly. She weaponized the existential terror of the youth. She had the entire state media apparatus at her disposal. Yet, the silent majority was never silent; they were just ignored. The realization hits her like a physical blow, heavy and suffocating: she is about to become the very first incumbent president in the democratic history of Taiwan to be thrown out of office after a single term. A historical footnote of failure. The sheer magnitude of this humiliation shatters the myth of the invincible DPP. The so-called ‘national doom’ evaporated the moment the working class decided they had suffered enough elite arrogance. In a few hours, she will have to walk down to the press room, bow her head, and surrender the nation.

`; endText += `

Back in the KMT war room, the trickle of data turns into a violent, unrelenting flood. The anchors on the pro-green television networks lose their arrogant smirks, their voices pitching upward in poorly concealed panic. The three-way split is brutally cannibalizing the progressive coalition. You watch the screen as the realization sets in. The populist outsider is not just surviving the slaughterhouse; you are steadily, bloodily chewing your way toward the throne.

`; endText += `

By eight o'clock, the final numbers solidify on the main broadcast screen: ${FINAL_VOTE_PERCENT.toFixed(1)}%. A collective, shuddering gasp echoes through the headquarters. It is a win. It is an incredibly fragile, mathematically fractured plurality, but in the ruthless game of thrones, plurality is the only God that matters. You did not convince the entire educated nation; you merely conquered the brutal arithmetic of a divided electorate. Power is power.

`; endText += `

You stand up, slowly smoothing out the wrinkles of your sweat-stained shirt. The room is paralyzed. You look across the space at the KMT aristocrats, and the power dynamic shifts instantly. Chairman Wu Den-yih approaches first. The patronizing edge is completely gone, replaced by a strained, incredibly fake smile that looks more like a grimace. He extends his hand. ‘A historic victory, President Han,’ Wu says, his voice noticeably tighter than before. ‘You have brought glory back to the Kuomintang. The central committee stands entirely behind your leadership.’ Right behind him is Ma Ying-jeou, the former president, offering stiff, polite praise. ‘You fought a hard campaign. The people have entrusted you with the Republic,’ Ma murmurs, his posture rigid.

`; endText += `

You shake their hands warmly, bowing your head in a flawless display of humility. ‘I could not have done it without the party's unwavering support, Chairman. Thank you, President Ma,’ you reply, your tone radiating respect. But internally, a dark, overwhelming wave of pure arrogance and supreme pride swells within your chest, threatening to burst. You look at Ma and feel nothing but absolute, visceral disdain for his weak, compromising, eight-year tenure that left the party hollowed out and disconnected from the common people. You look at Wu and mock his cowardly backroom calculations. They did nothing. You are the one who actually conquered the streets. You dragged their dying, bankrupt party out of the grave with your bare hands. You are the king now, and they are merely your subjects. However, you are far too shrewd to let the monster out just yet. You carefully mask this surging, terrifying arrogance, projecting only an aura of humble, radiant, and unstoppable confidence to the room. The men who spent their entire lives mastering the dark arts of institutional control realize their life’s work has just been seized by a man who compares political strategy to playing mahjong in a public bathhouse. The century-old dynasty has officially surrendered to the tavern.

`; endText += `

Standing exactly half a step behind you is your running mate, ${currentMateName}. They puff out their chest, flashing a highly disciplined, professional smile for the cameras, clearly believing they played an indispensable role in securing this historic victory. They nod sagely at the party elders, acting as if they are a crucial co-pilot in this new administration. It is almost tragic to watch. They have absolutely no idea that the raw, chaotic ‘Han Wave’ requires no co-pilot. They were merely a necessary prop to temporarily soothe the terrified intellectual elites and check a demographic box. For the next four years, ${currentMateName} is destined to become the most useless, ignored person in the Republic of China, left to rot in the ceremonial freezer while you dominate every waking second of the nation's news cycle.

`; endText += `

The heavy glass doors leading to the balcony are finally pushed open by your security detail. The humid night air rushes in, carrying the terrifying, earth-shattering roar of hundreds of thousands of fanatical believers chanting your name. You step out into the blinding glare of the stadium spotlights. The sea of red-and-blue flags violently surges below you like a stormy ocean, stretching as far as the eye can see. You raise your hands, and the crowd screams with the raw, deafening devotion of a cult witnessing a living miracle. Across the capital, urban intellectuals and progressive youth are staring at their phones in sheer, apocalyptic terror, weeping as Tsai delivers her bitter concession speech. Over half the country views your very existence as a catastrophic threat, ready to paralyze your administration on day one.

`; endText += `

But standing on this balcony, bathed in the light, you do not care. You grab the microphone, your voice hoarse but echoing like thunder across the island. ‘They called us uneducated! They called us spies! They tried to use foreign ghosts to steal our country! But today, the grassroots have spoken! The elites who eat steak and drink wine while you starve are gone! From tomorrow on, the Republic of China belongs to the common people! We will sweep out the corrupt bureaucrats! We will tear down the ideological walls! We have only one goal, one belief, one destiny: Taiwan stays safe, and the people get rich!’

`; endText += `

The roar that follows shakes the very foundations of Taipei. It is a primal scream of vindication from the forgotten corners of the island. You conquered the palace by setting the establishment on fire. Tomorrow, you must rule over the smoldering, deeply divided ashes of a fractured nation. But tonight, the Bald Greengrocer is the absolute, undisputed King of Taiwan.
