The immaculate white marble floors of the Kuomintang central headquarters had never seen so much mud. For decades, this VIP suite on Bade Road had been a sanitized sanctuary for the blue-blooded aristocracy—a place where Ph.D. scholars, retired generals, and corporate tycoons calmly divided the nation over cups of premium high-mountain tea. But tonight, the aristocratic silence was dead, violently murdered by the chaotic, suffocating heat of the southern grassroots.

`; endText += `

You sit sprawled on the centerpiece leather sofa, your signature blue shirt unbuttoned at the collar, a cheap plastic bottle of mineral water dangling loosely from your hand. The air in the room reeks of stale sweat, heavy cheap tobacco, and the faint, unmistakable tang of Kaoliang liquor carried in by your inner circle of local warlords. You take a slow sip of water, your eyes locked on the massive LED broadcast screens. The numbers ticking upward are not a mathematical anomaly. They are a brutal, undeniable verdict. You have crossed the fifty percent threshold. This is no longer a fragile, lucky plurality. This is a hostile, democratic takeover of the Republic of China.

`; endText += `

Across the city, within the sterile, progressive echo chambers of the Presidential Office, the cognitive dissonance is shattering minds. President Tsai Ing-wen and her Ivy-League-educated strategists stare at the bleeding electoral map in sheer, paralyzed horror. They had poured millions into a sophisticated cyber-warfare campaign. They had weaponized the tragic tear gas of Hong Kong to preach an apocalyptic sermon of 'national doom.' They had treated the electorate as a grand geopolitical seminar. But they had profoundly misunderstood the physics of starvation. You cannot feed a desperate, struggling family with diplomatic white papers, and you cannot lecture an unemployed factory worker about liberal democratic values. The DPP's pristine ivory tower has just been violently demolished by a tsunami of forgotten night-market vendors, angry farmers, and exhausted laborers. The working class did not just reject Tsai Ing-wen; they humiliated her, handing her the historically catastrophic disgrace of being the first one-term president in modern democratic history.

`; endText += `

Back in the KMT war room, the realization of your absolute mandate drops like an anvil. The final numbers solidify: ${FINAL_VOTE_PERCENT.toFixed(1)}%. A solid, unshakeable majority. A roar of primal, predatory triumph erupts from your southern aides, vibrating the expensive glass windows.

`; endText += `

You do not stand up immediately. You let the silence stretch, forcing the old guard to come to you. And they do. The physical manifestation of their surrender is almost sickeningly beautiful to watch. Chairman Wu Den-yih, the master manipulator who had spent eighteen months trying to secretly orchestrate your downfall, walks over with shoulders practically hunched. The cunning machinations in his eyes have been entirely replaced by the hollow, glassy stare of a defeated man. He offers his hand, his voice dry and trembling. 'A magnificent mandate, President Han. The party... the party is yours to command.' Following him is Ma Ying-jeou. The former president, the ultimate symbol of polished, Harvard-educated elitism, looks physically ill as he forces a polite bow to the Bald Greengrocer. They had spent their entire lives treating politics like a delicate, surgical game of chess, only for you to flip the board and smash their legacy to pieces with a bottle of water. You smile warmly, grasping their hands with theatrical affection. 'We are one family, Chairman, President Ma. The Republic of China needs your wisdom.' The words taste like ash in their mouths, but they nod vigorously. Your internal arrogance swells into a dark, towering colossus. You have not just defeated the DPP; you have broken the spine of the Kuomintang establishment. You own their history now.

`; endText += `

Standing perfectly still in the corner, resembling a highly decorative, incredibly expensive porcelain vase, is your running mate, ${currentMateName}. They offer a flawless, politically calibrated smile, adjusting their tie, trying desperately to project the illusion of a co-pilot. It is a pitiful sight. In their academic or bureaucratic minds, they still believe they were the crucial 'rational anchor' that won over the middle class. They do not realize that in a holy war of this magnitude, logic is worthless. The fanatical wave of populism carried the ticket entirely on its own back. For the next four years, ${currentMateName} will be nothing more than a constitutional ghost, trapped in the freezing silence of the vice-presidential office, watching helplessly as you rule the island through sheer, chaotic willpower.

`; endText += `

It is time to face your congregation. The heavy glass doors to the balcony are thrown open. The humid, electric night air of Taipei hits you, carrying a sound so massive, so terrifyingly loud, that it vibrates in your very teeth. Hundreds of thousands of fanatical believers, a surging, endless ocean of red, white, and blue, stretch down the boulevard into the horizon. As you step into the blinding glare of the spotlights, the crowd erupts into a state of sheer, apocalyptic religious ecstasy. They are weeping. They are screaming. To half the nation watching on television, this balcony scene looks like the terrifying dawn of a populist dictatorship. But to the sea of faces below, you are the messiah who finally saw their suffering.

`; endText += `

You grab the microphone, refusing to use a script. Your voice is raw, coarse, and echoes like artillery fire across the capital. 'They called us uneducated! They called us spies! They tried to use foreign ghosts to steal our country! But today, the grassroots have spoken! The elites who eat steak and drink red wine while you starve are gone! From tomorrow on, the Republic of China belongs to the common people! We will sweep out the corrupt bureaucrats! We will tear down the ideological walls! We have only one goal, one belief, one destiny: Taiwan stays safe, and the people get rich!'

`; endText += `

The roar from the masses threatens to crack the sky. But you are not finished. You lower the microphone slightly, looking out over the endless sea of weeping, screaming faces. The atmosphere instantly shifts from a political victory rally to something infinitely more profound, something deeply martial and terrifyingly loyal. You raise the microphone again, your eyes gleaming with an intense, fiery fervor. Slowly, deliberately, you begin to sing. Your voice is rough, unpolished, yet filled with an undeniable, magnetic power.

`; endText += `

'The night is vast, the stars and moon are dim...'

`; endText += `

For a split second, the crowd is stunned. And then, a massive, collective shockwave of recognition ripples through the hundreds of thousands of people below. It is 'Night Attack'—the legendary, blood-pumping military anthem of the Republic of China armed forces. It is the song of the underdog, the song of the soldiers crawling through the mud to launch a desperate, victorious ambush against an entrenched enemy. As you sing the second line, a few thousand veterans in the front rows join in. By the third line, ten thousand voices are harmonizing with you.

`; endText += `

'Strict silence, conceal our tracks... We wait for the signal, we wait for the signal...'

`; endText += `

The sound swells into a terrifying, unified roar. The entire boulevard, packed with working-class heroes, street vendors, taxi drivers, and weeping grandmothers, transforms into a massive, fanatical military choir. The melody echoes off the concrete towers of Taipei, drowning out the traffic, drowning out the progressive commentators on television, drowning out the entire old world order. You stand at the edge of the balcony, acting as the supreme commander of this phenomenal, populist symphony.

`; endText += `

'Like swift lightning, like a thunderbolt... Piercing straight into the enemy’s heart! Piercing straight into the enemy’s heart!'

`; endText += `

The final lyrics erupt from the crowd like a physical shockwave. You raise your fist into the night sky, and the sea of flags violently erupts in response. You have pierced the heart of the establishment. You conquered the palace by setting the old political order on fire. He did not see that ruling a deeply divided, terrified nation with the sheer heat of populism is like holding a starving tiger by the ears. The fire he started will eventually demand more fuel. But tonight, there are no consequences. There is only the deafening, fanatical chorus of your believers singing in the dark, and the absolute certainty that the Bald Greengrocer is the unquestioned King of Taiwan. The coronation is complete.

There was no suffocating tension in the war room. There was no agonizing wait for the rural districts to report their margins. Long before the heavy steel doors of the polling stations slammed shut at four o'clock, the entire island already knew the verdict. The air in the Kuomintang central headquarters was not filled with anxiety, but with the terrifying, vibrating certainty of an impending avalanche. The ruling party was not just defeated today; they were subjected to a historic, merciless democratic execution.

`; endText += `

For months, the Democratic Progressive Party had unleashed the most sophisticated, obscenely funded electoral smear campaign in the history of the island. They weaponized the geopolitical tragedy of Hong Kong to preach an apocalyptic sermon of national doom. They deployed their notorious internet cyber-armies to mock your intellect and sabotage your rallies. They orchestrated the fabricated Wang Liqiang spy hoax, a desperate, third-rate dirty trick designed to permanently brand you as a traitor to the state. But it all shattered like fragile glass against the impenetrable, unyielding wall of working-class fury. The progressive elites in Taipei had profoundly miscalculated the physics of starvation. They believed they could distract a hungry man with geopolitical ghost stories. But the Shumin—the forgotten commoners, the street vendors, the exhausted laborers, the marginalized veterans—had simply had enough. You became the living, breathing vessel for their decades of accumulated resentment.

`; endText += `

As the broadcast screens illuminate with the first wave of counting, the numbers are so overwhelmingly one-sided that the pro-green news anchors physically stumble over their words. The map of Taiwan is not just leaning blue; it is drowning in a massive, uninterrupted ocean of it. The traditional DPP strongholds in the deep south fall like dominoes. The agricultural belt revolts with staggering margins. The urban centers, supposedly the bastions of the educated youth, are effortlessly overrun by the sheer turnout of the silent majority. The myth of Tsai Ing-wen’s invincibility evaporates on live television. She is left isolated in the Presidential Office, watching her political legacy be violently dismantled by the very grassroots citizens her party once swore to protect. The progressive era has been buried alive under a mountain of angry ballots.

`; endText += `

The final, historic tally permanently locks onto the main screen: ${FINAL_VOTE_PERCENT.toFixed(1)}%. A supermajority. A landslide of such colossal proportions that it completely rewrites the fundamental laws of Taiwanese politics. This is no longer an election; it is a mandate from heaven.

`; endText += `

You sit in the center of the VIP suite, radiating a quiet, terrifyingly absolute authority. There is no need to mask your arrogance today, because arrogance implies a need to prove oneself. You have nothing left to prove. You are the undisputed master of the island. The blue-blooded Kuomintang aristocrats in the room—Ma Ying-jeou, Wu Den-yih, the Ivy-League technocrats who once sneered at your vulgarity—do not even dare to approach you with hypocritical handshakes. They stand at a respectful, fearful distance, their heads bowed, utterly subjugated by the sheer magnitude of your mandate. They realize with crushing clarity that the century-old KMT is dead. What remains is the Han Kuo-yu Party. They are merely guests in your house now.

`; endText += `

Somewhere in the periphery of your vision stands your running mate, ${currentMateName}. They look incredibly small against the backdrop of this historic tsunami. A landslide of this magnitude brutally exposes the reality of the ticket: ${currentMateName} brought absolutely nothing to the table that you did not already conquer yourself. They are a phantom, a ceremonial vestige of the old establishment, already fading into total political irrelevance before the inauguration has even begun. You do not even glance in their direction.

`; endText += `

The heavy glass doors leading to the balcony are thrown open. The humid night air of Taipei hits you, but it is instantly drowned out by a sound that defies physical description. It is a primal, earth-shaking roar from millions of fanatical believers. The streets below are entirely consumed by a surging, infinite sea of red, white, and blue. Men and women are weeping openly, falling to their knees, waving flags with the manic devotion of a liberated people. You step into the blinding glare of the stadium spotlights. You do not wear a suit. You wear your simple, rolled-up blue shirt—the armor of the working class.

`; endText += `

You grab the microphone. You do not read from a teleprompter. You look down at the endless sea of faces, your eyes shining with unspeakable intensity. Your hoarse voice echoes like artillery fire across the capital.

`; endText += `

‘They looked down on us!’ you roar, pointing a finger fiercely toward the distant, dark silhouette of the Presidential Office. ‘For years, the arrogant elites sat in their air-conditioned rooms, drinking their expensive wine, telling us what to think! They used their dirty tricks, their fake news, their state machinery to crush us! They thought the Shumin were stupid! They thought we were blind! But the heavens have eyes! Today, the grassroots of Taiwan stood up and smashed their ivory tower to pieces!’

`; endText += `

The crowd erupts in a deafening, hysterical frenzy. You grip the microphone tighter, your voice trembling with raw, unfiltered emotion.

`; endText += `

‘I do not thank the politicians tonight. I do not thank the tycoons. I thank the taxi drivers sweating in the summer heat! I thank the night market vendors boiling soup at midnight! I thank the farmers whose hands are covered in the soil of this island! You are the true masters of this country! From tomorrow on, there will be no more green terror. There will be no more ideological witch hunts. There will only be the sweat of our brows and the wealth in our pockets!’

`; endText += `

You take a deep breath, raising your fist high into the Taipei night sky. The energy in the air is apocalyptic.

`; endText += `

‘Long live the Republic of China! Long live the Republic of China! Long live the Republic of China!’

`; endText += `

The three roars tear through the city like a shockwave, instantly echoed by millions of voices chanting in perfect, terrifying unison. The old political order has been burned to ash. Tomorrow, a new, unpredictable era begins. But tonight, standing on the balcony above a conquered capital, the Bald Greengrocer is the absolute, unquestioned Emperor of Taiwan.

`; s_name = "General's Order - Mayday (2013)"; s_cover = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/jiangjun.jpg?v=1782593638746'; s_url = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/%E5%B0%87%E8%BB%8D%E4%BB%A4%20-%20Mayday%20(youtube).mp3?v=1782593600785'; endImage = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/zhanghan.jpg?v=1782593106875'; mainTitle = 'POPULIST EMPEROR'; subTitle = 'An unstoppable tsunami consumes the establishment.'; } } // 2. 朱立伦 (Eric Chu) else if (Number(campaignTrail_temp.zhulilun) === 1) { if (pct < 50.0) { endText += `

Four o'clock in the afternoon. The LED screens in the Kuomintang central headquarters flicker with agonizingly tight margins, casting a pale, clinical glow over the VIP suite. The air in the room is suffocating, thick with the scent of expensive dark roast tea, starched cotton, and the sharp, undeniable stench of aristocratic panic. You stand near the back of the room, your posture impeccably straight, your arms crossed over your perfectly tailored suit. Beside you, your wife, Kao Wan-chien, reaches out to gently adjust your silk tie. Her perfectly manicured fingers linger on your collar for a brief second. 'Four years of swallowing glass for this party, Eric,' she whispers, her voice barely audible over the hum of the air conditioning, her eyes carrying a quiet, fierce intensity. 'Don't let them see you sweat.' You offer her a tight, highly practiced smile. 'I won't. We have endured too much to break now.'

`; endText += `

For three agonizing hours, the gap refuses to widen beyond a few tens of thousands of votes. This is your third showdown with Tsai Ing-wen, and the ghost of 2016 haunts every shadow of this building. You remember the crushing humiliation of that year, the frantic, desperate 'Change Hung' debacle, and the infamous 'Grandma from Tamsui' anecdote that the internet youth ruthlessly weaponized into a national joke. Tonight was supposed to be your ultimate, cleansing vindication, but the electorate is making you bleed for every single inch. The DPP's geopolitical fearmongering clashes violently with your pragmatic, centrist appeals. You are not surfing a massive wave of populist adoration; you are extracting a victory through cold, mathematical attrition, heavily relying on a split opposition to cannibalize the green vote.

`; endText += `

Then, just past eight-thirty, the dam finally breaks. The central Taiwan firewall holds, and the massive suburban vote banks in New Taipei City swing decisively in your favor. You cross the threshold—not a majority, but an undeniable plurality. The room collapses into an exhausted, undignified state of hysterical relief. Chairman Wu Den-yih visibly sags, his shoulders dropping as he wipes a thick layer of sweat from his forehead with a monogrammed handkerchief. 'Heavens above,' Wu breathes out, dropping his cunning, Machiavellian facade for a split second of pure, unfiltered relief. 'We dodged a bullet. We actually survived.' Former President Ma Ying-jeou steps forward, his usual rigid, patrician posture softening as he grasps your hand with uncharacteristic fervor. 'A miraculous defense of the Republic, Eric. You pulled us back from the brink,' Ma murmurs, his eyes wide with the realization that his legacy will not be entirely erased. You nod graciously, projecting the aura of a humble savior. But internally, your gaze is ice. You know their profound relief is not for you, but for their own institutional survival. You were their shield, their sacrificial lamb who somehow managed to slaughter the butcher.

`; endText += `

Your running mate, ${currentMateName}, steps to your side, eyes already scanning the incoming data on an electronic tablet. There is no wild celebration, only a grim, professional acknowledgment of the battlefield. 'We secured the presidential mandate, but the legislative margins are going to be a nightmare,' ${currentMateName} mutters, lowering the tablet. 'Governing tomorrow is going to be brutal trench warfare.' You stare at your reflection in the darkened glass window. Your jaw tightens. You issue a silent, fierce warning to yourself: The Kuomintang cannot repeat the same catastrophic mistakes. There can be no return to the arrogant complacency of the old guard. If this century-old party does not ruthlessly reform itself tonight, this fragile victory will merely be a delayed death sentence.

`; endText += `

You step out of the headquarters and approach the podium set up on Bade Road. There is no unhinged, deafening roar of a populist mob. The applause that greets you is disciplined, polite, and deeply relieved—the sound of the anxious middle class breathing again. You adjust the microphone, projecting absolute, unwavering stability. 'Tonight, the people of Taiwan have made a profound choice,' you declare, your voice smooth, practiced, and radiating technocratic competence. 'I want to humbly thank every single voter who stood with us. Tonight, we rejected extremism and embraced the middle path. Let me be clear: there is no blue or green tonight, there is only ONE Taiwan! We must unite this divided nation. And to my own party—we must reform, and we must deliver. If you are going to do it, you must do it right! (做，就要做好!)'

`; endText += `

The crowd cheers, waving their flags in rhythmic, orderly satisfaction. It is a flawless, clinically executed end to a vicious political war. Yet, as the camera flashes blind you, the chilling constitutional reality of your victory sets in. You are a minority president holding a razor-thin mandate. The deep-blue ideological purists behind you still harbor bitter resentment for your moderation. The progressive youth watching on their screens still view your party as a rotting relic. And across the city, the wounded DPP is already preparing a ruthless legislative blockade to paralyze your administration on day one. You have successfully reclaimed the crown, but the throne is made of fragile glass, suspended perilously over a deeply fractured, hostile nation. The technocrat is finally holding the scalpel, but the patient is actively resisting the surgery.

`; endImage = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/zhu.jpg'; mainTitle = 'A HOLLOW VINDICATION'; subTitle = "The establishment survives on a razor's edge."; s_name = 'Simon Says - No Party For Cao Dong (2016)'; s_cover = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/caodong.jpg?v=1782597709415'; s_url = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/%E8%8D%89%E6%9D%B1%E6%B2%92%E6%9C%89%E6%B4%BE%E5%B0%8D%20No%20Party%20For%20Cao%20Dong%20-%20%E5%A4%A7%E9%A2%A8%E5%90%B9%20Simon%20Says%E3%80%90Official%20Music%20Video%E3%80%91%20-%20No%20Party%20For%20Cao%20Dong%20%E8%8D%89%E6%9D%B1%E6%B2%92%E6%9C%89%E6%B4%BE%E5%B0%8D%20(youtube).mp3?v=1782597648221'; } else if (pct <= 55.0) { endText += `

Two o'clock in the afternoon. The Taipei sky is a bruised, suffocating gray, threatening a winter rain that refuses to fall. Inside the VIP suite of the Kuomintang central headquarters, the waiting has become an excruciating psychological torture device. The air reeks of stale coffee, premium oolong tea, and the sharp, undeniable scent of aristocratic anxiety. You pace the marble floor, your perfectly tailored suit feeling like a suffocating straitjacket. On the glass coffee table, a highly classified sheet of early exit polls sits like an unexploded bomb. It whispers a lead of 2.5 percentage points over Tsai Ing-wen. Two and a half percent. In any normal democracy, it would be a cause for cautious optimism. A few junior staffers are already exchanging quiet, hopeful glances by the water cooler, daring to smile. But you are a trained actuary. You know the brutal, unforgiving truth of Taiwanese politics: 2.5 percent is dangerously embedded within the margin of error. It is a statistical phantom. The deep-green fortresses in the south have not fully reported, and the youth turnout at the high-speed rail stations looks terrifyingly massive. You stare at the paper, feeling a sickening knot twist in your stomach. The ghost of your crushing 2016 landslide defeat—the endless internet mockery, the sheer humiliation of being wiped out by three million votes—is permanently etched into your very bones. You dare not celebrate. You barely dare to breathe.

`; endText += `

Four o'clock. The heavy steel doors of the polling stations across the island finally slam shut. The agonizing crawl of actual data begins. The televisions are unmuted, and the anchors' voices pitch upward in nervous excitement. ‘Are the early numbers from New Taipei holding?’ you ask, your voice barely above a whisper, shattering the heavy silence. Your campaign manager nods nervously, wiping a bead of sweat from his forehead. ‘It is tight, Mayor. Excruciatingly tight. But we are holding the line.’ You rub your temples. This is your third showdown with Tsai Ing-wen. Your names are permanently chained together in the history books. If you lose today, your political career is not just over; it becomes a permanent, tragic footnote.

`; endText += `

By seven o'clock, the agonizing trickle of votes turns into a relentless, unstoppable flood. The numbers do not just lean blue; they surge. The central Taiwan firewall holds flawlessly, breaking the back of the DPP’s momentum. You definitively cross the fifty percent threshold. ‘Look at Taichung,’ Chairman Wu Den-yih mutters, gripping his teacup so tightly his knuckles turn white. ‘And Changhua. The DPP’s arrogant pension cuts finally caught up with them. They dug their own graves.’ The realization that washes over the room is stark and coldly pragmatic. The electorate has not suddenly fallen madly in love with the Kuomintang again. They are simply furious at Tsai Ing-wen’s economic stagnation and ideological warfare. They are using you as a highly efficient, sterile weapon to punish the ruling party.

`; endText += `

The unbearable tension finally shatters into loud, immensely relieved applause. The party heavyweights gather around you like sharks smelling blood in the water. Former President Ma Ying-jeou steps forward, a familiar, highly self-satisfied smile playing on his lips. ‘Over fifty-one percent,’ Ma says, patting your shoulder with paternal pride. ‘Eric, I told you. The people still trust our orthodox brand. This feels exactly like my reelection in 2012.’ You force a flawless, polite smile, violently swallowing the urge to remind him that his 2012 victory led directly to the party's most catastrophic historical collapse. ‘It is different this time, Mr. President,’ you reply quietly. ‘We barely survived.’ Wang Jin-pyng chuckles from the corner, his eyes crinkling. ‘Do not overthink it, Eric. The southern factions delivered exactly what we negotiated. A win is a win.’ Wu Den-yih is already frantically typing on his phone. ‘If we secure the cabinet, we need to immediately consolidate the resources. The local bosses are going to want their rewards.’

`; endText += `

Your wife, Kao Wan-chien, steps to your side. Her eyes are red, but they shine with the fierce, quiet vindication of a family that endured four years of bitter political exile and relentless media ridicule. Beside her, your running mate, ${currentMateName}, nods with the crisp, professional satisfaction of a corporate executive who just closed the deal of a lifetime. ‘The Taipei stock market futures are already surging,’ ${currentMateName} says smoothly. ‘The business sector is profoundly relieved. You gave them stability.’ You adjust your tie. ‘Let us go give them a government,’ you reply.

`; endText += `

You step out onto the podium on Bade Road. There is no unhinged, populist screaming here—only the rhythmic, thunderous applause of the middle class and business elites desperate for a return to normalcy. You retrieve your wire-rimmed glasses and slide them onto your face. It is a deliberate aesthetic choice: the rational actuary is officially back in the office. ‘Four years ago, I stood on a stage very much like this one and apologized for our devastating defeat,’ your voice rings out, smooth and commanding. ‘You punished the Kuomintang because we lost touch with reality. We learned our lesson in the freezing wilderness. Today, you have chosen economic sanity over green terror. I promise you this: we will build a highly competent government that serves every citizen with flawless precision. It is time to get to work.’

`; endText += `

The crowd roars in highly disciplined approval. The era of ‘Normal Chu’ has spectacularly begun. Yet, as the blinding camera flashes wash over you, your analytical mind is already calculating the grim reality ahead. You have reclaimed the throne, but the electorate's anger is merely a rented weapon. You must govern flawlessly, because the exact same ruthless fury that destroyed Tsai Ing-wen tonight will inevitably come for you next.

`; mainTitle = 'RETURN OF NORMALCY'; subTitle = 'The technocrat quietly reclaims the throne with a solid mandate.'; s_name = 'Bombardment - Wei Bird (2012)'; endImage = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/2942598_1_1.jpg?v=1782600229574'; s_cover = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/500x500.jpg?v=1782599937761'; s_url = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/%E8%BD%9F%E7%82%B8%20-%20%E9%9F%A6%E7%A4%BC%E5%AE%89%20(youtube).mp3?v=1782599873467'; } else { endText += `

Crossing the fifty-five percent threshold does not feel like a triumphant political victory; it feels like a violent, island-wide exorcism. The electorate did not wake up this morning harboring a sudden, passionate romance for the Kuomintang. They simply vomited the Democratic Progressive Party out of their collective system. After four grueling years of relentless ideological lecturing, arrogant administrative overreach, and suffocating economic stagnation, the voters essentially dragged Tsai Ing-wen out of the Presidential Office by her political hair. You won entirely by default. You are nothing more than the sober, deeply unexciting designated driver for a republic that is violently hungover and completely sick of the green party’s endless circus. The sheer volume of the landslide is actually terrifying. It proves that traditional party loyalty is dead. The voters are no longer loyal subjects; they are ruthless consumers, and they just initiated a hostile refund policy against the incumbent regime.

`; endText += `

Inside the hyper-air-conditioned VIP lounge of the party headquarters, the stench of premature arrogance is suffocating. The KMT heavyweights are popping open premium champagne and brewing vintage tea, suffering from a miraculous, incurable case of collective amnesia. Former President Ma Ying-jeou nods sagely to the flashing cameras of the friendly press, taking full personal credit for a public mood he fundamentally misreads. He is whispering to anyone who will listen that the glorious, golden days of 2008 have officially returned, completely blind to the fact that his own 2012 victory laid the exact groundwork for the apocalyptic ashes of 2016. In the far corner, Chairman Wu Den-yih and the ‘King of Deals’ Wang Jin-pyng are already huddled over a glass table, carving up the incoming cabinet seats, national banks, and state-owned enterprises like starving butchers eyeing a prized pig. They honestly, genuinely believe their archaic, rust-covered political machine won this race. You look at these grinning, self-congratulatory relics and a wave of pure, cynical dread washes over your chest. They have learned absolutely nothing from the wilderness. They are actively preparing to repeat every single catastrophic mistake that got the party slaughtered four years ago. You did not just defeat the DPP; you now have to babysit an entire nursing home of delusional aristocrats.

`; endText += `

Your wife, Kao Wan-chien, finally lets out a breath she has been holding in her lungs for four bitter, humiliating years. She manages a tired but genuinely relieved smile, the silent vindication of a family that endured endless internet mockery and political exile. Stepping up eagerly beside you is your running mate, ${currentMateName}. The newly minted Vice President-elect is already practicing their royal wave for the mirrors, visibly intoxicated by the sudden realization that they are now officially the second most powerful person in the Republic of China. Or, perhaps far more accurately, a highly glorified ribbon-cutter trapped in an air-conditioned office, quietly waiting for the president to catch a fatal cold. Still, they play the part beautifully, soaking in the blinding, intoxicating lights of a historic landslide they merely rode shotgun for. They are already mentally measuring the drapes in their new office, blissfully unaware of the absolute administrative nightmare awaiting the executive branch. You pat their shoulder, offering a hollow congratulation, knowing full well you will assign them the most meaningless, ceremonial tasks imaginable for the next four years.

`; endText += `

Walking out onto the massive stage on Bade Road, you adjust your wire-rimmed glasses with cold, mechanical precision. The crowd screams, completely starved for any sign of administrative normalcy. You do not offer them poetic democratic dreams. You do not offer them fiery populist fury. You deliver a spectacularly dry, painfully pragmatic, brutally honest audit of the nation. ‘The ideological circus is permanently closed,’ you declare flatly into the microphone, your voice devoid of any theatrical emotion. ‘You hired an accountant, and tomorrow morning, we are ruthlessly auditing the books.’ The sheer, unadulterated boredom of your promise sends the middle-class crowd into rapturous applause. It is hilariously depressing that basic ‘competence’ is now considered a revolutionary, groundbreaking concept in Taiwanese politics. You drone on about fiscal responsibility, cross-strait trade stabilization, and bureaucratic efficiency. Every sentence is a bucket of ice water poured directly onto the burning embers of Taiwan's culture wars. The people cheer because they are finally allowed to go to sleep without checking the news for a national crisis.

`; endText += `

Yet, as the blue and white confetti rains down upon your shoulders, a chilling, metallic truth freezes your blood. A fifty-five percent mandate means absolutely zero excuses. There is no viable opposition left to blame. There is no legislative gridlock to hide behind. The state apparatus is entirely yours. The very same voters who gleefully used you as a razor-sharp guillotine to decapitate the DPP tonight will not hesitate for a single second to drag you to the exact same bloody scaffold the moment the economy stumbles. The honeymoon will last exactly until the first power outage or the first sluggish quarterly earnings report. You have inherited a ticking time bomb, wrapped in a golden ribbon, and the timer just started counting down. You look up into the night sky, smiling perfectly for the cameras, knowing that in the ruthless game of Taiwanese democracy, every landslide victory is merely the prologue to the next catastrophic betrayal. The burden of normalcy is the heaviest crown of all.

`; endImage = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/sizhu.jpg?v=1782682968511'; mainTitle = 'ACCOUNTANT’S BURDEN'; subTitle = 'A massive mandate built entirely on exhaustion.'; s_name = 'The Pawnshop of Dark Clouds - Omnipotent Youth Society (2020)'; s_cover = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/%E4%B9%8C%E4%BA%91.jpg?v=1782601848678'; s_url = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/%E8%90%AC%E8%83%BD%E9%9D%92%E5%B9%B4%E6%97%85%E5%BA%97%20%E7%83%8F%E9%9B%B2%E5%85%B8%E7%95%B6%E8%A8%98%20-%20puffdad%20(youtube).mp3?v=1782601825547'; } } // 3. 郭台铭 (Terry Gou) else if (Number(campaignTrail_temp.guotaiming) === 1) { if (pct < 50.0) { endText += `

Three-thirty in the afternoon. The ultra-luxury penthouse suite overlooking Taipei 101 is suffocatingly quiet. You pace the imported Persian rugs, your hands clasped tightly behind your back. You have conquered global supply chains, negotiated with the world’s most powerful heads of state, and built a multi-billion-dollar empire from scratch. You are used to absolute control. But democracy is terrifyingly unmanageable. The thought of losing today—of pouring billions of your own wealth into a campaign only to be publicly humiliated and branded a naive, arrogant rich fool by Tsai Ing-wen—makes your stomach churn with physical nausea. The early internal polls are a disorganized mess. You are barking orders at your data analysts, demanding exact margins, furious that they cannot give you a guaranteed ROI on your political investment. For the first time in decades, Terry Gou is genuinely terrified of losing face.

`; endText += `

By six o'clock, the agonizing trickle of data turns into a flood. The race is a brutal, agonizing seesaw. Tsai Ing-wen’s ideological firewall in the south is holding terrifyingly firm. For an hour, you watch your political obituary being written on live television. But then, the economic hubs begin to report. Hsinchu, Taichung, and the middle-class suburbs of New Taipei pull through. The pragmatists, the small business owners, and the tech sector—people who care more about their wallets than political poetry—rally behind your CEO aura. The numbers inch past the DPP. You break a sweat, exhaling a heavy, trembling breath as the final margin settles into a fragile plurality. You did not conquer the nation’s heart; you simply outbid the competition in a fractured market. But in the corporate world, fifty-point-one percent of the shares makes you the absolute dictator of the board. You wipe your forehead. The hostile takeover is complete.

`; endText += `

The heavy oak doors swing open. Former President Ma Ying-jeou and Chairman Wu Den-yih enter the suite, flanked by their aides. They look relieved, but subtly uncomfortable in your opulent, non-traditional war room. Ma puts on his signature, polite smile, extending a hand. ‘Terry, congratulations. The Kuomintang has successfully returned to power. We reclaimed the mandate.’ You stand up and shake his hand—not with hostility, but with the cold, measured grip of a chairman evaluating acquired assets. ‘We closed the deal, Mr. President,’ you reply evenly. ‘But let us be clear: the traditional party brand did not save us today. The Foxconn economic dividend did.’ Wu Den-yih clears his throat, attempting to assert his institutional authority. ‘Chairman Gou, the local factions delivered the ground game. We should discuss the cabinet allocations soon to stabilize the party ranks.’ You look at Wu with a faint, detached smirk. ‘I appreciate the ground game, Chairman. But moving forward, this government operates on strict KPIs. Send me their resumes. I do not care about their factional pedigree; I care if they can read a balance sheet and execute a business plan.’ The KMT elders exchange a nervous glance. They have not won an election; they have merely been retained as middle management by a highly demanding new boss.

`; endText += `

You turn away from the seasoned politicians and look at your real inner circle. Your mother, Chuchu, sits quietly in a leather armchair, tears of immense pride welling in her eyes. You walk over and gently squeeze her shoulder. Your wife, Delia Tseng, stands elegantly by the window, already adapting flawlessly to her impending role as First Lady. Standing a respectful step behind you is your running mate, ${currentMateName}. The newly elected Vice President looks completely professional, acting less like a political partner and more like a highly paid Executive VP awaiting board instructions. ‘The transition memos are being drafted, Sir,’ ${currentMateName} reports crisply. You nod in approval. On the massive television screens, Zhao Shao-Kang is practically radiating euphoric joy on his evening talk show. ‘The era of green poverty is dead! Terry Gou is going to restructure Taiwan into a global powerhouse!’ Jaw has effectively transformed his broadcasting empire into your personal PR department. The corporate propaganda machine is running flawlessly.

`; endText += `

You step out onto the victory stage set up in the sprawling plaza. The crowd below is a bizarre, chaotic mixture of pragmatic businessmen in suits and desperate working-class voters hoping for an economic miracle. You grab the podium, projecting the aggressive, undeniable posture of an apex predator. ‘Listen to me very carefully!’ your voice booms, instantly silencing the plaza. ‘The political circus is officially bankrupt! Tsai Ing-wen and her cronies drove this island into the ground because they are professional talkers. I am a professional builder. Starting tomorrow, the Republic of China is open for business!’ The crowd screams in absolute frenzy. You unleash a barrage of impossible, reality-bending promises. ‘I will personally bring trillions of foreign capital back to Taiwan! I will double the GDP! Anyone in the government who tries to stop me with bureaucratic red tape will be fired before lunch!’

`; endText += `

The roar of the masses is deafening, fueled entirely by the intoxication of your extreme confidence. You look at the final numbers on the ticker: ${FINAL_VOTE_PERCENT.toFixed(1)}%. You smile coldly, soaking in the adulation. You bought the presidency with sheer financial force, bypassing the traditional democratic soul of the nation. Yet, beneath the blinding strobe lights, a chilling reality lingers. Over half the country voted against you. Progressive youth and civil society groups are horrified, genuinely terrified that you will sell the island’s sovereignty to Beijing to protect your massive Foxconn empire. You are the undisputed CEO of Taiwan now. But managing a wildly polarized, fiercely democratic island of 23 million people is not like running a sweatshop assembly line. The voters are not your employees; they are angry, unpredictable shareholders. In the ruthless game of politics, even the wealthiest CEO can face a terrifyingly violent hostile takeover.

`; endImage = 'https://cc-image-resizer.cwg.tw/resize/uri/https%3A%2F%2Fstorage.googleapis.com%2Fwww-cheers-com-tw%2Farticle%2F201904%2Farticle-5cb57b3339008.jpg/?format=webp'; mainTitle = 'HOSTILE TAKEOVER'; subTitle = 'The Republic, purchased by a fragile plurality.'; s_name = 'The higher being - Dou Wei (1994)'; s_cover = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/douwei.jpeg'; s_url = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/%E7%AB%87%E5%94%AF%20Dou%20Wei%E3%80%90%E9%AB%98%E7%B4%9A%E5%8B%95%E7%89%A9%20The%20higher%20being%E3%80%91Official%20Music%20Video%20-%20%E6%BB%BE%E7%9F%B3%E5%94%B1%E7%89%87%20ROCK%20RECORDS%20(youtube).mp3?v=1782591736671'; } else if (pct <= 55.0) { endText += `

Exit polls and blackout data had projected a slight edge for the billionaire all week, but you do not trust political science. You only trust ledgers. Sitting in the ultra-luxury penthouse suite overlooking the Taipei skyline, you pace the imported Persian carpets like a caged tiger. The internal numbers gave you a two to three percent lead over Tsai Ing-wen. In the corporate world, data is absolute. In democracy, data is a terrifyingly fragile illusion. You despise this uncertainty. You have built a transnational manufacturing empire, negotiated with the world’s most powerful dictators, and bent global supply chains to your will. Yet today, your entire destiny rests in the hands of millions of ordinary, unpredictable citizens marking pieces of paper. What if the pollsters are wrong? The sheer thought of losing—of spending billions of your personal fortune only to be publicly humiliated by a career academic—makes your stomach churn with a sickening, violent pride. You bark at your data analysts, demanding updates every five minutes, completely terrifying the junior staff. You do not just want to win; you need to crush her.

`; endText += `

Across the sprawling penthouse, the atmosphere is chillingly different from a traditional political campaign. There are no frantic grassroots organizers, only highly paid corporate strategists and media mercenaries. Lounging gracefully on a velvet sofa is your wife, Delia Tseng. She sips sparkling water, exuding the flawless, untouchable elegance of a woman preparing to become the ultimate First Lady of Taiwan. Standing awkwardly near the entrance are the wives of the Kuomintang elite—the spouses of faction leaders and former cabinet ministers. For decades, these women were the undisputed queens of the pan-blue social circles. But today, the hierarchy has been brutally upended. Delia speaks to them with a polite, razor-thin smile, her tone laced with the terrifying, subtle condescension of a billionaire looking down on bankrupt aristocrats asking for a handout. The KMT wives nod sycophantically, completely subjugated. They know their husbands’ political careers now depend entirely on the financial charity of the man pacing across the room.

`; endText += `

By seven o'clock, the agonizing trickle of data turns into an overwhelming, undeniable avalanche of blue and gold. You cross the fifty percent threshold. A solid, absolute majority. You did not just scrape by; you executed a flawless, absolute acquisition of the national apparatus. The DPP’s ideological fortress has been completely pulverized by your limitless war chest and your ruthless, economic-first populism. The working class bought your CEO pitch wholesale, choosing the promise of wealth over the fear of Beijing. You watch the numbers soar, feeling an intoxicating rush of pure, unadulterated supremacy. You proved that money, when weaponized with a ruthless corporate vision, can pave a direct, unassailable road to supreme power. The century-old Kuomintang, a decaying, bankrupt antique shop of a party, was merely the vehicle you purchased to drive into the Presidential Office. You bought them, you rebranded them, and you won.

`; endText += `

Your private cell phone rings. The caller ID is hidden, but you know exactly who is begging for your ear. You let it ring three times before slowly, arrogantly picking it up. ‘Chairman Gou,’ Tsai Ing-wen’s voice comes through the speaker, strained and painfully exhausted. ‘The voters have made their choice. I am calling to concede the elect—’ You do not even let her finish the sentence. ‘You are fired, Tsai,’ you interrupt, your voice dripping with absolute, freezing contempt. ‘You ran this island into the ground. Pack your desk. I am taking over the company.’ You press the end call button, tossing the phone carelessly onto the glass table. The ultimate disrespect. You do not care about democratic sportsmanship or political grace. You are a winner dealing with a loser. She is history.

`; endText += `

Sitting back in the heavy executive chair, you close your eyes for a moment, letting the sheer magnitude of your new power wash over you. The transition from businessman to Commander-in-Chief is completely finished. Your mind drifts to the international stage. You picture yourself stepping off Air Force One, shaking hands with Donald Trump, two billionaire outsiders who bypassed the political swamp to conquer their nations. You imagine the furious, scrambling panic in Beijing. Xi Jinping knows he can no longer bully Taiwan with cheap military threats, because the man sitting in Taipei controls the absolute lifelines of the global tech supply chain. Both sides of the Pacific desperately need you now. You are the ultimate geopolitical linchpin. The fantasy is intoxicating, bordering on delusions of grandeur, until a polite voice pulls you back to reality. ‘Mr. President-elect,’ your running mate, ${currentMateName}, says softly, standing a respectful distance away. ‘The party elders have arrived.’

`; endText += `

The heavy oak doors swing open. Former President Ma Ying-jeou and Chairman Wu Den-yih enter the suite, flanked by their aides. They look relieved, but subtly uncomfortable in your opulent, non-traditional war room. Ma puts on his signature, polite smile, extending a hand. ‘Terry, congratulations. The Kuomintang has successfully returned to power.’ You do not stand up. You remain seated, staring at him with the cold eyes of an apex predator. ‘Correction, Ma,’ you say, your voice echoing like a whip. ‘I returned to power. I bought your bankrupt, obsolete antique shop of a party. I paid for the advertisements. I funded the local factions.’ Ma’s face turns pale. Wu Den-yih clears his throat, frantically trying to negotiate cabinet allocations. You cut him off instantly. ‘There are no political rewards. You are no longer political warlords; you are my regional managers. You are all dismissed.’ They stand frozen in absolute humiliation. You turn your back on them, looking at your mother, Chuchu, who weeps with immense pride. Delia stands beside you, offering a chillingly victorious smile to the dismissed KMT elders. On the massive televisions, Zhao Shao-Kang is screaming on his talk show, practically worshipping your name. ‘Terry Gou has saved the Republic! The golden era of Taiwan Inc. begins tomorrow!’

`; endText += `

Stepping onto the blindingly lit stage, you stare down at a roaring ocean of hundreds of thousands of fanatical believers. They are chanting your name like a corporate deity. You grab the podium, radiating the aggressive, unrestrained arrogance of a tycoon completely off the leash. ‘The pathetic political circus is dead!’ you roar, your voice echoing off the skyscrapers. ‘Tsai Ing-wen bankrupted this island, but tomorrow morning, Taiwan Incorporated opens for business! I do not care about your factions, I do not care about your feelings! I only care about KPIs!’ The crowd screams in apocalyptic euphoria. You unleash a torrent of reality-bending, Trumpian promises. ‘I will personally force foreign capital to flood our markets! We are going to build factories that make Silicon Valley look like a joke! I will fire any useless bureaucrat who stands in my way! We will be the richest, most untouchable island on Earth!’ You raise both fists into the air as the confetti rains down. The voters did not elect a president; they elected a dictator of economics. The boardroom has officially superseded the parliament.

`; endImage = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/370326138_851155399715491_1170147914084660165_n-1.png?v=1782589811282'; mainTitle = 'TAIWAN INCORPORATED'; subTitle = 'The boardroom supersedes the parliament.'; s_name = 'Princess - Jam Hsiao (2009)'; s_cover = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/Jam_Hsiao_2009_Album_Cover_%2528Princess%2529.jpg'; s_url = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/%E8%95%AD%E6%95%AC%E9%A8%B0%20%E7%8E%8B%E5%A6%83-%E8%8F%AF%E7%B4%8Dofficial%20HQ%E5%AE%98%E6%96%B9%E7%89%88MV%20-%20%E8%8F%AF%E7%B4%8D%E9%9F%B3%E6%A8%82%20Warner%20Music%20Taiwan%20(youtube).mp3?v=1782589710793'; } else { endText += `

The sprawling, ultra-luxury penthouse suite atop the Xinyi District skyscraper feels entirely disconnected from the gravity of the island below. It is four o'clock in the afternoon. The voting booths have just closed, but in this room, there is no air of democratic anxiety, only the cold, sterile hum of corporate anticipation. You pace the length of the imported Persian carpet, your hands clasped tightly behind your back. Spread across the massive mahogany conference table are the final, heavily encrypted internal polling projections compiled by the most expensive political data scientists money can buy. The numbers are staggering. They project a landslide of historic proportions, pushing past the fifty-five percent threshold. According to the spreadsheets, you are completely obliterating Tsai Ing-wen. The green fortress in the south has supposedly collapsed under the weight of your economic promises. Yet, looking at the impeccably dressed campaign managers and data analysts standing nervously around the table, a dark, venomous wave of paranoia violently churns in your stomach.

`; endText += `

In the corporate world, you trust the balance sheets because you own the factories. In politics, you are swimming in an ocean of professional liars. You narrow your eyes, scrutinizing the sycophantic smiles of the political mercenaries you hired. Are they telling you the truth? Or are they simply massaging your ego, treating the legendary founder of Foxconn as the ultimate political sucker? You have poured an astronomical, frankly obscene amount of your personal fortune into this campaign. You bought the billboards, you bought the airtime, you bought the silence of the factions, and you literally funded the Kuomintang's payroll when they were bankrupt. You have paved a road of solid gold straight to the Presidential Office. But the terrifying thought lingers: what if the Taiwanese electorate took your money, attended your lavish rallies, ate your catered bentos, and then walked into the voting booths to silently stab you in the back? The sheer thought of being scammed by the political establishment makes your blood boil with a violent, terrifying pride. You do not just demand a victory today; you demand a total, unquestionable return on your investment.

`; endText += `

Across the opulent room, completely oblivious to your silent, raging paranoia, a different kind of theater is playing out. The atmosphere resembles a high-society salon rather than a war room. Your elderly mother, Chuchu, sits quietly in her wheelchair near the window, a silent, comforting anchor to your humble origins. Your adult children are already gathered around the crystal wet bar, laughing and popping early bottles of vintage Dom Perignon, reveling in the intoxicating proximity to ultimate state power. But the true spectacle is unfolding on the velvet sectional sofa in the center of the room. Your wife, Delia Tseng, sits with the flawless, terrifyingly relaxed posture of a queen who has already been crowned. Surrounding her, perched awkwardly on the edges of their seats, are the wives of the Kuomintang's highest-ranking elite—the spouses of former ministers, faction bosses, and central committee members. For decades, these women were the undisputed, blue-blooded aristocrats of Taipei society. Today, they are nothing more than terrified courtiers.

`; endText += `

You watch Delia out of the corner of your eye. She sighs, a perfectly calibrated, theatrical sound of exhaustion, delicately adjusting a diamond bracelet that costs more than a legislator's lifetime salary. ‘It is just so incredibly exhausting,’ Delia complains, her voice dripping with that uniquely terrifying, passive-aggressive arrogance of the newly supreme. ‘The lawyers from the Control Yuan are being so pedantic about the asset declarations for the First Family. I have had my assistants working until midnight just to catalog the Hermes Birkins, the limited-edition Patek Philippes, the custom Chanel perfumes... Every single piece of jewelry has to be appraised and filed. Honestly, becoming First Lady feels like being audited by peasants.’ The KMT wives, women who once wielded immense social power, force sycophantic, strained smiles, nodding vigorously in agreement, completely humiliated by the sheer, unbridgeable financial chasm between them and your empire. They are being treated like lowly clerks, and they must swallow the insult with a smile.

`; endText += `

Suddenly, looking at Delia, a profound and unexpected wave of irritation washes over you. Her voice, usually a pleasant background hum, suddenly grates on your nerves like scratching metal. The superficiality of it all—the bags, the perfumes, the endless vanity—feels grotesquely cheap against the historical weight of what you are about to accomplish. For a split second, a cold, ruthless thought flashes across your mind: I should divorce her. The thought is sharp and violent. A CEO optimizing a poorly performing asset. You quickly brush the thought aside; a divorce scandal right before the inauguration would be a catastrophic PR nightmare. But the resentment lingers, quickly giving way to a deep, agonizing pang of melancholy. You look away from the sofa, staring out at the gray Taipei sky. You think of Serena. Serena Lin. Your late wife. The woman who actually built the empire with you, who swallowed the bitter dust of the early factory days, who mortgaged her own family's dignity to fund your first ambitions. She was the true matriarch of Foxconn. A bitter, heavy sorrow twists in your chest. Serena should be the one sitting on that sofa. Serena should be the one walking into the Presidential Office as the First Lady of the Republic of China, not this noisy, superficial dancer complaining about paperwork. You clench your jaw, burying the grief under a thick layer of cold, capitalist anger.

`; endText += `

By six-thirty, the anxiety in the room is violently incinerated by the brutal, undeniable mathematics of democracy. The early polls were not a lie; they were an understatement. The trickle of data turns into an apocalyptic avalanche of blue and gold. The news anchors on the television screens look physically stunned, stumbling over their words as the maps bleed into your colors. You cross the fifty percent threshold. Then fifty-two. Then fifty-five. It is a supermajority landslide of terrifying proportions. You have not just defeated the Democratic Progressive Party; you have completely and utterly annihilated them. Tsai Ing-wen’s supposedly impenetrable fortress of progressive ideology, built on the fear of Beijing and the tear gas of Hong Kong, has been effortlessly crushed by the overwhelming, undeniable gravity of your wealth. The forgotten working class, the pragmatic middle class, the terrified business owners—they all abandoned traditional politics and submitted to your CEO pitch. You promised them money, and they handed you the country.

`; endText += `

The final, historic tally permanently locks onto the main screen: ${FINAL_VOTE_PERCENT.toFixed(1)}%. The room erupts into chaotic, hysterical cheering, but you remain perfectly, terrifyingly still. The arrogance swelling inside you is no longer a dark secret; it is an absolute, undeniable reality. You look at the number. Over fifty-five percent. The last time the Kuomintang saw numbers like this was Ma Ying-jeou in 2008. But Ma was a polished, career politician riding a wave of anti-corruption sentiment against a crippled DPP. You did this as an outsider, against a fully entrenched, hostile state apparatus. You bought a decaying, bankrupt century-old political party, ripped out its failing engine, rebranded it with your personal logo, and drove it straight over the opposition.

`; endText += `

A new, deeply satisfying thought crosses your mind. You think of Donald Trump. The media loves to compare you to the American President—two billionaire outsiders who shocked the world. But standing here, watching your landslide, you realize you are infinitely superior to Trump. Trump barely scraped by the electoral college; he lost the popular vote by millions, despised by the majority of his own citizens. You, however, have absolutely conquered the popular vote. You did not sneak through a constitutional loophole; you mathematically crushed your opponent and forced the entire nation to explicitly, democratically submit to your rule. You are not just a populist accident; you are the undisputed, universally acknowledged Emperor of Taiwan Incorporated.

`; endText += `

Your chief of staff approaches, his hands physically shaking as he holds a clipboard. ‘Mr. President-elect... Chairman Wu Den-yih, Former President Ma Ying-jeou, and Speaker Wang Jin-pyng are downstairs. They are requesting to come up to the suite to offer their formal congratulations and discuss the transition.’ You do not even turn your head to look at him. You stare blankly at the Taipei 101 tower in the distance. ‘Tell the security desk to deny them entry,’ you say, your voice flat, cold, and echoing with absolute authority. ‘Tell them the CEO is busy. If they want to wait, they can wait in the underground parking garage. I will summon them when I need them to take dictation.’ The chief of staff turns pale, nodding frantically before scurrying away. The ultimate, unthinkable humiliation of the Kuomintang establishment is complete. They thought you were their savior; they realize too late that you are their liquidator. You glance sideways at your running mate, ${currentMateName}, who is standing awkwardly by the wall, trying to look important. You mentally dismiss them. A decorative paperweight. For the next four years, ${currentMateName} will do absolutely nothing but attend ribbon-cutting ceremonies while you run the boardroom.

`; endText += `

The room suddenly falls completely silent. Your private, highly encrypted cell phone, sitting on the mahogany desk, begins to vibrate. The caller ID simply reads: Presidential Office. It is Tsai Ing-wen. The defeated incumbent, calling to deliver her agonizing, humiliating concession. The ultimate surrender of the progressive era. Every eye in the room is locked on the vibrating device. Delia stops talking. The children freeze. You stand over the desk, looking down at the glowing screen. A cold, predatory smile slowly spreads across your face.

`; endText += `

You do not pick it up.

`; endText += `

You let it ring. Once. Twice. Three times. You let the leader of the free world on this island wait in agonizing, unanswered humiliation. The ringing echoes through the opulent penthouse, a ringing declaration that the era of polite, democratic sportsmanship is dead. You are a winner dealing with a loser, and the CEO does not take calls from bankrupt competitors. As the phone finally goes silent, transitioning to voicemail, you adjust your suit jacket. It is time to go down to the balcony. It is time to address the shareholders of your newly acquired nation.

`; endImage = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/_130921808_gettyimages-1628187411.jpg'; mainTitle = 'ABSOLUTE MONOPOLY'; subTitle = 'The billionaire CEO claims his ultimate crown.'; s_name = "I Don't Care - Hua Chenyu (2015)"; s_cover = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/HuaChenYu-Alien.jpg'; s_url = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/%E8%8F%AF%E6%99%A8%E5%AE%87%20-%E3%80%8A%E7%95%B0%E9%A1%9E%E3%80%8B-%20%E6%88%91%E7%AE%A1%E4%BD%A0%20-%20JJY%20Music%20Channel%20(youtube).mp3?v=1782582746520'; } } // 4. 王金平 (Wang Jin-pyng) else if (Number(campaignTrail_temp.wangjinping) === 1) { if (pct < 50.0) { endText += `

Four o'clock in the afternoon. Inside the deeply insulated VIP suite of the Kuomintang central headquarters, the atmosphere is heavy with the scent of aged Alishan Oolong tea and old leather. You sit at the center of a mahogany table, surrounded by the true, invisible power brokers of the island: the faction bosses of Changhua, the agricultural association chiefs of Yunlin, and the temple directors of Kaohsiung. Your running mate, ${currentMateName}, sits quietly beside you, repeatedly checking a muted smartphone. The exit polls leaked earlier were a chaotic, contradictory mess. Half the pundits projected a narrow survival for Tsai Ing-wen; the other half whispered of a shocking blue upset. You maintain your signature, impenetrable smile, your eyes crinkling at the corners in perpetual, Buddha-like benevolence. ‘We accept whatever the people decide with a calm heart,’ you murmur to the room, pouring another round of tea. Yet, the way your aged, spotted fingers grip the delicate porcelain teacup with white-knuckled intensity betrays the violent, racing anxiety tearing through your chest. You have survived in the political trenches for four decades, but today is the ultimate gamble. There is no middle ground left.

`; endText += `

As the first hour of counting passes, the news anchors on the massive LED screens appear visibly confused. The urban, progressive elites in Taipei had spent the entire campaign treating you like a prehistoric joke. They believed Tsai Ing-wen’s sophisticated cyber-warfare and international sovereignty rhetoric would easily crush a boring, archaic, southern old man whose campaign consisted mostly of temple visits and banquet handshakes. But the screens tell a radically different story. The Choshui River line is holding. The rural machinery is grinding out votes with terrifying, silent efficiency. Townships that the DPP assumed were safely green are suddenly flipping blue by margins of a few hundred votes each. By six-thirty, the arrogant smirks vanish from the pro-green commentators’ faces. The media narrative aggressively shifts in real-time. Suddenly, they are no longer mocking your age; they are breathlessly praising the unparalleled, terrifying organizational mastery of the ‘King of Deals.’ Your invisible network of patronage and favors has quietly strangled the DPP’s air war.

`; endText += `

By eight o'clock, the agonizingly tight race reaches its mathematical conclusion. The numbers stabilize at ${FINAL_VOTE_PERCENT.toFixed(1)}%. You did not capture a majority of the nation; you merely stitched together a fragile, hyper-localized coalition to secure a razor-thin plurality. But in the ruthless calculus of the Republic of China, a plurality is all it takes to claim the throne. The television switches to a live broadcast of Tsai Ing-wen stepping up to a podium, her face pale and exhausted, delivering a bitter, formal concession speech. The VIP suite erupts. The local bosses slam their hands on the mahogany table, cheering hoarsely. You slowly set your teacup down. The smile on your face remains exactly the same, but the weight of a lifetime of political survival has finally lifted. The eternal legislator has just become the President.

`; endText += `

You step out of the suite and walk into the main reception hall of the headquarters. The entire Kuomintang establishment is waiting to greet you. Chairman Wu Den-yih approaches first, his eyes calculating the new distribution of power as he warmly pumps your hand. Eric Chu offers a highly polished, respectful bow. Your running mate, ${currentMateName}, beams with the immense pride of a politician who knows they have just secured their place in history, blissfully unaware that for the next four years, they will be nothing more than a ceremonial ghost in an administration governed by your backroom deals. Then, the crowd parts slightly, and you see him. Former President Ma Ying-jeou.

`; endText += `

The man who had mercilessly tried to politically execute you during the infamous September Strife of 2013 stands before you. He looks noticeably uncomfortable, his aristocratic posture agonizingly stiff. The deep, poisonous grudge between you two is the worst-kept secret in Taiwanese politics. Yet, today is not the day for outbursts. You are the ultimate master of harmony. With your signature, unyielding smile, you walk directly toward him and extend both hands, grasping his right hand warmly. ‘Thank you for your tireless guidance, President Ma. The party is finally whole again,’ you say, your voice dripping with weaponized, passive-aggressive magnanimity. Ma forces a polite, incredibly hollow smile, his eyes devoid of warmth. ‘Congratulations, President-elect Wang. The party endures,’ he replies tersely, quickly withdrawing his hand. You both know the truth. You have not just defeated the DPP; you have finally, permanently defeated him. You have outlasted the princeling.

`; endText += `

The heavy glass doors open, and you step out onto the balcony overlooking Bade Road. The crowd below is a vast, roaring ocean of traditional supporters and mobilized local factions. You grab the microphone. You do not speak in the polished, sterile Mandarin of the Taipei elites. You speak in fluent, deeply resonant Taiwanese Hokkien. ‘My fellow folks! The fighting is over!’ your voice booms across the humid night. ‘We have had enough of this blue and green ideological warfare! Starting tomorrow, we throw away the political hatred! We will protect the peace across the strait, we will open the doors to trade, and we will focus on one thing only: developing the economy so everyone can put food on the table!’ It is the ultimate, cliché-ridden manifesto of the KMT localist faction, but to the exhausted, mobilized masses below, it sounds like absolute salvation.

`; endText += `

The crowd erupts into a deafening, thunderous applause, chanting your name into the Taipei night. You stand at the edge of the balcony, waving your hands slowly. The flashbulbs of the cameras blur your vision, or perhaps it is the sudden, overwhelming sting of tears. You blink them away, maintaining your eternal smile. It is an ugly, unglamorous, violently pragmatic victory. But looking down at the conquered capital, the King of Deals knows that a fragile crown is still a crown.

`; endImage = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/wangjp.jpg'; mainTitle = 'KING OF DEALS'; subTitle = 'A fragile coalition forged in the shadows.'; s_name = 'White dove - Wu Bai & China Blue (1999)'; s_cover = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/wubai.jpg'; s_url = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/%E4%BC%8D%E4%BD%B0%20Wu%20Bai%26China%20Blue%E3%80%90%E7%99%BD%E9%B4%BF%20White%20dove%E3%80%91Official%20Music%20Video(4K)%20-%20%E6%BB%BE%E7%9F%B3%E5%94%B1%E7%89%87%20ROCK%20RECORDS%20(youtube).mp3?v=1782684957641'; } else if (pct <= 55.0) { endText += `

The afternoon sun casts long, golden shadows across the VIP suite of the Kuomintang central headquarters. You sit comfortably at the head of a heavy mahogany table, methodically rinsing a set of delicate porcelain teacups with boiling water. Your running mate, ${currentMateName}, sits across from you, rapidly scrolling through an encrypted electronic tablet. 'The blackout polling data is incredibly consistent, President Wang,' ${currentMateName} says, a hint of breathless excitement breaking through their professional facade. 'Aside from the most hardcore deep-green media outlets, almost every mainstream network is quietly projecting a victory for us. The southern margins are holding.' You pause, pouring the amber liquid with practiced, unwavering precision. You offer your signature, impenetrable, Buddha-like smile. 'We listen to the polls with a humble heart, but we never presume,' you reply, your voice a perfectly calibrated mask of veteran political humility. 'Ultimately, we accept whatever the people decide. The true verdict lies entirely inside the ballot boxes.' It is the classic, evasive rhetoric of a man who has spent forty years surviving the treacherous currents of the Legislative Yuan.

`; endText += `

At four o'clock, the counting begins. The early hours are a terrifyingly tight, suffocating tug-of-war. For a fleeting moment, the green commentators on television dare to project an air of relief. But as evening descends, the quiet, terrifying efficiency of your ground game begins to strangle the Democratic Progressive Party. You maintain a fragile but utterly unbreakable lead. The urban progressive youth watching the broadcasts are in a state of absolute, paralyzed shock. They simply cannot comprehend how their sophisticated, internationalist incumbent president is being systematically dismantled by a boring, archaic old man whose entire campaign consisted of temple visits and banquet handshakes. But they have forgotten the oldest, most brutal rule of Taiwanese democracy: internet algorithms do not vote; patronage networks do. By eight o'clock, the suspense is unceremoniously executed. The numbers cross the fifty percent threshold. A solid, undeniable majority. Tsai Ing-wen steps up to a podium on live television, her face pale and rigidly composed, to deliver a bitter concession speech.

`; endText += `

The heavy doors of the VIP suite swing open, not for the Ivy-League-educated Taipei elites, but for the true lords of the island. The warlords have come to pay tribute. The heads of the Chang family from Yunlin, the Hsieh clan from Changhua, and the Yen family from Taichung stride into the room. They smell of expensive Kaoliang liquor, cigar smoke, and immense rural power. They laugh hoarsely, clapping you on the back with the rough familiarity of brothers in arms. You are the undisputed Godfather, and the families have delivered the nation. Standing quietly in the corner, Chairman Wu Den-yih watches the scene and offers a slow, deeply approving nod. He knows exactly what this means. The alliance of the two native Taiwanese, 'benshengren' old men has successfully executed the greatest electoral heist of the decade, effortlessly neutralizing the arrogance of the northern establishment.

`; endText += `

Then, the crowd parts slightly, and the mood in the room instantly drops a few degrees. Former President Ma Ying-jeou steps forward. The contrast is violently jarring. Ma’s face is a masterclass in conflicted, patrician agony. He is visibly relieved that the Kuomintang has reclaimed the executive branch, yet he looks deeply nauseated by the fact that the supreme crown now rests on the head of the man he despises most—the man he utterly failed to destroy during the September Strife years ago. Ma extends his hand, offering a tepid, painfully polite greeting. 'Congratulations on a hard-fought victory. The party has returned to its rightful place,' Ma murmurs, his eyes cold and evasive. You know exactly what is churning behind his rigid posture. Today is the ultimate vengeance, but a master politician never gloats. You match his icy detachment with a warm, flawlessly hypocritical smile, briefly shaking his hand. 'With your blessing, President Ma. The party is whole again.' You do not linger. A brief, suffocating exchange of pleasantries, and you seamlessly walk past him to join the local bosses. You have absolutely no time to entertain defeated aristocrats.

`; endText += `

You step out onto the brightly lit balcony overlooking Bade Road. The crowd below is a vast, disciplined ocean of mobilized supporters and factional loyalists. You approach the microphone and begin to speak in fluent, deeply resonant Taiwanese Hokkien. It is the exact same speech you have delivered a thousand times. You speak of discarding ideological warfare. You speak of protecting the peace across the Taiwan Strait. You promise to focus entirely on pragmatism, on developing the economy, on letting the common people make money in harmony. To the intellectual elites in the capital, it is a parade of exhausting, outdated localist clichés. But to the roaring masses below, it is the comforting, predictable gospel of stability.

`; endText += `

The applause erupts, a deafening wave that washes over the concrete canyons of the city. You stand at the edge of the balcony, your vision slightly blurring under the relentless assault of camera flashes and perhaps the faint, unspeakable emotion of a lifelong ambition finally realized. The camera seems to slowly pull back, lifting high above the Kuomintang headquarters. The cheering fades into the ambient hum of the Taipei metropolis, the neon lights blending with the distant, dark silhouette of the mountains. The Republic of China has not been saved by a shining ideological knight, but by the quiet, relentless, and shadowy gears of the ultimate political machine. The King of Deals stands alone at the summit.

`; endImage = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/wangjpd2.jpg'; mainTitle = 'TRIUMPH OF THE GODFATHER'; subTitle = 'The quiet machinery of local factions claims the ultimate prize.'; s_name = 'Great Ship Enters Port - Jody Chiang (1990)'; s_cover = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/250px-Emblem_of_the_Kuomintang.svg.png'; s_url = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/%E5%A4%A7%E8%88%B9%E5%85%A5%E6%B8%AF%20-%20Jody%20Chiang%20(youtube).mp3?v=1782685597507'; } else { endText += `

It is two o'clock in the afternoon, mere hours before the polls officially close. You and your running mate, ${currentMateName}, are conducting a final, leisurely walking tour through a bustling traditional market in southern Taiwan. The humid air is thick with the scent of incense, fried shallots, and crushed asphalt. A group of elderly women and weathered local men press against the police barricades, their faces flushed with absolute devotion, desperately reaching out to grab your hands. ‘President! Dong-suan! Dong-suan!’ they chant in rapid, fiery Taiwanese Hokkien. A swarm of reporters shoves microphones into your face, breathlessly noting that Tsai Ing-wen’s campaign seems to have completely collapsed and asking if you are ready to declare a historic victory. You pause, adjusting your collar with a slow, practiced grace. You flash your signature, impenetrable Buddha-like smile. ‘We listen to the polls with a humble heart,’ you murmur, deploying the timeless, evasive vocabulary of the veteran statesman. ‘But ultimately, we accept whatever the people decide. The true verdict lies entirely inside the ballot boxes.’ It is a masterclass in false modesty, perfectly masking the surging, electric certainty in your chest.

`; endText += `

When the heavy steel doors of the polling stations slam shut at four o'clock, the agonizing suspense lasts barely thirty minutes. The numbers do not just trickle in; they detonate. The Choshui River line is completely obliterated. Your invisible, subterranean empire of agricultural associations, temple networks, and local faction bosses executes its mandate with terrifying, mechanized precision. By seven o'clock, the map is drowned in an overwhelming ocean of orthodox blue. You cross the fifty percent threshold, then fifty-two, then effortlessly smash past fifty-five percent. It is a supermajority landslide of apocalyptic proportions, mirroring the invincible momentum of the 2008 Kuomintang wave. In the progressive, hipster coffee shops of Taipei, the urban youth are staring at their smartphones in sheer, paralyzed horror. They are weeping openly, cursing the heavens, and venting their furious hatred against the 'Black Gold' politics, the corrupt local patronage, and the factional warlords. They simply cannot comprehend how Tsai Ing-wen’s sophisticated, internationalist crusade was just brutally, mathematically slaughtered by a boring, archaic old man who barely understands the internet. But reality is a ruthless executioner. Algorithms do not vote; organized local networks do.

`; endText += `

Inside the VIP suite of the KMT central headquarters, the atmosphere is a chaotic, intoxicating frenzy of absolute power. The sheer magnitude of the mandate proves a profound political truth: Taiwan does indeed desire local, native identity (bentuhua), but the electorate profoundly distrusts the DPP's ideological, war-baiting version of it. They chose your version instead—a pragmatic, conservative, and highly localized network of mutually beneficial compromises that protects cross-strait peace and focuses solely on economic prosperity. Chairman Wu Den-yih rushes toward you, his usual cunning demeanor entirely replaced by a breathless, almost sycophantic enthusiasm. The two native Taiwanese, 'benshengren' old men exchange vigorous handshakes, Wu nodding deferentially to the new supreme leader of the Republic.

`; endText += `

You and ${currentMateName} are practically glowing, your faces plastered with radiant, unstoppable smiles as you warmly embrace the true lords of the island who have come to pay tribute. The Chang family from Yunlin, the Hsieh clan from Changhua, the Yen family from Taichung—they all crowd around you, smelling of victory and cigar smoke. The Democratic Progressive Party has not just been defeated; it has been suppressed and utterly humiliated. Tsai Ing-wen is already on television, bowing deeply to deliver her bitter concession speech.

`; endText += `

Yet, amidst the deafening cheers and the clinking of champagne glasses, your razor-sharp political instincts detect a glaring anomaly.
