You subtly scan the crowded room, looking past the shoulders of the sycophants. Someone is missing. The tall, patrician figure of former President Ma Ying-jeou is nowhere to be found. The man who tried to politically execute you during the brutal September Strife of 2013 has vanished from the headquarters. Perhaps the sheer psychological trauma of watching his most despised internal rival achieve a presidential mandate equal to his own legendary 2008 victory was simply too much for his aristocratic pride to stomach. A fleeting, cold realization washes over you: the Kuomintang has reclaimed the nation, but the blood feud between the princeling and the Godfather is far from over.

`; endText += `

You take a half-step forward, intending to ask an aide about Ma’s whereabouts, but you are instantly swallowed. Another wave of jubilant, red-sashed faction leaders and ecstatic local politicians surges forward, lifting their glasses, shouting your name, and blocking your view of the door. The King of Deals smiles, raising his own glass, completely and permanently engulfed by the immense, chaotic gravity of his own unstoppable political empire.

`; endImage = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/mawang.jpg'; mainTitle = 'SUPREME UNIFIER'; subTitle = 'The ultimate backroom master takes all.'; s_name = "World's Number One - Andy Lau (1997)"; s_cover = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/shijiediyideng.jpg'; s_url = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/%E4%B8%96%E7%95%8C%E7%AC%AC%E4%B8%80%E7%AD%89%20%E5%88%98%E5%BE%B7%E5%8D%8E%20(%E6%AD%8C%E8%AF%8D%E7%89%88)%20-%20GM%20Lyric%20(youtube).mp3?v=1782686294876'; } } // 5. 吴敦义 (Wu Den-yih) else if (Number(campaignTrail_temp.wudunyi) === 1) { if (pct < 50.0) { endText += `

‘What is the exact turnout rate in the coastal townships of Changhua?’ Chairman Wu Den-yih’s voice was a low, terrifyingly calm murmur, yet it made the junior data analyst physically tremble. You leaned over the desk, your eyes locking onto the glowing spreadsheets. ‘Did the local factions deliver the quotas we negotiated? Filter the cross-tabs for the fifty-plus demographic. Now.’

`; endText += `

‘Chairman, the... the turnout is holding at sixty-five percent, but James Soong is siphoning slightly more of our orthodox veteran votes than we projected—’ the analyst stammered, frantically adjusting the metrics on the screen.

`; endText += `

‘Let Soong have the stubborn old men,’ you replied, your voice cold and meticulously calculated, wiping a thin layer of sweat from your forehead with a monogrammed handkerchief. ‘As long as our patronage networks hold the central counties, Soong’s spoiler campaign is nothing but a localized nuisance. Focus on Taichung.’

`; endText += `

‘Den-yih, you are making yourself sick,’ whispered your wife, Tsai Ling-yi. Her voice was brittle with anxiety as she paced the imported carpet of the VIP suite, clutching her designer handbag like a shield against the agonizing wait. Standing stiffly by the window, your running mate, ${currentMateName}, attempted a robotic projection of confidence. ‘The organizational machine is fully deployed, Chairman. We just need to trust the ground game.’ You did not even look up from the monitors. ‘There is no such thing as trust in an election,’ you replied, adjusting your glasses. ‘There are only mobilization targets, resource allocations, and cold, hard votes. A political machine is only as effective as the discipline of its operators.’

`; endText += `

For the first two agonizing hours of counting, the discipline of that machine was severely tested. The southern green strongholds reported their numbers with brutal efficiency, painting the screens in a suffocating sea of green. Tsai Ing-wen took a terrifying early lead. The VIP suite felt like a morgue. ‘We are bleeding in the urban centers,’ a faction boss muttered darkly from the corner. ‘The youth vote is punishing us.’

`; endText += `

But then, the geographical gravity of the island violently shifted. The massive, working-class belts of northern and central Taiwan began dumping their ballots into the system. The DPP’s arrogant, progressive cultural crusades had finally backfired, causing moderate and swing-voter turnout to completely collapse. Meanwhile, your meticulously engineered local alliances kicked into high gear. ‘Look at Nantou!’ a strategist yelled. Your ancestral home—your impenetrable fortress—was delivering a massive, overwhelming surge of blue votes. The race tightened into a suffocating, decimal-by-decimal trench war. The blue and green lines twisted and intertwined like a braided rope of mathematical agony. The lead changed hands three times in forty minutes.

`; endText += `

Then, just before eight o'clock, the green line hit a ceiling. Without a high youth turnout to save her, Tsai Ing-wen was stranded. The final number flashed across the main broadcast: ${FINAL_VOTE_PERCENT.toFixed(1)}%. A razor-thin, incredibly fragile plurality. James Soong had indeed bled your margins, but your brutal, relentless organizational leverage had dragged the Kuomintang across the finish line.

`; endText += `

‘We got her,’ someone whispered. Then, louder: ‘We got her!’

`; endText += `

The unbearable tension shattered into a deafening, hysterical explosion of relief. You, a man famous for your rigid, joyless discipline, finally let the mask slip. You let out a raw, guttural laugh of pure vindication. ‘Bring the Kaoliang! Pour the drinks!’ you ordered, your face flushed dark red with absolute triumph. The calculating, cold-blooded Chairman vanished, temporarily replaced by a man intoxicated by supreme power.

`; endText += `

The heavy oak doors were violently thrust open. Former President Ma Ying-jeou strode into the room. The usual patrician stiffness was completely gone; he was practically glowing with a desperate sense of salvation. ‘You did it, Den-yih!’ Ma shouted over the roaring crowd, walking straight up to you and clapping you heavily on the shoulder—a gesture of profound, unprecedented camaraderie. ‘You saved the Republic!’

`; endText += `

You handed him a heavy glass of liquor, clinking it against his with staggering force. ‘We stabilized the foundation, President Ma! The 2016 humiliation is permanently erased!’ you replied, drinking the burning alcohol in a single gulp. Soon, Wang Jin-pyng and a procession of powerful local faction bosses crowded into the suite, their faces flushed with alcohol and greed. ‘The machine still works, Chairman!’ Wang laughed hoarsely, raising his glass. The old men patted each other on the back, entirely consumed by the euphoria of their own resurrection.

`; endText += `

Yet, this deafening celebration was a dangerous, blinding narcotic. They were cheering for a miraculous escape, entirely masking the terrifying reality beneath their polished Italian leather shoes. The foundation of the Kuomintang was severely rotting. The deep-seated corruption, the arrogant disconnect from the younger generation, the absolute refusal to modernize their cross-strait ideology—all the fatal flaws remained completely unresolved. They had learned absolutely nothing from their time in the political wilderness, saved today only by Tsai Ing-wen's failure to mobilize her base and your brutal, archaic organizational mechanics.

`; endText += `

Amidst the chaotic, roaring chorus of ‘Ganbei!’ and the clinking of crystal glasses, a secure mobile phone resting on the edge of your mahogany desk began to vibrate. The screen lit up with an incoming call from the Presidential Office. It was Tsai Ing-wen, calling to officially concede her agonizing defeat. The phone vibrated intensely against the polished wood, its screen blinking silently in the shadows. But no one noticed. You were too busy pouring another glass for the former President, negotiating future cabinet seats with the warlords, entirely consumed by the arrogant illusion that the golden dynasty had returned forever. The phone rang until it automatically disconnected, lost in the triumphant noise of an empire celebrating upon its own fragile ruins.

`; endImage = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/wudunyi1.jpeg'; mainTitle = 'CALCULATED SURVIVOR'; subTitle = 'A fragile victory masks the rotting foundation.'; s_name = 'Mr. Almost - MC HotDog (2008)'; s_cover = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/regou.jpg?v=1782688995780'; s_url = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/MC%20HotDog%20%E7%86%B1%E7%8B%97%E3%80%90%E5%B7%AE%E4%B8%8D%E5%A4%9A%E5%85%88%E7%94%9F%E3%80%91Official%20Music%20Video%20-%20%E6%BB%BE%E7%9F%B3%E5%94%B1%E7%89%87%20ROCK%20RECORDS%20(youtube).mp3?v=1782688971965'; } else if (pct <= 55.0) { endText += `

You stand quietly by the floor-to-ceiling window of your private office in the Kuomintang central headquarters, your hands clasped loosely behind your back. It is late afternoon, and the sprawling concrete canopy of Taipei stretches out beneath a heavy, gray sky. Behind you, the wall-mounted television is blaring. The political talk shows are in a state of frenzied, speculative overdrive. You can hear the aggressive, booming baritone of Zhao Shao-Kang clashing with the cynical, raspy analysis of Shen Fu-hsiung as they dissect the projected turnout models, arguing endlessly about the cross-tabs in the suburban districts. The noise is a chaotic, speculative mess. It grates on your nerves. You do not deal in speculation; you deal in machinery. With a sharp exhale of annoyance, you pick up the remote and kill the power to the television. The sudden silence in the room is profoundly comforting.

`; endText += `

You walk back to your mahogany desk, sitting down to study a printed copy of the final, unreleased TVBS internal tracking poll. It shows you holding a two-point lead over Tsai Ing-wen. Two percent. In the volatile ecosystem of Taiwanese elections, a two-point margin is completely swallowed by the statistical margin of error. It is a terrifyingly thin tightrope, yet your pulse remains steady. You adjust your glasses, tapping your pen against the paper. The Democratic Progressive Party has spent the entire year deploying the full, terrifying weight of the state apparatus to crush you. They weaponized the tear gas of Hong Kong and the fabricated Wang Liqiang spy scandal. Yet, your mathematical models told you that the silent, working-class frustration over economic stagnation would ultimately override the geopolitical fearmongering. Now, it is simply a matter of waiting for the gears of the party machine to turn.

`; endText += `

The heavy oak door creaks open. Your chief data analyst steps in, his face pale but his eyes burning with adrenaline. ‘Chairman, it is four o'clock. The polls have officially closed.’

`; endText += `

You nod once, signaling him to turn the television back on. The agonizing wait for the early returns begins, but this time, the narrative unfolds exactly according to your meticulous blueprint. The early, chaotic trickle of green votes from the deep south is quickly and violently neutralized. Then, the floodgates open. Nantou County—your ancestral home, your impenetrable political fortress—erupts with a massive, overwhelming wave of orthodox blue ballots. The Hakka belt across Miaoli and Hsinchu follows suit, reporting spectacularly high turnout that bleeds the progressive coalition dry. Taichung and the central plains deliver their quotas with mechanical perfection. And finally, the crushing blow: the traditional, ironclad voting blocs of Taipei and the northern suburbs drop their massive tallies into the system. The blue line on the screen shoots upward, effortlessly crossing the fifty percent threshold and stabilizing into a solid, undeniable majority.

`; endText += `

You lean back in your chair, a slow, deeply satisfied smile spreading across your face. The final projection hovers at ${FINAL_VOTE_PERCENT.toFixed(1)}%. Watching the numbers, a sudden, vivid memory flashes through your mind. It feels exactly like the evening in 2012, standing on the stage alongside Ma Ying-jeou, celebrating the retention of the executive branch and your own ascension to the Vice Presidency. But tonight is profoundly different. In 2012, you were a highly effective lieutenant executing another man's vision. Today, you are the undisputed architect of the victory. You pulled this party from the ashes of 2016, starved the populist insurgents, unified the warring factions, and masterminded the destruction of Tsai Ing-wen.

`; endText += `

You button your suit jacket, smooth your tie, and open the door to the main reception hall. The moment you step across the threshold, the room erupts into a deafening, hysterical roar of triumph. You are instantly engulfed in a sea of adulation. The power dynamic of the entire island has shifted, and you are its new gravitational center. Your wife, Tsai Ling-yi, rushes forward, her eyes brimming with tears of absolute vindication, grasping your arm. Your running mate, ${currentMateName}, stands tall beside you, offering a deeply respectful, deferential bow, acknowledging your supreme authority. The heavyweights who once plotted against you now crowd around like eager courtiers. Wang Jin-pyng approaches, offering his signature Buddha-like smile, patting your arm with the deep, unspoken respect of a fellow factional survivor. Then, former President Ma Ying-jeou steps into your orbit. Ma grasps your hand warmly, his face glowing with relief. He knows that by defeating Tsai, you have retroactively salvaged his eight-year legacy. They surround you like stars orbiting the sun, showering you with praise. You shake their hands one by one, offering modest, perfectly calibrated replies, soaking in the absolute submission of the Kuomintang elite.

`; endText += `

The time for pleasantries concludes. Escorted by a phalanx of security and party elders, you step out onto the brightly lit stage on Bade Road. A roaring ocean of supporters stretches into the Taipei night, waving flags in a disciplined, euphoric frenzy. You approach the podium. You do not offer a speech of humble reconciliation; you are here to deliver a political execution.

`; endText += `

‘My fellow citizens, tonight the Republic of China has been rescued from the brink of the abyss!’ your voice booms across the concrete canyons, sharp, cold, and dripping with righteous vindication. ‘We did not just win an election today. The people of Taiwan have delivered a crushing, undeniable verdict against the arrogance, the corruption, and the relentless ideological warfare of the Democratic Progressive Party! They tried to divide us with fear! They tried to silence us with their state machinery! But today, the voters have loudly declared that they are sick of the economic stagnation and the manufactured hatred!’

`; endText += `

The crowd screams in fierce agreement. You adjust your glasses, your eyes locking onto the television cameras, speaking directly to the defeated administration. ‘This catastrophic defeat is entirely of their own making. The DPP’s profound arrogance blinded them to the suffering of the common people. Starting tomorrow, the Kuomintang will restore the dignity of this nation. We will rebuild the economy, we will restore peace across the strait, and we will clean up the rot left behind by this incompetent regime!’ The deafening roar of the crowd washes over you. You stand firmly at the center of the stage, the undisputed, calculated master of the Republic.

`; mainTitle = 'GRANDMASTER’S DESIGN'; endImage = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/wudunyi2.jpg?v=1782691899083'; subTitle = 'Ruthless mechanics crush internet rhetoric.'; s_name = 'Leave Earth Surface - Mayday (2007)'; s_cover = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/JUMP_THE_WORLD.JPG'; s_url = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/%E9%9B%A2%E9%96%8B%E5%9C%B0%E7%90%83%E8%A1%A8%E9%9D%A2%20-%20Mayday%20(youtube).mp3?v=1782689481956'; } else { endText += `

The heavy leather executive chair in the Chairman's office was not designed for sleeping, yet at three o'clock in the afternoon, barely an hour before the polling stations officially closed, the next President of the Republic of China was fast asleep. The grueling, punishing marathon of the eve-of-election mega-rallies had completely drained you. Your seventy-one-year-old bones ached, and your usually sharp, calculating mind was clouded with a profound, overwhelming exhaustion. You had ordered the junior staff out of the room. The air conditioning hummed a steady, freezing drone. In the corner, the television was left running on a prominent news channel. You rested your head against the leather, your eyes closed, listening to the shrill, chaotic debates of the political pundits filling the empty room.

`; endText += `

‘It is a bloodbath, a complete repudiation of the ruling party,’ a famous commentator sneered from the screen, his voice cutting through your half-sleep. ‘The DPP governed so atrociously, their arrogance so entirely out of touch with the grassroots, that the electorate is literally punishing them with a supermajority for the opposition. Think about the sheer absurdity of this moment! Tsai Ing-wen is about to be utterly crushed by Wu Den-yih. Wu Den-yih! The boring, gaffe-prone old man! The infamous White Dolphin, the so-called White Thief, the walking, talking relic of the deeply unpopular Ma Ying-jeou era! And he is going to win in a historic landslide! That tells you exactly how much the Taiwanese people currently despise the Democratic Progressive Party!’

`; endText += `

Hearing your most toxic, humiliating political nicknames broadcasted on national television would normally trigger a cold, vindictive rage. But sitting in the dim office, you merely let out a long, heavy yawn. You rubbed your tired eyes beneath your glasses. You could not even bring yourself to be angry at the insults, because the pundits were absolutely right. The DPP had dug their own grave with their progressive arrogance and economic failures. You did not need to inspire the nation; you just needed to be the vessel for their furious, collective punishment. The sheer inevitability of the outcome made the entire democratic process feel incredibly tedious. You adjusted your posture, leaned your head back against the chair, and let the droning voices of the television commentators lull you back into a deep, dreamless sleep.

`; endText += `

You are violently jolted awake hours later. The sky outside the floor-to-ceiling windows is pitch black, periodically illuminated by the explosive, blinding flashes of fireworks. The deafening, rhythmic crackle of firecrackers shakes the thick bulletproof glass of the headquarters. The heavy oak doors of your office are suddenly thrown wide open, and a tidal wave of noise, light, and people floods into the room. You blink rapidly, completely disoriented, instinctively reaching to straighten your slightly wrinkled suit jacket as the harsh glare of camera flashes hits your face.

`; endText += `

You are instantly surrounded by a suffocating mob of euphoria. Your wife, Tsai Ling-yi, is weeping openly, throwing her arms around you. Your running mate, ${currentMateName}, is shaking your hand with a manic, almost terrifying enthusiasm. Former President Ma Ying-jeou, Wang Jin-pyng, and the powerful local faction bosses are crowding the doorway, raising glasses of champagne, hailing you as the absolute savior of the party. You stand up, your joints stiff, mechanically returning the smiles and the handshakes, still slightly groggy from the nap. Through the sea of rejoicing elites, you catch a glimpse of the massive LED screen in the hallway. The final, terrifyingly dominant number is locked on the broadcast: ${FINAL_VOTE_PERCENT.toFixed(1)}%. A supermajority. The green camp has been wiped off the electoral map.

`; endText += `

But as the champagne flows and the confetti falls around your shoulders, the sleepy fog in your mind completely dissipates, replaced by a sudden, chilling clarity. You look at the overwhelming landslide on the screen, and a profound, icy sense of dread washes over you. You remember 2008. You remember when Ma Ying-jeou won a historic mandate just like this one, sweeping the executive and legislative branches. You remember how that absolute, unchecked power eventually bred absolute complacency, leading the party straight into the apocalyptic slaughters of the Sunflower Movement and the 2016 elections. The pendulum of Taiwanese politics is a ruthless, unforgiving meat grinder.

`; endText += `

The millions of voters celebrating on the streets outside are not cheering for you. They do not love Wu Den-yih. They are cheering for the brutal execution of the DPP. But tomorrow morning, when the hangover fades, this angry, highly volatile electorate will turn their gaze to you, demanding immediate economic miracles and flawless governance. You have won the absolute monopoly of the state, which means you have absolutely no one left to blame when things inevitably go wrong. The luxury of being the opposition is gone. As you raise your glass of Kaoliang liquor to the cheering crowd, plastering on your signature, calculating smile, you realize the horrific truth of your victory: the countdown to the next slaughter has already begun.

`; endImage = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/mawuxiao.jpg'; mainTitle = 'CURSE OF THE SUPERMAJORITY'; subTitle = 'An overwhelming mandate leaves no room for excuses.'; s_name = 'Eat What You See - Yoga Lin (2009)'; s_cover = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/eat.jpg'; s_url = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/%E7%9C%8B%E8%A6%8B%E4%BB%80%E9%BA%BC%E5%90%83%E4%BB%80%E9%BA%BC%20-%20Yoga%20Lin%20(youtube).mp3?v=1782743428259'; } } else if (Number(campaignTrail_temp.hongxiuzhu) === 1) { endText += `

‘Go back to Beijing, you communist traitor!’ a university student screamed, his face flushed red, waving a green progressive banner just inches from your face. It was two o'clock in the afternoon on election day. While the KMT elites hid nervously inside their air-conditioned headquarters, you were standing on a humid Taipei street corner, surrounded by a mob of furious, progressive youth. You did not flinch. As the ‘Little Pepper’, you looked the young man dead in the eye, your expression a mask of absolute, freezing disdain. ‘You think screaming slogans stops missiles?’ you replied, your voice slicing through the street noise like a scalpel. ‘You enjoy the peace and prosperity my generation built with our blood, while you try to burn the house down with American slogans. When the war starts, your internet memes will not save you.’

`; endText += `

The student opened his mouth to shout again, but your running mate, ${currentMateName}, stepped seamlessly between you, gently touching your arm. ‘Chairwoman,’ ${currentMateName} whispered, leaning in close so the hostile crowd could not hear. ‘The final blackout tracking polls just came in from the campaign managers. Taichung is flipping. The northern suburbs are turning out in droves. They are swinging to us.’ You glanced back at the screaming youths, a cold, calculating realization settling in your chest. Perhaps this so-called ‘Natural Independence’ generation was just a loud, manufactured echo chamber. Perhaps the silent majority was not as easily brainwashed by fear as the media claimed.

`; endText += `

You returned to the VIP war room of the central headquarters. The contrast was jarring. Outside, the streets were alive with ideological warfare; inside, the establishment elites—men like Wu Den-yih and the local faction bosses—were sitting in terrified, agonizing silence, sweating through their tailored suits. You poured yourself a cup of hot tea, offering them a serene, almost eerie smile. ‘Why the long faces, gentlemen?’ you asked, taking a slow sip. ‘The people are voting on the ultimate destiny of the Republic of China today. If they choose the illusion of independence, we die with dignity. But if they choose the truth... we make history. I accept whatever verdict the heavens deliver.’ They stared at you, unnerved by your absolute, terrifying calm. This was not a mere election to you; it was a holy referendum.

`; endText += `

At four o'clock, the agonizing tally began. As expected, Tsai Ing-wen took a fierce, commanding early lead. The deep-green southern fortresses bled red on the screens. The room grew dead silent. But then, as the sun set, the geography of the vote violently shifted. The urban electorate in the north and the pragmatic middle class in the center were not turning green; they were swinging directly to your column. You watched the blue line surge upward. Could it be true? Did the endless months of DPP media smearing, the electoral dirty tricks, and the terrifying shadow of the Hong Kong riots truly fail? You remained deeply skeptical of the establishment's sudden, hyperventilating cheers, but the cruel mathematics of democracy did not lie.

`; endText += `

By eight o'clock, the impossible became an undeniable reality. The final tally locked in at ${FINAL_VOTE_PERCENT.toFixed(1)}%. You had officially overthrown Tsai Ing-wen. On the main television screen, Tsai stepped up to her podium, her face pale and exhausted, to deliver a bitter concession speech. The war room erupted into fanatical, tearful cheers. A few minutes later, your secure phone rang. You picked it up.

`; endText += `

‘Chairwoman Hung,’ Tsai Ing-wen’s voice came through the speaker, stripped of its usual bureaucratic arrogance, sounding incredibly hollow yet sharply composed. ‘The people have made their choice. I am calling to congratulate you. Despite our bitter ideological differences, this election was an unprecedented duel between two women... it marks a definitive step forward for Taiwan’s democracy.’ Tsai paused, her tone hardening into a chilling, genuine warning. ‘But I beg you, Chairwoman. Lead this country safely. Do not drag Taiwan down a dark, irreversible path toward Beijing.’

`; endText += `

You listened with cold detachment, a ruthless smirk forming on your lips. ‘Save your lectures for your memoirs, President Tsai,’ you replied sharply. ‘You poisoned the roots of this island with your independence lies and cultural destruction. I am simply administering the antidote. The Republic of China is returning to the right path.’ You hung up the phone without waiting for her response. The time for polite, centrist compromise was permanently dead.

`; endText += `

You stepped out onto the brightly lit balcony on Bade Road. The crowd below was a massive, weeping ocean of deep-blue veterans, ideological purists, and loyalists waving the Republic of China flag. They screamed your name with the fanatical devotion of a people who believed their stolen nation had just been resurrected. You grabbed the microphone, your voice echoing with uncompromising, historical authority. ‘We will end the decades of hostility!’ you roared to the masses. ‘We will tear up their toxic textbooks! We will sit down with Beijing, face-to-face, and negotiate a permanent peace for the Chinese nation!’

`; endText += `

The old soldiers wept, falling to their knees in religious ecstasy as your blueprint for unification echoed across the capital. But the camera of history pans away from the blinding lights of the balcony, drifting into the dark, labyrinthine alleys just a few blocks away. There, illuminated by the flickering orange glow of a small fire, a group of bitter, furious progressive youth were silently burning the Kuomintang flag alongside the flag of the People's Republic of China. Their faces were twisted not in terror, but in a simmering, irreconcilable resentment. You had won the ultimate ideological victory, but as the flames reflected in the dark Taipei night, a chilling reality set in: you were inheriting a profoundly fractured island, where the embers of today's political earthquake could very well ignite a silent, unforgiving social cold war.

`; endImage = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/hongzhuxi.webp'; mainTitle = 'CRUSADER AWAKENING'; subTitle = 'The soul of the Republic is purified, but the island divides.'; s_name = 'Speak Straight - A-Mei (2011)'; s_cover = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/amei.jpg'; s_url = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/%E9%96%8B%E9%96%80%E8%A6%8B%E5%B1%B1%20-%20aMEI%20(youtube).mp3?v=1782746767311'; } // ====================================================================== // 终极拼接与渲染 (2020年代 Apple / 现代 UI 极简风格版) // ====================================================================== let endingHTML = `

When Ma Ying-jeou pushed open the door to his home, the sensor light in the entryway failed to turn on.

`; endText += `

He stood instinctively in the dark for two seconds, waiting for that familiar click. Dead silence. Only then did he remember that last month Chow Mei-ching had hired someone to replace the entire lighting control system; the new system only recognized her phone’s Bluetooth. His had been removed from the paired device list. It wasn’t out of spite; it was simply because he had barely come home during those months. Even while in Taipei, he had slept on a folding cot in the campaign office, pillowed on leftover bento boxes from fundraising dinners, waking up with the taste of cold star anise from braised meats in his mouth.

`; endText += `

He kicked off his leather shoes without bending over to straighten them. As his feet touched the floor, the big toe of his left foot pressed against something through his sock—a dried cherry tomato, hard as a plastic bead, likely rolled out from his daughter's fruit bowl. He didn't pick it up, walking straight into the living room.

`; endText += `

Chow Mei-ching sat at the dining table with an iPad spread out before her, the screen paused on a YouTube replay of a political talk show. Hearing his footsteps, she didn't look up, merely using her finger to slide the screen brightness down to the lowest setting, like closing a half-read book.

`; endText += `

“Don't eat that,” she said.

`; endText += `

Ma’s hand was already resting on the lid of a box of mung bean pastries. It had been thrust upon his bodyguard this morning by a party committee chairman from Yunlin, who then shoved it into the back seat of his car with a single sentence: “The chairman said we ate these exact pastries during the magistrate election, and we won.” He hadn't replied at the time. Now, looking at the box, he suddenly felt that the red printed characters on the surface—“Traditional Handmade” and “Local Sentiment”—were mocking him.

`; endText += `

“Why can’t I eat it?” He lifted the lid, and the aroma of flaky pastry wafted out, making his stomach churn with acid instead.

`; endText += `

“You’ll get acid reflux if you eat it. Every time you get acid reflux, you wake up in the middle of the night to rummage through the fridge for soda crackers, making the kitchen look like it was ransacked by a burglar. Then tomorrow morning your face swells up like a giant dumpling, the reporters catch you on camera again, and the headline reads: ‘Ma Ying-jeou Binge-Eats After Defeat.’ Do you think I don't have enough troubles?”

`; endText += `

Ma closed the lid, his knuckles tapping lightly against the edge of the cardboard box. “I’ve already lost anyway. Gaining a little weight won't make me lose more.”

`; endText += `

Chow Mei-ching finally raised her head, taking off her reading glasses and setting them on the iPad, her movements deliberate like defusing a bomb timer. “Just tell me,” her voice wasn't loud, yet held the calm of a surgeon before the first incision, “why did you have to wade into this muddy water?”

`; endText += `

Ma looked at her and opened his mouth. The pendulum clock in the living room clicked through a second, yet he made no sound.

`; endText += `

“Wu Den-yih came to find you, and you just nodded? Or did you see a few meme images of your handshake online and think people actually missed you?” Chow Mei-ching pushed the iPad aside, leaning forward with her elbows on the table. “Could Eric Chu not go? Could Terry Gou not go? You’ve been retired for four years after serving eight years as president—what position haven't you held? Why did you have to collide head-on with an incumbent president who just suffered a crushing defeat in the local elections and even resigned as party chair?”

`; endText += `

Ma wanted to reply “that’s different,” but the words dissolved on the tip of his tongue before he could convince even himself. How it was different, he couldn't quite articulate. In the beginning, Wu Den-yih had indeed brought polling data, claiming only Ma could hold the northern base. Later, several old aides toasted him repeatedly at dinner tables, reminiscing about the days at the Zhongxing Residence. Eventually, he began believing it himself—that perhaps there really was a segment of voters waiting for him to return and set things right. That box of mung bean pastries was the physical manifestation of that illusion: thinking that the goodwill of local faction bosses was still spread thick across the table, only to lift the lid and find nothing but crumbled pastry crust.

`; endText += `

He sat down, the chair letting out a long creak. “This time the running mate was ${currentMateName}. We originally thought—”

`; endText += `

“Don't shift the blame to ${currentMateName},” Chow Mei-ching cut him off immediately, her tone like severing a redundant suture thread. “He ran across Taiwan with you and wore out several pairs of shoes. You were the one who wanted to run, not him.”

`; endText += `

Ma didn't argue further. He looked at the box of pastries on the table, suddenly remembering three or four years ago, shortly after he had stepped down, when Chow Mei-ching pulled him to Yongkang Street for mango shaved ice. Back then, passersby still asked for photos, but the flashbulbs had thinned significantly. She had said then: “Finally, we can relax a bit.” He remembered her expression—a genuine sigh of relief, like a string pulled taut for eight years suddenly untied from both ends. But today, the flashbulbs had returned. On the stage of campaign headquarters on election night, standing beside ${currentMateName} in front of sparse flags, the flashbulbs still popped incessantly, stinging his eyes. Those camera lenses weren't there to record his victory; they were there to document his downfall. The media never cared about the person—they cared about the drop.

`; endText += `

“I thought after this election, there’d be fewer reporters,” Chow Mei-ching said, turning her gaze toward the living room’s floor-to-ceiling window. The curtains weren't fully drawn, and red taillights flickered faintly on the driveway outside. “Turns out yesterday a paparazzi was hiding on the second floor of the convenience store across the street. You lost, and they’re even more thrilled, because a story about defeat sells far better than a story about a winner.”

`; endText += `

Ma suddenly laughed, a sound like a broken whistle. “Well, now you can relax. Nobody pays attention to a loser. In two weeks, they won't even spell my name right.”

`; endText += `

Chow Mei-ching stared at him for a few seconds, her lip twitching, unable to hold back a faint, helpless smile. “You really know how to find humor in misery.”

`; endText += `

“Otherwise what am I supposed to do? Sit here hugging your iPad watching political talk shows, listening to them analyze where I went wrong?” He leaned back against the chair, the chair legs scraping harshly against the terrazzo floor. “I don't even need to watch. Section one will be about my vague campaign narrative, section two about my small-circle decision-making, section three will invite some anonymous ‘party insider’ to declare that I lost touch with public opinion. And during the commercial break, they’ll run the public service ad I endorsed years ago. Truly ironic.”

`; endText += `

Chow Mei-ching tucked her reading glasses into their case with gentle movements. She wanted to say something, swallowed it back, and finally uttered a single sentence: “Do you want to go for a walk in the park tomorrow? I’ll accompany you.”

`; endText += `

Ma froze. The turn caught him more off-guard than any political headline. He had expected a far longer barrage of lectures—bringing up how his insistence on not interfering with the judiciary had angered certain factions, bringing up those nameless young legislators who called him an “old blue man” behind his back, bringing up that rainy day before the election when he knelt to pray at a temple entrance, the sharp snap in his knees still aching subtly now. Instead, she merely asked if he wanted to walk in the park.

`; endText += `

“Are you sure?” he asked. “Reporters might be camping out at the entrance of Daan Forest Park.”

`; endText += `

“Then we’ll go to a different park. The NTU Farm has a few newly paved trails, and the sweetgum trees are lovely. Nobody will recognize us.” Chow Mei-ching stood up, tucked the iPad under her arm, picked up the box of mung bean pastries, and walked into the kitchen.

`; endText += `

Ma heard her open the refrigerator and set the pastries inside. The low hum of the compressor as the fridge door sealed shut sounded unnaturally crisp in the quiet house.

`; endText += `

He stood up and walked to the large bookshelf in the living room. The shelves were packed with picture frames from over the years: receiving foreign dignitaries as president, employees lining the hallway to bid him farewell on his final day in office, participating in road races wearing short shorts. In every photo, he smiled conscientiously—a conscientiousness practiced countless times: how many degrees to curve the lips, how much to squint the eyes, all measured precisely. Now, looking at those photos, he felt his reflection in the glass was far more real: swollen eyelids, a loose collar, the line of his jaw sagging into a blurred curve.

`; endText += `

He unlocked his phone; the campaign group chat had fallen dead silent. The last message was sent by ${currentMateName}: “Thank you everyone, there is a long road ahead.” Only three people had liked it. He flipped his phone face down onto the bookshelf.

`; endText += `

The night sky outside was as thick as unbrewed black coffee. The upscale residential area of Daan District was overly quiet, with rarely even a dog bark. A number suddenly surfaced in his mind—not legislative seats, not vote margins in various cities, but his own final vote percentage. That figure hung on the massive screen at the counting center, a red bar shrunk to a tiny stub, like a clipped fingernail. Its exact value was ${FINAL_VOTE_PERCENT.toFixed(1)}%.

`; endText += `

He had stood by the second-floor window at campaign headquarters, watching that number cross the integer threshold as young volunteers beside him began to sob. He hadn't cried; he only felt several fingernail marks dug into his left palm. Standing before his bookshelf now, he looked down at his hand; the marks had faded, leaving only faint red traces.

`; endText += `

Chow Mei-ching emerged from the kitchen holding a mug. Printed on the mug was “Love My Taiwan,” a souvenir produced for a Double Tenth National Day years ago, from which he had drunk countless cups of hot cocoa. She placed the mug into his hands. He looked down—it wasn't cocoa inside, but warm water with a slice of lemon floating on top.

`; endText += `

“There was half a lemon left in the fridge. It would dry out if we didn't use it.” With that, she turned and walked upstairs, leaving him alone in the living room.

`; endText += `

Ma gripped the mug and sat on the sofa. He didn't turn on the television, merely gazing at the ceiling. There was a faint crack running from the base of the crystal chandelier toward the crown molding in the corner. It had been there when they moved into the house years ago. Back when he had just stepped down, he felt the crack represented an imperfection and seriously considered hiring a contractor to repair it. Later, busy with various foundation affairs and daily speaking invitations, the crack was forgotten. Now he realized the crack remained the same crack—it hadn't grown longer, nor shorter. They had lived in the house for nearly four years; everything had changed, except for it.

`; endText += `

He recalled a Zen koan he had read many years ago: an old monk pointed to a crack in the ceiling and asked his disciple what he saw. The disciple said he saw an imperfection; the old monk said he saw the sky. Back then he thought the koan was deep, but tonight he felt that old monk probably lived in an illegal rooftop extension to see the sky through a crack. Their building had another floor above them; through the crack, one could only see rebar and concrete dust.

`; endText += `

He finished the warm water, the slightly bitter tang of lemon skin clinging to the root of his tongue. Then he switched off the living room light and navigated the dark stairs. His feet stepped onto the wooden treads, every step letting out a low creak. The master bedroom door was ajar, letting out a sliver of yellow light. He pushed the door open to find Chow Mei-ching lying on her side, her back turned to him.

`; endText += `

He took off his jacket and trousers, lying down on the other side of the bed, facing the ceiling. The ceiling in this bedroom was smooth and flawless, without a single crack. Looking at that blank space, he suddenly laughed—a very soft chuckle, careful not to wake the person beside him. It wasn't bitter, nor self-deprecating; it was simply genuine amusement. Amused at himself for remembering a crack for so many years, believing it would become a metaphor—when in truth, it was merely an old house, having nothing to do with politics, nothing to do with the era, and nothing to do with whether he won or lost.

`; endText += `

Tomorrow, if it didn't rain, he would go with Chow Mei-ching to the NTU Farm to walk that new trail. The sweetgum leaves should be turning red. On the way, maybe a passerby or two would recognize them, maybe someone would take a sneaky photo, or maybe nobody would pay attention at all.

`; endText += `

So what.

`; endText += `

He closed his eyes. The white of the ceiling still shone through his eyelids. That patch of white had no cracks and no sky, merely hovering steadily above his head like a thin, light cocoon finally unbinding itself.

`; s_name = 'Proud Whale - Accusefive (2019)'; s_cover = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/zhuanji.jpg'; s_url = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/%E9%A9%95%E5%82%B2%E7%9A%84%E9%AF%A8%E9%AD%9A%20-%20%E5%91%8A%E4%BA%94%E4%BA%BA%20(youtube).mp3'; endImage = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/majiongaichi.jpg'; mainTitle = 'LIGHT COCOON UNBINDING'; subTitle = 'An unprecedented comeback ends in quiet reflection behind closed doors.'; } } // ====================================================================== // 1. 韩国瑜 (Han Kuo-yu) 败选分支 // ====================================================================== if (Number(campaignTrail_temp.hanguoyu) === 1) { if (pct < 40.0) { endText += `

The air inside your private holding room at the Kuomintang headquarters is stale, reeking of cold coffee and impending doom. You sit alone on the leather sofa, staring blankly at the muted television screen. Beside you, Lee Chia-fen sits in paralyzing silence. Her hands tremble slightly as she clutches a crumpled tissue, her eyes hollow and completely drained by the vicious, year-long media slaughterhouse that has torn your family apart. Standing awkwardly near the door, keeping a noticeable physical distance, is your running mate, ${currentMateName}. The person who eagerly joined your ticket, expecting to ride a populist rocket to the pinnacle of power, now constantly checks their phone with a grim, pale face, silently calculating how to salvage their own political career from this catastrophic, sinking submarine.

`; endText += `

For months, you orchestrated the most audacious psychological illusion in Taiwanese political history. When the scientific polls showed you bleeding out by double digits, you did not pivot; you doubled down. You stood on brightly lit stages and roared to the masses that ‘he who wins the polls gets hemorrhoids.’ You ordered an unprecedented ‘polling blackout,’ instructing your fanatical followers to deliberately lie to pollsters and shout ‘Only support Tsai Ing-wen!’ It was a brilliant, desperate mechanism of self-preservation. You convinced millions of people that the cold, hard data was fake, and that the suffocating, shoulder-to-shoulder sea of red-and-blue flags at your rallies was the only truth that mattered. You built an impenetrable, massive echo chamber. But sitting in this quiet room, looking at the silent despair of your wife and the evasive eyes of your running mate, you know the brutal reality: the bubble is about to burst.

`; endText += `

At four o'clock, the heavy steel doors of the polling stations close, and the illusion shatters violently on live television. The counting process is not a race; it is a methodical, unmerciful execution. Tsai Ing-wen is not just winning; she is mathematically dismantling you. The green line on the screen surges past six million, then seven million, climbing relentlessly toward a historic, unprecedented record of over eight million votes. The sheer numerical brutality of it takes the breath out of the room. You are witnessing the creation of a towering democratic monument, and you realize with sickening clarity that you are nothing but the bloody stepping stone beneath it. The progressive youth, the educated middle class, the moderate swing voters—they did not attend your massive street rallies. They stayed home, watched your populist circus with growing horror, and then quietly, ruthlessly marched to the ballot boxes to annihilate your campaign.

`; endText += `

Downstairs on Bade Road, the scene is a grotesque, heartbreaking tragedy. The impenetrable ocean of red-and-blue flags has collapsed into a desolate graveyard of crushed hopes. Elderly women—the fiercely loyal aunties wrapped in Republic of China flag jackets—are collapsing onto the wet asphalt, weeping uncontrollably, their makeup running down their faces in dark streaks. Hardened, working-class uncles who followed your campaign bus across the island are sitting on the curbs, staring into the void, letting their massive banners drag through the mud. The triumphant blasts of air horns have been replaced by a collective, suffocating wail. Almost immediately, desperate, angry whispers ignite through the grieving crowd. ‘Election fraud.’ ‘They rigged the computer systems in the central election commission.’ ‘They stuffed the ballot boxes.’ It is a pathetic, desperate coping mechanism—a phantom conspiracy of stolen elections that has never been proven since the year 2000. But tonight, this baseless rumor is the only psychological shield these broken, deceived believers have left to protect themselves from the unbearable truth.

`; endText += `

The era of raw, unchecked populism is officially dead. You put on your signature windbreaker, give Lee Chia-fen’s hand one last, heavy squeeze, plaster a forced, dignified smile onto your face, and step out onto the stage to face the music. You deliver your concession speech, urging your weeping supporters to respect the democratic process. But as the microphone cuts out and you wave to the desolate crowd, your mind is already consumed by a far darker, more terrifying reality. The election is over, but your punishment has only just begun. You have to go back to Kaohsiung. You know the people of the south will never, ever forgive the ‘runaway mayor’ who abandoned them for the presidential palace after a mere six months in office. The Democratic Progressive Party, now completely politically invincible, will show absolutely no mercy. The recall petitions are already being printed. The political guillotine is waiting for you down south. The Han Wave did not just crash tonight; it drowned you.

`; mainTitle = 'BURSTING OF THE BUBBLE'; subTitle = 'The populist illusion shatters against a historic green wall.'; s_name = 'God Bless Taiwan - The Chairman (2010)'; s_cover = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/taiwan.jpg?v=1782754641848'; s_url = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/%E7%9C%BE%E7%A5%9E%E8%AD%B7%E5%8F%B0%E7%81%A3%20God%20Bless%20Taiwan%EF%BD%9C%E8%91%A3%E4%BA%8B%E9%95%B7%E6%A8%82%E5%9C%98%EF%BD%9C%E3%80%90%20The%20Chairman%20Official%20Music%20Video%20%E3%80%91%20-%20%E8%91%A3%E4%BA%8B%E9%95%B7%E6%A8%82%E5%9C%98%20The%20Chairman%20Band%20(youtube).mp3?v=1782754592084'; endImage = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/hankuoyu.jpg?v=1782754688574'; } else { endText += `

You stand quietly by the tinted glass window of the Kuomintang central headquarters, looking down at Bade Road. The scene below is staggering. A terrifying, endless sea of red-and-blue flags undulates under the streetlights, accompanied by the deafening, rhythmic blasts of plastic air horns. The sheer volume of human bodies, the visceral, fanatical energy radiating from the asphalt—it feels exactly like the electric, miraculous eve of your 2018 Kaohsiung mayoral victory. Your running mate, ${currentMateName}, steps up beside you, handing you a tablet with the final blackout polling data. You are trailing. But it is not a blowout; the gap hovers agonizingly on the razor edge of the statistical margin of error. Deep down, the pragmatic political survivor in you knows the math is grim. But looking at the roaring masses below, a desperate, defiant hope flickers in your chest. What if the pollsters are wrong just this once? What if this overwhelming, unprecedented grassroots mobilization simply shatters their sterile data models?

`; endText += `

At four o'clock, the heavy steel doors of the polling stations close, and the agonizing reality begins to unfold on the massive LED screens. This is not a sudden, catastrophic collapse; it is a slow, suffocating political asphyxiation. It feels like a cruel, reversed mirror image of the 2012 presidential election—only this time, you are the one watching the incumbent slowly, methodically grind out a narrow, insurmountable lead. The blue line and the green line twist together in a tense, decimal-by-decimal trench war, but Tsai Ing-wen remains persistently, frustratingly out of reach. The passion on the streets did not magically generate new votes; it merely created a deafening echo chamber. The working-class fury was potent, but the silent, cautious middle class—terrified by your unpredictable populism and the geopolitical shadow of Hong Kong—formed a quiet, impenetrable wall against your campaign.

`; endText += `

As the night deepens, the inevitable verdict crystallizes on the screen. You lost. Downstairs, the triumphant roars slowly devolve into a stunned, weeping silence. The religious fanaticism of the crowd curdles into bitter, helpless rage. Hardened military veterans and loyal aunties are sobbing openly into their Republic of China flags, unable to comprehend how their undeniable momentum was defeated by invisible ballots. In their desperation, they search frantically for a scapegoat to rationalize the death of their miracle. Curses ring out in the humid air. Some fiercely denounce James Soong, bitterly blaming the eternal spoiler who they believe has been robbing the Kuomintang of its rightful, razor-thin margins since the year 2000. Others violently accuse the DPP of utilizing dark, unseen electoral tricks, whispering the same exhausted, unproven rumors of rigged voting computers and stuffed ballot boxes that surface after every agonizing defeat. But standing in the quiet VIP room, you know the cold, unromantic truth: you simply did not have the numbers.

`; endText += `

The grand, chaotic theater of the Han Wave has reached its final curtain call. The populist dream has shattered against the cold realities of presidential demographics. You cannot play the role of the invincible outsider anymore; the show simply cannot go on. You turn away from the window, buttoning your trademark windbreaker, and prepare to face the cameras. Despite the raging grief of your supporters, you know you must maintain the final, crucial shred of political dignity. You will walk out onto that stage, urge your heartbroken followers to accept the democratic verdict, and call for national unity in the face of defeat.

`; endText += `

But as you mentally rehearse the concession speech, a much darker, immediate crisis looms over you. You lost the presidency, but the punishment is not over. You have to return to the deep south. The people of Kaohsiung are waiting, and they are not in a forgiving mood. The recall petitions are already piling up, fueled by a deeply vengeful progressive machine that will not rest until the 'runaway mayor' is completely stripped of power and utterly humiliated. The national stage is lost; tomorrow morning, you must return to the municipal trenches and brace for a brutal, bloody battle just to survive the political winter.

`; mainTitle = 'A DIVIDED NATION'; subTitle = 'The grassroots weep as the establishment burns.'; s_name = 'Long Night Train - Fire EX. (2017)'; s_cover = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/miehuoqi.jpg'; s_url = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/%E6%BB%85%E7%81%AB%E5%99%A8%20Fire%20EX.%20-%20%E9%95%B7%E9%80%94%E5%A4%9C%E8%BB%8A%20Southbound%20Night%20Bus%20Lyric%20Video%20-%20%E6%BB%85%E7%81%AB%E5%99%A8%20Fire%20EX.%20(youtube).mp3?v=1782755281390'; endImage = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/hanguoyubaixuan2.jpg'; } } // ====================================================================== // 2. 朱立伦 (Eric Chu) 败选分支 // ====================================================================== else if (Number(campaignTrail_temp.zhulilun) === 1) { if (pct < 40.0) { endText += `

The air inside your private VIP suite at the campaign headquarters feels as heavy and cold as a tomb. The late afternoon sun struggles to pierce through the gray, overcast Taipei sky, casting long, fading shadows across the room. You sit perfectly still, staring down at the final internal blackout polling data handed to you just moments ago by Chairman Wu Den-yih. The numbers printed on the crisp white paper are an absolute, undeniable bloodbath. Less than forty percent. It is a grotesque, agonizing echo of your catastrophic 2016 campaign. The moderate, technocratic middle path you banked your entire political resurrection on has been utterly rejected by the electorate.

`; endText += `

You look up, your eyes locking onto the Chairman standing across the coffee table. The polished, unoffensive mask you have worn for years finally slips, revealing a cold, exhausted bitterness. ‘Why didn't you run in 2016, Chairman?’ you ask, your voice dropping to a chilling, razor-sharp murmur. ‘Why did you hide in the shadows and let me walk alone into that slaughterhouse?’ Wu Den-yih pauses. A slow, sinister, and entirely evasive smile creeps across his aged, calculating face. He offers a meaningless, philosophical platitude about party duty and the unpredictable tides of history, smoothly and shamelessly dodging the question. You stare at him with absolute contempt. He knew 2016 was a suicide mission, and he gladly let you take the bullet. Now, through his machinations, he has let you take it twice.

`; endText += `

You turn your gaze back to the window, watching the distant skyline of New Taipei—the city you once governed with such pride for eight years—fade into the encroaching dusk. You know exactly what these abysmal numbers mean. Your political life is effectively terminated. The Kuomintang, a party obsessed with vengeance and winning, will never, ever nominate a man who led them to two consecutive, historic presidential annihilations. 2024 is a permanently closed door. You are a walking political corpse.

`; endText += `

There is no need to sit through the agonizing theatricality of the television broadcasts. You do not need to watch the green line surge past yours on the LED screens, or listen to the pro-green pundits mock your failure. You already know exactly how this script ends. You stand up, buttoning your suit jacket with mechanical, robotic precision. You call for your wife, Kao Wan-chien, whose eyes are red but dry, and your running mate, ${currentMateName}, who looks completely shell-shocked by the scale of the impending disaster. They follow you out of the suite in a solemn, funereal silence.

`; endText += `

You do not wait for the news networks to officially call the race. You walk straight out to the election night rally stage set up on Bade Road. The atmosphere is not one of fiery outrage or weeping despair; it is just devastatingly empty. You step up to the microphone, adjusting your glasses, and deliver the exact same, hollow concession speech you were forced to give four years ago. You utter the exhausted, polite clichés, congratulating Tsai Ing-wen on securing her reelection, and calling for national unity in the face of a divided society. But as you look out into the dark square, the bitterest reality of all sets in. The few remaining supporters are not crying. They are quietly rolling up their banners and walking toward the subway station. The journalists are already packing up their tripods. Nobody is truly listening anymore. The era of Eric Chu ends not with a dramatic explosion, but with a profound, deafening apathy.

`; mainTitle = 'HISTORY REPEATS ITSELF'; subTitle = 'The technocrat falls into the exact same abyss.'; s_name = 'Blank Space - Tanya Chua (2008)'; s_cover = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/konbgbaige.jpg'; s_url = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/%E7%A9%BA%E7%99%BD%E6%A0%BC%20-%20Tanya%20Chua%20(youtube).mp3?v=1782758061264'; endImage = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/zhushibai1.jpg?v=1782760870094'; } else { endText += `

The war room feels less like a political campaign headquarters and more like an exhausted accounting firm. You sit alone at the head of the conference table, your eyes darting across endless rows of cross-tabs, demographic breakdowns, and margin-of-error calculations. A single, highly optimistic pro-blue tracking poll shows you leading Tsai Ing-wen by exactly one percentage point. The remaining dozen independent surveys, however, paint a grim picture of a persistent green advantage. As the consummate actuary of the Kuomintang, you obsessively run the numbers, searching desperately for a mathematical pathway to victory. You calculate the tipping points in Taichung, the required turnout thresholds in the Hakka belt, and the exact number of swing voters needed in the northern suburbs. You believe that if the machinery works perfectly, the equation can still be solved.

`; endText += `

But as the late afternoon sun casts long, melancholic shadows across the polished mahogany desk, a cold, clinical realization settles in your chest. You can calculate sample sizes and standard deviations, but you cannot quantify the human heart. The Taiwanese electorate is simply exhausted. They are deeply tired of the Kuomintang's endless, archaic infighting, its suffocating conservatism, and its arrogant entitlement. You presented yourself as the rational, reformist face of the establishment, offering a polite, moderate alternative to the chaotic populism of the extremes. Yet, this polished mask was not enough to disguise the rotting, decaying structure of the century-old party beneath it. The voters do not necessarily love the DPP, but they have fundamentally lost faith in the KMT's ability to genuinely evolve.

`; endText += `

The heavy wooden door clicks open. Your wife, Kao Wan-chien, steps quietly into the room, holding a cup of hot, fragrant oolong tea. She sees the rigid tension in your shoulders, the defeated slump of your posture, and softly asks what is wrong. You take the porcelain cup from her hands, the warmth seeping into your cold palms. You take a slow, deliberate sip, letting the bitter, earthy taste wash over your tongue. You do not show her the spreadsheets. You simply look at her with a quiet, devastating resignation. 'You are going to have to walk out there and concede with me again,' you say, your voice perfectly flat, entirely devoid of any remaining illusions. 'Oh. And tell the Vice President to get ready.'

`; endText += `

You step out onto the brightly lit stage on Bade Road, flanked by your wife and ${currentMateName}. The night air is thick and heavy. You do not wait for the final, agonizing decimal points to be tallied on the news networks. You adjust your glasses, looking out at the subdued crowd, and deliver the inevitable. You apologize for letting them down, announce that you will shortly call President Tsai Ing-wen to congratulate her on her reelection, and formally admit defeat. There are no wailing cries of despair, no angry riots, no fanatical tears. The audience responds with a dead, suffocating silence. The people standing in the dark square look back at you with profound apathy. They know that tomorrow morning, they will still have to clock into their jobs, pay their rent, and navigate their ordinary, grueling lives. Tsai Ing-wen won, but the harsh, unromantic truth is that an Eric Chu presidency was never going to fundamentally change their reality anyway. It is the quietest, most tragically ordinary death a political campaign can suffer.

`; mainTitle = 'LIMITS OF MORTAL'; subTitle = 'Pragmatism fails to overcome the green tide.'; s_name = 'King of Comedy - Li Ronghao (2014)'; s_cover = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/lironghai.jpg'; s_url = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/%E3%80%8A%E5%96%9C%E5%89%A7%E4%B9%8B%E7%8E%8B%E3%80%8B%E6%9D%8E%E8%8D%A3%E6%B5%A9-%20Lyrics%20%E6%AD%8C%E8%AF%8D%E7%89%88%20-%20Lyrics%20Channel%20%E5%92%8C%E4%BD%A0%E4%B8%80%E8%B5%B7%E5%90%AC%E9%9F%B3%E4%B9%90%20(youtube).mp3?v=1782760684748'; endImage = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/2016.webp?v=1782760853033'; } } // ====================================================================== // 3. 郭台铭 (Terry Gou) 败选分支 // ====================================================================== else if (Number(campaignTrail_temp.guotaiming) === 1) { if (pct < 40.0) { endText += `

The sprawling, ultra-luxury penthouse office of your campaign headquarters sits high above the suffocating smog of Taipei, encased in thick, soundproof glass. It is a fortress suspended in the sky, designed to isolate the apex predator from the noise of the streets below. The time is four-thirty in the afternoon. The ballot boxes have only just been sealed, but the verdict has already been ruthlessly delivered to your mahogany desk. You stand alone by the floor-to-ceiling window, your hands resting on the cold glass, staring blankly out at the gray, overcast horizon. The towering silhouette of Taipei 101 pierces the clouds in the distance, a monument to capital and ambition, yet today, it looks like a giant, mocking needle pointing straight at your monumental failure. You are completely, utterly alone. You had specifically ordered the campaign managers, the data analysts, and even your closest family members out of the suite. You needed the absolute, freezing silence to process the apocalyptic reality unfolding on the papers scattered across your desk. Less than forty percent. You are trailing Tsai Ing-wen by at least ten, perhaps twelve percentage points. It is not just a defeat; it is a mathematical massacre. It is a public, historical execution of your ego.

`; endText += `

You are a man who does not understand the concept of losing. For forty years, you have built a transnational manufacturing empire from the mud and sweat of assembly lines. You idolized Genghis Khan. You viewed yourself as the modern incarnation of the great conqueror, sweeping across the globe, bending supply chains, foreign presidents, and local economies to your absolute will. When you set your sights on the Presidential Office, you approached it like just another hostile corporate takeover. You believed that capital was the ultimate weapon, that the electorate was merely a board of shareholders waiting to be bought off with the promise of soaring dividends. But looking at the cold, hard numbers bleeding across the page, a sickening, unfamiliar sensation begins to violently churn in your stomach. You do not know what went wrong. You physically cannot comprehend how a nation of wage-earners would reject the most successful CEO in their history in favor of a career academic.

`; endText += `

Your eyes drift to a glossy, leather-bound folder resting on the edge of the desk. It is the final internal tracking poll, handed to you just yesterday by the highly paid, so-called ‘elite’ political consultants you hired. The cover sheet boldly, confidently declared that the gap had narrowed to a mere four or five points, well within the margin of a silent majority upset. You stare at that folder, and a low, guttural, agonizing sound escapes your throat. It is a laugh. A dry, hideous, self-deprecating laugh that echoes off the expensive walls. You, the legendary Terry Gou, the man who ruthless negotiated Apple’s supply margins down to the cent, had been played for an absolute fool. You had poured billions—literally billions of your personal, hard-earned fortune—into this campaign. You bought the billboards, you bought the prime-time advertisements, you flooded the local factions with endless campaign subsidies. And what did it buy you? Nothing. Absolutely nothing. Your subordinates, the sycophantic political mercenaries, had simply treated you as a fat, bottomless ATM. They fed you fabricated, sugar-coated data to keep the cash flowing, smiling to your face while knowing you were driving a gold-plated train straight off a cliff. You feel incredibly stupid. The sheer, overwhelming embarrassment of being scammed by third-rate political hacks burns your chest like swallowing battery acid.

`; endText += `

The laughter dies, replaced by a pure, suffocating, blinding rage. If you are a god of business, then someone else must be responsible for this desecration. Your mind instantly violently pivots, searching for a target, and it locks onto the only logical culprit. The Kuomintang. That rotting, parasitic, decaying zombie of a political party. It was their fault. You bought their debt, you bailed out their frozen bank accounts, you draped their century-old, moth-eaten flag over your shoulders, and their toxic, completely unsalvageable brand dragged you straight into the abyss. The voters did not reject Terry Gou; they rejected the Kuomintang, and you were collateral damage in their historical execution. You think of Chairman Wu Den-yih, sitting in his office a few miles away, likely calculating how to survive the fallout. The sheer hatred you feel for Wu in this moment is almost physical. He is a scavenger. The KMT’s victory in 2018 was not a testament to his leadership; it was a pure, unadulterated stroke of dumb luck, a localized spasm of populist anger that Wu shamelessly took credit for. The party is a hollow shell of corruption, infighting, and arrogant incompetence. They should be liquidated. They should be dismantled and sold for scrap.

`; endText += `

The pressure in your skull reaches a critical mass. The veins in your neck throb. Your face flushes a deep, burning crimson. You turn away from the window, your eyes locking onto a priceless, intricately painted Ming-dynasty replica vase resting on a marble pedestal near the door. Without a single conscious thought, driven entirely by the primal, violent fury of a thwarted conqueror, you step forward, grab the heavy porcelain by its neck, and hurl it with all your strength against the reinforced glass wall. The impact is deafening. The vase shatters into a thousand jagged, glittering shards, raining down across the imported carpet like broken teeth. You stand there, your chest heaving, your breath ragged and heavy, staring at the destruction. For a brief, fleeting second, the physical exertion offers a tiny release valve for the pressure. But it evaporates instantly. The silence returns to the room, heavier and more mocking than before. The broken vase changes absolutely nothing. The numbers on the desk remain exactly the same.

`; endText += `

The true horror of the evening finally begins to solidify in your mind. The vote counting will soon end. The television networks will officially call the race. And then, tradition and protocol will demand the ultimate, unthinkable sacrifice. You will have to call her. You will have to pick up the phone, dial the Presidential Office, and verbally submit to Tsai Ing-wen. You will have to admit defeat to a woman whose administrative skills you profoundly, unapologetically despise. The mere visualization of that moment causes a physical wave of nausea to wash over you. The blood rushes to your face again, burning with the heat of an unbearable, historic humiliation. In the darkest, most irrational corner of your mind, a fleeting, desperate thought whispers to you: it would be easier to die. It would literally be easier to end it all, right here in this penthouse, than to stand before the cameras, bow your head, and admit to the world that the great Terry Gou is a loser.

`; endText += `

But you do not move. You stare at the broken porcelain on the floor. You are a businessman. You calculate the margins of every action. If you refuse to concede, if you throw a tantrum, if you scream about fake polls and rigged systems, you will not look like a cheated emperor. You will look like a gigantic, spoiled infant. The internet trolls, the very people who destroyed your campaign, would feast on your meltdown for decades. They would turn your legacy, your empire, and your entire family into a pathetic, laughing meme. Your children would bear the stigma of a patriarch who could not take a punch. The social humiliation of being a sore loser in front of the entire international business community is a fate far worse, far more terrifying than a simple electoral defeat. You are a titan. Titans do not throw tantrums when the market crashes; they absorb the loss, cut the dead weight, and maintain their terrifying composure.

`; endText += `

You close your eyes, forcing the hot, suffocating rage down deep into the pit of your stomach, locking it away behind a vault of iron discipline. You must act like an adult. You must swallow the glass and smile. You slowly walk back toward the mahogany desk, your expensive leather shoes crunching softly over the shattered pieces of porcelain. You reach out and pick up the secure mobile phone. Your hand—the same hand that confidently signed billion-dollar corporate mergers across the globe—is visibly, uncontrollably trembling. It takes every ounce of your legendary willpower to steady your fingers. You unlock the screen. You find the contact number for the Presidential Office. You take one last, shuddering breath, staring into the dark reflection of the screen, and you press call. The line begins to ring.

`; mainTitle = 'COLLAPSE OF THE KHANATE'; subTitle = 'The billionaire’s empire shatters against the shores of reality.'; s_name = 'Brave - No Party For Cao Dong (2016)'; s_cover = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/caodong.jpg?v=1782824800463'; s_url = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/%E5%8B%87%E6%95%A2%E7%9A%84%E4%BA%BA%20-%20No%20Party%20for%20Cao%20Dong%20(youtube).mp3?v=1782824782043'; endImage = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/guodongbaixuan.webp'; } else { endText += `

The atmosphere inside the ultra-luxury penthouse suite overlooking the Xinyi District is deliberately, almost aggressively casual. It is late afternoon, the hours just before the ballot boxes are sealed, and you have chosen to completely isolate yourself from the suffocating, sweat-stained panic of the Kuomintang central headquarters. Instead, you are lounging at the massive, custom-built Italian marble bar in your private residence, surrounded by your adult children and your wife. To mask the intense, acidic knot of anxiety twisting in your stomach, you are doing what you always do: projecting absolute, unbothered supremacy.

`; endText += `

‘The labor costs in Shenzhen are creeping up again,’ your eldest son remarks, swirling a glass of sparkling water, leaning against the edge of the marble counter. ‘We are looking at accelerating the land acquisitions in Chennai and Hanoi. But the local bureaucrats in India are dragging their feet on the tax exemptions. They keep asking for more environmental reviews.’

`; endText += `

You do not even look up from your wine glass. ‘Tell the regional directors to issue a hard ultimatum,’ you reply, your voice flat and utterly devoid of anxiety. ‘If the permits are not cleared by Friday morning, we pull the capital entirely and move the assembly lines to Mexico. I do not have the patience to negotiate with third-rate provincial politicians. They need our jobs far more than we need their land. You have to squeeze them until they bleed, otherwise they will never respect your authority.’

`; endText += `

Your daughter laughs softly, tapping her manicured nails on the counter. ‘Uncle Chen was saying the exact same thing at the golf club yesterday. He said everyone in his circle voted for you. All the tech executives, all the shipping magnates. He thinks Tsai Ing-wen will be packing her bags by eight o'clock tonight.’

`; endText += `

You reach out, using a pair of silver tongs to drop three thick, crystalline ice cubes into your vintage red wine—a stubborn, barbaric personal habit that horrifies sommeliers but asserts your absolute dominance over conventional rules. ‘Of course they did,’ you say, watching the ruby liquid splash against the ice. ‘I spent billions injecting actual efficiency into this island's dying political machine. The internal data gives us a three-point lead. In business, numbers are absolute. The voters are not stupid; they know who actually signs the paychecks. Tsai knows nothing but empty slogans.’

`; endText += `

Yet, the illusion of unbothered tranquility is constantly punctured by the massive, eighty-inch OLED television mounted on the far wall. The screen is split into multiple feeds, broadcasting the frenzied, ear-piercing chatter of Taiwanese political talk shows. Pundits with flushed faces are screaming over each other, frantically analyzing voter turnout, weather patterns, and blackout polling rumors. The shrill, low-brow, chaotic noise of the broadcasts feels entirely alien in this silent, climate-controlled mansion. You swirl your glass, the ice cubes clinking softly. You desperately want the upper hand.

`; endText += `

At four o'clock, the counting begins. The casual corporate banter around the bar slowly dies out, replaced by a tense, heavy silence. The numbers start rolling across the bottom of the television screen. It is not a blowout. It is a grueling, decimal-by-decimal trench war. For the first two hours, the red and green lines on the graphic trackers are practically intertwined. But as the evening drags on, a terrifying, irreversible trend begins to form. Tsai Ing-wen begins to pull ahead. Not by ten percent, not by a landslide, but by a steady, persistent margin of three, then four, then five percentage points. The gap is small enough to keep hope agonizingly alive, but wide enough to be mathematically fatal.

`; endText += `

You stop talking entirely. You sit frozen on the barstool, staring at the screen. You gently swirl your glass. The ice cubes in the red wine have begun to melt, shrinking slowly, losing their sharp, crystalline edges. The vote gap is widening, and the ice is melting. The two processes seem brutally synchronized. You watch your presidential ambitions, your billions of dollars spent, and your colossal ego slowly dissolving into the warm, red liquid. Sensing the sudden, lethal drop in the room's temperature, your adult children instinctively recognize the danger. Without saying a word, they quietly, swiftly scatter, retreating into the deeper, safer corridors of the sprawling penthouse, leaving you alone at the bar.

`; endText += `

Alone, except for your wife. Delia Tseng leans against the opposite side of the marble counter, completely misreading the apocalyptic tension in the room. She lets out a long, theatrical, highly exasperated sigh. ‘I simply cannot believe this,’ she complains, her voice whining with the superficial annoyance of a socialite inconvenienced. ‘Do you have any idea how many hours my assistants spent filing those ridiculous asset declarations with the Control Yuan? The lawyers made me document every single Hermes Birkin bag, every limited-edition Patek Philippe watch, my entire custom jewelry collection from Paris... They treated us like criminals just because we are wealthy. We spent weeks doing all that humiliating, exhausting paperwork for the government, and now you might not even get elected? What a complete and utter waste of my time.’

`; endText += `

The words hit your ears like scraping metal. A sudden, blinding surge of violent, uncontrollable rage explodes in your chest. The sheer, breathtaking ignorance of her complaint—equating the catastrophic failure of your ultimate historical ambition with the inconvenience of declaring her luxury handbags—pushes you to the absolute brink. For one terrifying, suspended second, a dark, primal impulse floods your brain. You want to reach across the marble bar. You want to strike her. You want to physically shatter that obnoxious, ungrateful, shallow voice. The urge for domestic violence is hot and acidic in your throat. You close your eyes. You force yourself to breathe. You swallow the violence down, burying it under a thick, suffocating layer of bitter restraint. You do not say a single word. You just glare at her with dead, empty eyes until she nervously turns on her heel and walks away.

`; endText += `

A deep, agonizing pang of melancholy twists in your chest. You look out at the dark city. You think of Serena. Your late wife. The woman who actually built the empire with you, who swallowed the bitter dust of the early factory days, who understood the brutal weight of conquest. She should be the one standing here. Instead, you are stuck with a noisy, superficial dancer complaining about paperwork. You clench your jaw, taking a heavy drink of the diluted wine. The ice is completely gone now.

`; endText += `

Your mind begins to race, spiraling into the dark, paranoid corners of a defeated tycoon. Where did it go wrong? You spent more money than any candidate in Taiwanese history. Did the Kuomintang set you up? Was Chairman Wu Den-yih secretly sabotaging your ground game to protect his own factional power? Did those decaying, corrupt KMT local bosses take your campaign subsidies and simply refuse to mobilize the vote? Or... was it the DPP? Did Tsai Ing-wen manipulate the central election commission? You think of the infamous two bullets of 2004, the stolen elections of the past. The thought of widespread electoral fraud flickers in your mind, a tempting, comforting conspiracy. But the rational CEO inside you quickly kills the thought. No one has seriously proven mass voter fraud in Taiwan since 2004.
