You were not cheated by the computers; you were simply rejected by the people. The realization is a bitter, indigestible pill.

`; endText += `

On the massive television screen, the scene cuts to the Democratic Progressive Party headquarters. Tsai Ing-wen steps up to the podium, bathed in the flashing lights of victory. The crowds are roaring. She begins her calm, measured, triumphant victory speech, thanking the voters for choosing sovereignty over economic submission. Her voice echoes through your empty, silent mansion. The sheer political exhaustion of the past year suddenly crashes down on you like a collapsed building. You are seventy years old. You are a billionaire. But right now, you feel incredibly, profoundly tired. You cross your arms on the cold marble surface of the bar. You rest your heavy head on your sleeves. The television continues to drone on, but the words blur into meaningless static. The tycoon who wanted to buy a nation closes his eyes, sinking into a deep, sullen, and lonely sleep on the bar counter, leaving the victorious progressive era to celebrate without him.

`; mainTitle = 'MELTING CROWN'; subTitle = 'The billionaire watches his political ambitions dissolve into the night.'; s_name = 'Surfing with the Chairman - Lin Sheng-xiang (2017)'; s_cover = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/dafopulasi.jpg'; s_url = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/%E5%A4%A7%E4%BD%9B%E6%99%AE%E6%8B%89%E6%96%AF%20%20%E8%B7%9F%E8%91%97%E8%91%A3%E4%BA%8B%E9%95%B7%E5%8E%BB%E8%A1%9D%E6%B5%AA%20-%20Peiyo%20Lin%20(youtube).mp3?v=1782828562225'; endImage = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/20190416-035429_U720_M513332_77ef.jpg%26g%3Dsm%26h%3D675%26resize%3Dfill%26w%3D1200%26format%3Dwebp'; } } // ====================================================================== // 4. 王金平 (Wang Jin-pyng) 败选分支 // ====================================================================== else if (Number(campaignTrail_temp.wangjinping) === 1) { if (pct < 40.0) { endText += `

The scent of aged Alishan high-mountain tea fills the dimly lit private suite of the Kuomintang headquarters. You sit alone at the heavy mahogany table, taking a slow, measured sip from a delicate porcelain cup. The television in the corner is muted, but the flashing red graphics and plunging bar charts tell the entire, brutal story. Less than forty percent. An absolute, humiliating slaughter. Yet, your heart rate does not spike. There is no shock, no sudden, paralyzing realization of doom. The cold, unromantic truth is that the King of Deals knew he was walking into a graveyard long before the first ballot was ever cast.

`; endText += `

You were fighting a war on two impossible fronts. First, the ideological rebellion. The deep-blue purists, the aging veterans of the Huang Fu-hsing, absolutely refused to march for you. To them, you have always been blue skin, green bone—a treacherous opportunist who collaborated with the DPP and sabotaged their beloved Ma Ying-jeou during the infamous September Strife. They chose to stay home, letting the party burn to the ground rather than hand the crown to a man they viewed as a traitor. You could not negotiate with pure, unadulterated hatred.

`; endText += `

But the deeper, more fatal wound was structural. The Taiwan you once mastered is dead. The relentless, suffocating march of urbanization has paved over the agricultural patronage networks you spent decades building. The temple directors, the water irrigation chiefs, and the local faction bosses who once commanded tens of thousands of votes with a single phone call are now aging relics. They are completely powerless to sway a new generation of youth who organize on the internet, not in banquet halls. The traditional, rural society of human connections and backroom favors—your absolute, unquestioned domain—has been swept away by the cold, digital wave of modern progressive politics. You are a king whose kingdom simply ceased to exist.

`; endText += `

You take another sip of the bitter tea. A faint, almost imperceptible smile touches your lips as a memory from four decades ago surfaces. An old, blind fortune teller in a Kaohsiung temple once traced the lines of your palm and declared you were destined to be a great minister, a man who would sit at the very pinnacle of the state. The prophecy was not entirely false; you navigated the martial law era and eventually ruled the Legislative Yuan like an absolute monarch for an unprecedented seventeen years. But the presidency? That requires the Mandate of Heaven.

`; endText += `

Your mind drifts to Ma Ying-jeou. The handsome, Harvard-educated princeling. The man who sailed through his political career with a flawless, one hundred percent electoral win rate. You spent your entire life mastering the dark, complex arts of compromise, navigating the mud and blood of local politics, yet you could never replicate the effortless, sweeping, nationwide mandates that Ma commanded. You let out a quiet, bitter chuckle, the sound evaporating into the empty room. You outlasted him in the party's internal trench warfare, but in the end, you must admit defeat. He possessed the historical, aesthetic destiny that you fundamentally lacked.

`; endText += `

The heavy wooden door slowly creaks open. Your running mate, ${currentMateName}, steps into the room. Their face is pale, completely drained of the political ambition that burned so brightly just months ago. ‘Speaker Wang,’ they say softly, instinctively reverting to your old, familiar title, as if the presidential campaign was already a faded illusion. ‘The final metropolitan districts just reported. We are completely buried. There is no mathematical path left. The campaign team believes it is time for you to go out there. We need a concession speech to call for national unity before the base completely turns on itself.’

`; endText += `

You nod slowly, placing the empty teacup precisely in the center of its saucer. The game is finally over. You stand up, smoothing out the wrinkles of your suit jacket, your face effortlessly returning to its signature, impenetrable, Buddha-like mask. ‘Let us go, then,’ you reply calmly. You walk out of the quiet sanctuary and down the sterile hallway, stepping into the blinding, relentless flashbulbs of the press corps and the desolate, weeping silence of a fading political empire that will never rise again.

`; mainTitle = 'END OF AN ERA'; subTitle = 'The King of Deals finally runs out of favors.'; s_name = 'Vanity Is a Dream - Jody Jiang (2000)'; s_cover = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/jianghui2.jpg?v=1782831732859'; s_url = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/%E7%B9%81%E8%8F%AF%E6%94%8F%E6%98%AF%E5%A4%A2%20-%20Jody%20Chiang%20(youtube).mp3?v=1782831740156'; endImage = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/wjp2.jpg'; } else { endText += `

The atmosphere inside the private briefing room of the Kuomintang headquarters is strangely subdued, lacking the frantic, suffocating panic usually associated with an impending defeat. You sit at the head of the long table, your hands resting comfortably on your lap, listening as the chief data analyst nervously breaks down the final tracking polls. He details the shrinking margins in the central counties and the unbreakable green firewall in the south. You absorb the data with a solemn, heavy expression, but a familiar, faint smile still plays at the corners of your lips. ‘Ah, I see,’ you murmur softly, interrupting the analyst. ‘So, the gap is roughly five to six points. It is playing out almost exactly like the 2012 election margins. I suppose it does not really matter anymore. We accept the people’s verdict.’

`; endText += `

The young analysts exchange confused glances, expecting rage or despair from their presidential nominee. But your mind has already moved past the executive branch. You wave your hand dismissively at the presidential charts. ‘Take those down. Show me the legislative projections,’ you command, your voice suddenly infused with sharp, calculating authority. ‘What are our estimates for the at-large party-list seats? Walk me through the regional battles in Taichung and Changhua. Who is surviving?’ Even on the eve of your own presidential defeat, your true obsession remains the Legislative Yuan. You are, and always will be, a creature of the parliament. You stare at the projected seating charts, a deep, hollow ache forming in your chest. How wonderful it would be if you could just return to the Speaker's chair, holding the gavel, mediating the factions, running the country from the shadows. But the brutal 2016 election had permanently shattered that dream. The DPP had conquered the legislature, and your era was over.

`; endText += `

Looking at the projected legislative map, a rare moment of cold, brutal self-awareness washes over you. You know exactly why you are losing tonight. You are simply too old, too deeply entangled in the archaic web of patronage and favors to connect with the modern, digitized Taiwanese electorate. You had lost touch with the grassroots a long time ago. In fact, you had not fought a grueling, direct district election in Kaohsiung for years; your local base had eroded so badly that the only way you maintained your legislative supremacy was by repeatedly strong-arming the KMT central committee into placing you safely at the top of the at-large list. You were an emperor of the backrooms, but a stranger to the streets.

`; endText += `

As the official vote counting begins on the television monitors, the reality of the race mirrors the polls. It is a respectable showing—a solid consolidation of the traditional blue base that keeps the margins tight—but the distance to Tsai Ing-wen remains persistent, teasing, and ultimately insurmountable. It is close enough to preserve the party's dignity, but far enough to definitively deny you the presidency. Watching the green line maintain its lead, a bitter, cynical chuckle escapes your lips. Your mind drifts to the massive, roaring pre-election rally held just twenty-four hours ago. You think of former President Ma Ying-jeou. He had sent a polite, terribly formal message claiming a sudden ‘physical illness’ prevented him from attending your final night on the stage. You shake your head, the smile turning sour. ‘Hmph. After all these years, he still hasn't let go of the grudge,’ you whisper to yourself. The petty, aristocratic prince could not even stomach standing on a stage to endorse the man who had outlasted him.

`; endText += `

The final outcome is no longer in doubt. You adjust your suit jacket, nodding to your silent, disheartened aides. The black town car is already waiting in the underground garage. You step into the vehicle, the tinted windows shielding you from the flashing lights of the press as the motorcade glides through the rainy Taipei streets toward your campaign stage. The ride is completely silent.

`; endText += `

You step out of the car and walk onto the stage. The crowd is subdued, a sea of disappointed faces gripping damp flags. You step up to the microphone, projecting the image of the eternal, harmonious elder statesman. You deliver your concession speech with flawless, practiced grace, congratulating President Tsai Ing-wen on her reelection, urging the nation to abandon ideological hatred, and calling for the Kuomintang to unite for the sake of the Republic. It is a perfect, textbook political farewell. But as you bow deeply to the crowd, the blinding glare of the camera flashes catches something the journalists miss. In the quiet, exhausted solitude of the stage, as the King of Deals realizes his forty-year reign has finally reached its definitive, permanent end, a single, solitary tear slips from your eye, disappearing instantly into the dark fabric of your suit.

`; mainTitle = 'FRACTURED COALITION'; subTitle = 'The local factions fight a desperate, losing war.'; s_name = 'Desperado - Superband (2009)'; s_cover = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/zongguanxian.jpg'; s_url = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/%E7%B8%B1%E8%B2%AB%E7%B7%9A%20Superband%E3%80%90%E4%BA%A1%E5%91%BD%E4%B9%8B%E5%BE%92%20Desperado%E3%80%91Official%20Music%20Video%20(%E5%B0%8E%E6%BC%94%E7%89%88)%20-%20%E6%BB%BE%E7%9F%B3%E5%94%B1%E7%89%87%20ROCK%20RECORDS%20(youtube).mp3?v=1782834046525'; endImage = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/wjp312.jpg'; } } // ====================================================================== // 5. 吴敦义 (Wu Den-yih) 败选分支 // ====================================================================== else if (Number(campaignTrail_temp.wudunyi) === 1) { if (pct < 40.0) { endText += `

‘That sue-tsa-boo!’ you hiss, the sharp, bitter Taiwanese Hokkien curse for an unlucky woman echoing through the private suite of the Kuomintang central headquarters. You slam your hand against the mahogany desk, glaring at the massive LED screen. ‘Her governance is a complete, unmitigated disaster! A total trainwreck! How in the world is she getting these numbers?’ The reality on the broadcast is mathematically terrifying. You are barely scraping the absolute bottom of the orthodox blue base. Less than forty percent. It is an apocalyptic collapse.

`; endText += `

Your wife, Tsai Ling-yi, walks over and gently places a hand on your trembling shoulder. She offers a sad, wry smile, her eyes reflecting the exhaustion of the campaign trail. ‘Nobody likes a stubborn old man like you anymore, Den-yih,’ she teases softly, trying to break the suffocating tension. ‘Well, nobody except me.’ You pause, the anger deflating slightly, and bark out a loud, hollow laugh, waving your hand to brush off the grim reality of the moment. The heavy oak doors open, and your running mate, ${currentMateName}, walks in, looking pale and thoroughly defeated. ‘I am so sorry, Chairman,’ ${currentMateName} says, bowing their head slightly. ‘I wish I could have brought more momentum to the ticket.’ You immediately wave away the apology, your face softening into the mask of a benevolent elder. ‘Nonsense. You fought hard. I appreciate everything you sacrificed for this party. The tides simply were not with us.’

`; endText += `

On the television, a prominent political talk show host is practically jumping out of his chair, furiously tapping a graphic whiteboard with a red marker. ‘Look at this collapse! It is a complete and absolute slaughter!’ the pundit screams into the camera, his face flushed. ‘What was the Kuomintang central committee smoking? They literally put up a walking fossil from the Ma Ying-jeou era and expected the youth to buy it! You cannot sell the White Dolphin in 2020! You cannot win an election with a White Thief who dodges every question with archaic political riddles! He is crashing right through Eric Chu’s pathetic 2016 floor! The KMT is officially being wheeled into the ICU tonight!’ You roll your eyes, finding the sensationalist, exaggerated screaming profoundly boring. You have heard these slurs for decades. With a heavy sigh, you pick up the remote and click the screen to a dead, silent black.

`; endText += `

You glance down at your luxury wristwatch. It is time. Time to walk out there and face the executioners. You slowly button your suit jacket. You know exactly what the press, the progressive youth, and even the furious members of your own party will scream tomorrow. They will say you were blinded by greed. They will say you selfishly played both referee and player, manipulating the primary rules to satisfy your own vanity and ruining the party's chances.

`; endText += `

But as you adjust your tie in the mirror, a cold, calculating clarity washes over you. What the hell were the alternatives? You mentally run through the roster of so-called saviors. Han Kuo-yu? He would have been slaughtered in a national race as a runaway mayor, burning his Kaohsiung base to the ground. Terry Gou? Handing the reins to him would mean surrendering the century-old party to a volatile, uncontrollable corporate dictator. Eric Chu? He possessed zero populist charm and was actively despised by the deep-blue purists. Hung Hsiu-chu? Complete, unapologetic political suicide. And Wang Jin-pyng was just as old and boring as you were. There were absolutely no good choices. You stepped up because you were the only architect capable of holding the fractured, dying machine together. If the house was destined to burn down anyway, you preferred to be the one holding the matches. ‘Fine,’ you whisper to your reflection. ‘If they need a villain, let them blame me.’ With your head held high and your signature, impenetrable smile plastered back onto your face, the grandmaster walks out of the room to deliver his final concession.

`; mainTitle = 'FALL OF THE ARCHITECT'; subTitle = 'The grandmaster takes the blame for an impossible war.'; s_name = 'Infernal Affairs - Andy Lau & Tony Leung (2002)'; s_cover = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/andylau.jpg'; s_url = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/%E7%84%A1%E9%96%93%E9%81%93%20(%E5%9C%8B)%EF%BC%8D%E5%8A%89%E5%BE%B7%E8%8F%AF%EF%BC%8F%E6%A2%81%E6%9C%9D%E5%81%89%20-%20Miss%20(youtube).mp3?v=1782837295310'; endImage = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/wudunyidefeat2.jpg'; } else { endText += `

The sprawling VIP suite of the Kuomintang central headquarters is surprisingly quiet. The frenzied staff have been dismissed to the outer halls. You sit deeply sunken into a plush leather armchair, your tie loosened. Sitting across the small glass coffee table from you is former President Ma Ying-jeou. Between you rests a large, traditional ceramic plate piled high with roasted peanuts and sunflower seeds. The only sound in the room, aside from the muted television broadcasting the election returns, is the sharp, rhythmic crack of seeds being split open. It is a scene of jarring, almost absurd domesticity amidst a national political earthquake. The two most powerful, calculating men of the orthodox blue establishment look like two retired uncles whiling away a Sunday afternoon.

`; endText += `

‘Remember that trip to Yunlin back in 2014?’ Ma asks, cracking a peanut shell and offering a rare, genuinely relaxed smile. ‘The local faction bosses were so terrified of my so-called death grip handshake that they literally tried to wear gloves. I had to stand there acting like I didn't notice.’ You let out a raspy, genuine laugh, tossing a sunflower seed shell into the ashtray. ‘How could I forget, President Ma? You stood there looking like a perfectly starched Taipei scholar, and I had to stay up until three in the morning drinking lethal amounts of Kaoliang liquor with them just to smooth over your awkwardness. You nearly cost us the agricultural association votes just by being too polite.’ Ma chuckles, shaking his head at the memory. For a fleeting moment, the suffocating pressure of the present dissolves into the comfortable, bittersweet nostalgia of their shared eight-year administration.

`; endText += `

You brush the salt from your fingertips and lean back, your eyes drifting toward the television screen. The green and blue lines are agonizingly close, twisting around each other, but the gap is stabilizing. ‘I ran the numbers an hour ago,’ you say quietly, the warmth draining from your voice, replaced by the cold, precise tone of a lifelong actuary. ‘We are not going to make it. The math simply does not close. We are going to lose by somewhere between five hundred thousand and a million votes.’ Ma stops chewing, looking at you intently. ‘The local factions did their job,’ you continue, staring blankly at the screen. ‘The ground game is flawless. But it is not enough to plug the hole. The youth demographic... we completely lost them. The internet, the geopolitical fear, the cultural shift. No amount of patronage or local favors can mathematically overcome that kind of generational deficit.’

`; endText += `

Ma Ying-jeou slowly wipes his hands on a napkin, his expression softening into a look of profound, empathetic understanding. ‘I know the feeling, Den-yih. Believe me, I know,’ Ma murmurs softly. ‘Back in 2012, right up until the final week, the media and the progressive youth swore I was a dead man walking. They said Tsai Ing-wen was going to completely overthrow me. It was terrifying. I barely scraped by with a few percentage points. It is a terrible weight to carry.’ Ma leans forward, his tone turning earnest. ‘But you have done an incredible job this time. Truly. You held the fundamental line. You completely boxed out James Soong and stopped him from stealing our orthodox votes. You protected the core base. You kept the Kuomintang alive so that it actually has a future to fight for.’

`; endText += `

You let out a dry, cynical laugh, shaking your head as you pick up another peanut. ‘A lot of good that will do me tomorrow morning. They will not care about the margins. They will not care that we prevented a total collapse. I am the Chairman who lost the presidency. They are going to curse me to death, demand my resignation, and blame me for every single thing that went wrong.’ You crack the peanut with a sharp snap. ‘Well, let them. Let us see who has the stomach and the skill to clean up this absolute mess in 2024.’

`; endText += `

The conversation naturally dies out. There is nothing left to say. On the television, Tsai Ing-wen maintains her relentless, persistent lead. You are trailing. It is a gap of several hundred thousand votes—a margin so agonizingly narrow that a slightly different campaign strategy, a few less gaffes, or a slightly weaker green turnout could have completely turned the world upside down. But close does not count in the Republic of China. The reality is ironclad. You failed to reclaim the throne. The two old statesmen sit side by side in the dim light, the plate of seeds forgotten between them. They just stare quietly at the glowing screen, enveloped in a heavy, absolute silence, watching as their political era officially and permanently fades into history.

`; mainTitle = 'DYING OF THE LIGHT'; subTitle = 'Two veterans watch their era quietly slip away.'; s_name = 'Broken Guitar - A-Yue (2011)'; s_cover = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/haiyagumu.jpg'; s_url = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/%E5%BC%B5%E9%9C%87%E5%B6%BD%20A-Yue%E3%80%90%E7%A0%B4%E5%90%89%E4%BB%96%E3%80%91Official%20Music%20Video%20HD%20-%20%E6%BB%BE%E7%9F%B3%E5%94%B1%E7%89%87%20ROCK%20RECORDS%20(youtube).mp3?v=1782838503584s'; endImage = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/W020170612748910491729.jpg?v=1782838171033'; } } // ====================================================================== // 6. 洪秀柱 (Hung Hsiu-chu) 败选分支 // ====================================================================== else if (Number(campaignTrail_temp.hongxiuzhu) === 1) { if (pct < 30.0) { endText += `

You always knew this was a suicide mission. From the moment you hijacked the nomination to wage an ideological holy war, you understood that preaching ultimate cross-strait unification was walking straight into a political furnace. But staring at the agonizingly slow ticker on the LED screens in your private war room, a rare, chilling sense of disbelief actually pierces your iron facade. Less than thirty percent. You have actually crashed through the pathetic, humiliating floor that Eric Chu set in 2016. You anticipated defeat, but you profoundly underestimated the absolute, visceral terror the Taiwanese public harbors toward Beijing. The sheer scale of the rejection takes the breath out of the room.

`; endText += `

The realization of what just happened is brutally clear. The blue-blooded establishment, the moderate economic voters, the local factions—they did not just passively refuse to march for you. They actively, intentionally defected. They stayed home, they bled votes to James Soong, and some even held their noses and voted for Tsai Ing-wen just to ensure your absolute political extermination. To them, you were a dangerous radical, a ticking time bomb who threatened their comfortable, ambiguous survival in Taiwan. You recognize this now. Your rebellion has been proven a catastrophic failure, and the cowardly establishment has successfully used the electorate to slaughter you.

`; endText += `

Your secure mobile phone vibrates on the desk. You pick it up, knowing exactly who is on the other end. Tsai Ing-wen’s voice comes through the speaker, calm and dripping with the unbearable, patronizing grace of an untouchable victor. She begins to lecture you, softly preaching about the democratic resilience of Taiwan, the progress of the nation, and warning you not to lead your followers down the wrong historical path. You feel a surge of absolute disgust. You do not want to hear this hypocritical wind blowing past your ears. You coldly cut her off, formally acknowledging the mathematical reality of the vote, and hang up the phone. The Democratic Progressive Party is surely laughing uncontrollably at the self-immolation of the Kuomintang, but you will not give them the satisfaction of your submission.

`; endText += `

You button your jacket, your spine perfectly straight. The establishment counter-attack will be swift and merciless. By midnight, they will be coming for your head. You will be forced to resign the chairmanship in absolute disgrace, stripped of all public office, and exiled to a quiet, forced retirement. You can only hope that the century-old party of Sun Yat-sen is not permanently annihilated by the flames of the rebellion you started. Your running mate, ${currentMateName}, stands by the door, completely shattered by the apocalyptic numbers, silently watching as you prepare to face the executioners.

`; endText += `

You step out onto the stage. It is not a crowd of mourning, weeping supporters; it is a chaotic, hostile mob. The centrist factions and angry party members have gathered in the dark square to demand blood. ‘Communist bandit, get out of the KMT!’ someone screams viciously from the darkness. ‘Go die in Beijing!’ Death threats and furious curses rain down on the podium. You stand there, bathed in the harsh spotlights, staring down at the raging faces. You do not apologize. You do not shed a single tear. You lean into the microphone, your voice as cold and hard as forged steel, echoing the exact, defiant words you spoke during your betrayal in 2015. ‘A lone minister may be abandoned, but my integrity shall never be broken!’ You turn and walk off the stage, your head held high, leaving the burning, fractured ruins of the Kuomintang behind you.

`; mainTitle = 'ASHES OF PURITY'; subTitle = 'The unyielding crusade burns down the house, leaving nothing but dust.'; s_name = 'Good Night! Formosa! - Fire EX. (2007)'; s_cover = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/wanantaiwan.jpg'; s_url = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/%E6%BB%85%E7%81%AB%E5%99%A8%20Fire%20EX.%20-%20%E6%99%9A%E5%AE%89%E5%8F%B0%E7%81%A3%20Good%20night!%20Formosa!%20-%20%E6%BB%85%E7%81%AB%E5%99%A8%20Fire%20EX.%20(youtube).mp3?v=1782842654979'; endImage = 'https://file.garden/Z9XHdyLGHwUEZPS4/ROC%202020/huanzhu.jpg'; } else { endText += `

The atmosphere inside the VIP suite of the Kuomintang central headquarters is remarkably, almost unnervingly still. While your campaign aides pace the hallways in a state of quiet, suffocating panic over the early exit polls, you sit calmly in a high-backed leather chair by the window. A pair of reading glasses rests on the bridge of your nose. In your hands is a thick, dog-eared historical volume detailing the bloody, protracted wars between the Ming loyalist Zheng regime in Taiwan and the encroaching Qing Dynasty across the strait. You are not reading it to pass the time; you are reading it to find clarity in the cyclical, tragic nature of Chinese history.

`; endText += `

Your eyes trace the detailed accounts of the late Zheng era, specifically the internal decay during the reign of Zheng Jing and the final collapse under Zheng Keshuang. The author vividly describes the fatal delusion of the island regime. Isolated across the sea, the Zheng court was consumed by bitter factional infighting, stubbornly clinging to the illusion of a phantom empire while entirely ignoring the overwhelming, crushing demographic and military reality of the continent. The hawkish ministers in Tainan constantly screamed for war and resistance, refusing any pragmatic negotiations for a peace treaty, ultimately forcing the Qing admiral Shi Lang to launch a devastating naval invasion at Penghu. The result was not a glorious martyrdom; it was the pointless slaughter of common soldiers and the complete, humiliating surrender of the island. You close the book gently, the historical revelation settling cold and heavy in your chest. The parallels to today's political climate are horrifyingly exact. The Democratic Progressive Party is playing the exact same suicidal role as the delusional Ming loyalists. They provoke Beijing, they whip up populist frenzy, and they sell the youth the romantic lie of independence, entirely ignoring the catastrophic bloodshed it will inevitably bring. You firmly believe that your vision—the pursuit of a formalized cross-strait peace accord and the bravery to seek unification without war—is the only pragmatic path to save Taiwan from repeating the tragedy of the Zheng regime. You are not a radical; you are the only realist left in the room.

`; endText += `

You remove your glasses and look out at the gray Taipei sky, your mind drifting back four years. You remember the bitter, agonizing humiliation of 2015. You had miraculously shattered the party's cynical anti-brick clause polling threshold, officially securing the presidential nomination against all odds. But the cowardly, calculating Kuomintang establishment, terrified of your ideological purity, orchestrated a brutal, televised political assassination at the Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall, unceremoniously stripping you of your candidacy. Today, you have finally secured your vindication. You forced the party to stop hiding behind ambiguous lies, stepping onto the grand stage for the first-ever female-versus-female presidential showdown in Taiwanese history. You are facing Tsai Ing-wen not just as a political opponent, but as an ideological mirror image. It is a battle for the ultimate soul of the island.

`; endText += `

The heavy oak doors open gently, and your running mate, ${currentMateName}, steps into the room. Their face is tight with disappointment, holding a tablet displaying the final blackout tracking data. The numbers hover around ${FINAL_VOTE_PERCENT.toFixed(1)}%. It is a highly respectable consolidation of the deep-blue base, far better than a total collapse, but still a definitive, undeniable defeat. Tsai Ing-wen maintains a steady, insurmountable lead. You look at the numbers and offer a serene, knowing smile to your pale running mate. You do not feel the agonizing sting of personal failure. You know exactly why you are losing today.

`; endText += `

You refuse to believe that the silent majority of the Republic of China fundamentally rejects your orthodox path. The voters did not reject peaceful unification; they were simply suffocated and blinded by a massive, unprecedented wave of progressive fearmongering. The DPP shamelessly weaponized the tragic tear gas of the Hong Kong protests, deploying their internet cyber-armies and endless electoral dirty tricks to launch a relentless, island-wide red-smearing campaign. They successfully painted your genuine pursuit of cross-strait peace as an act of treason, whipping the electorate into a hysterical panic. You know the truth: your ideology did not deviate from the core of the Republic; the people were simply terrified by the shadows the ruling party cast upon the wall.

`; endText += `

When the broadcast networks officially call the race for Tsai Ing-wen, your expression does not change. You slowly place the history book perfectly square on the desk. There will be no desperate denial, no hysterical claims of electoral fraud, and no tearful breakdowns. You are the Little Pepper, and you will face this defeat with the absolute, unyielding dignity of a true statesman. You turn to ${currentMateName} and nod gracefully. It is time to walk out there and conclude this chapter.

`; endText += `

You walk up the narrow steel steps of the stage on Bagude Road. The damp night wind bites at your jacket. Below you, the sight is heartbreaking: a sea of blue flags drooping heavily in the dark. Hardened military veterans are weeping openly, their tears catching the harsh glare of the media spotlights. You step up to the podium and adjust the microphone. It lets out a brief, sharp whine that instantly cuts through the sobbing of the crowd. You look straight into the wall of flashing camera lenses, your spine straight as a bayonet. ‘My fellow citizens of the Republic of China, good evening,’ your voice rings out, completely steady, utterly devoid of any despair. ‘The numbers are in. I, Hung Hsiu-chu, accept the decision made by the people of Taiwan today. I formally congratulate President Tsai Ing-wen on her reelection. We are a democracy, and I respect the constitutional system. I sincerely wish her a safe and stable term.’ It is a flawless, dignified concession. The hostile press corps, who came expecting a hysterical, radical meltdown, are stunned into a confused silence.

`; endText += `

But you are not finished. You grip the edges of the wooden podium, your knuckles turning white. The polite, statesman-like aura suddenly hardens into something terrifyingly sharp. ‘However!’ your voice suddenly cuts through the night air like a blade, making the journalists in the front row physically flinch. ‘I concede the ballot box tonight, but I will never, ever concede that the Democratic Progressive Party is right!’

`; endText += `

You point a finger directly at the cameras, as if pointing a spear straight through the screens into the Presidential Office. ‘President Tsai, you know exactly how you won today! You weaponized the tragedy in Hong Kong to manufacture mass panic! You used fabricated spy scandals to smear anyone who dares to pursue peace! You hijacked the anxieties of our youth and twisted them into a blind, suicidal hatred toward Beijing just to harvest cheap votes. You won the election, yes, but you are actively severing the cultural roots of the Republic of China and dragging this island straight toward the abyss of a catastrophic war!’

`; endText += `

The crowd below is no longer weeping; they are staring up at you in absolute, breathless awe. You deliver your final verdict, every word dripping with historical gravity. ‘A victory built on manufactured fear and dirty smears will eventually be judged by history. The illusion of independence may have blinded the majority today, but the ironclad reality of cross-strait peace will not change because of an election. I may have lost tonight, but as long as the true soul of the Republic of China breathes, my fight will never end. A lone minister may be abandoned, but my integrity shall never be broken!’ You turn sharply and walk off the stage. You do not look back. Behind you, the dead silence shatters into a roaring, fanatical wave of applause that pierces the dark Taipei sky.

Anchor Liu: Good evening, Taiwan! Welcome to the Critical Moment! I am your host, Baojie! Are you looking at the electoral map behind me?! Are you seeing these terrifying numbers?! We are not just witnessing a Kuomintang defeat tonight; we are witnessing the complete, anatomical disassembly of a century-old political machine! Mr. Kuo, I am looking at the live returns from the Central Election Commission right now. The Kuomintang won a pathetic, humiliating ${kmtSeats} seats! ${kmtSeats} seats across the entire island of Taiwan! Even during their absolute lowest point in 2016, they still managed to hold onto a respectable minority. Today, they have been politically evaporated. Meanwhile, the Democratic Progressive Party has secured a monstrous ${dppSeats} seats. That officially crosses the three-quarters supermajority! They can literally rewrite the Constitution of the Republic of China tomorrow morning if they want to! How did this absolute apocalypse happen?!

`; reportBody += `

Analyst Kuo: Baojie, you have to look past the presidential race and look at the absolute structural, demographic, and psychological collapse of the Kuomintang’s ground game. This is not just a standard electoral defeat; this is an extinction-level event for the blue camp. What we are witnessing tonight is the permanent death of the KMT's traditional political ecosystem. Let us start by looking at central and southern Taiwan. Look at the regional district maps. The local factions—the absolute, iron-fisted masters of the coastal patronage networks for decades, families whose temple connections and agricultural association influence were considered mathematically invincible—just got washed away by DPP rookies parachuted in from Taipei! When the local warlords cannot even mobilize their own backyards, you know the KMT national brand has become utterly radioactive.

`; reportBody += `

Anchor Liu: It is unbelievable! We all thought the local factions were immune to national ideological winds. We thought they ran on pure patronage, water irrigation budgets, and local favors. How did the DPP breach the absolute core of the KMT's subterranean networks?

`; reportBody += `

Analyst Kuo: Because the local faction bosses are ruthless, calculating businessmen, Baojie. They are not ideological martyrs willing to die for the party central. When they saw the presidential candidate's polls crashing weeks ago, and when they saw the terrifying, unprecedented mobilization of the progressive youth triggered by the Hong Kong anti-extradition protests, they immediately executed a severe triage strategy. They realized the national KMT ticket was an infectious disease. If a local warlord tied their regional legislative campaign to the presidential nominee, they would drown together in the progressive tsunami. So, they completely cut off the financial pipelines. They stopped organizing the massive, expensive banquet rallies. They told their local neighborhood wardens and precinct captains to stand down and save their resources for the upcoming mayoral and city council elections next cycle. They intentionally let the KMT regional legislative candidates be slaughtered to preserve their own local power bases. The KMT central headquarters was entirely, maliciously abandoned by its own ground troops.

`; reportBody += `

Anchor Liu: This is absolutely ruthless! But Kuo, what about the north? What about the absolute, impenetrable fortresses in Taipei and New Taipei? I am looking at districts in Daan, Wenshan, and Zhonghe—districts where a KMT candidate could historically win just by putting a blue flag on a watermelon—and they are flashing bright green! How did the intellectual, middle-class blue voters abandon the party so completely?

`; reportBody += `

Analyst Kuo: That brings us to the most brutal, self-inflicted wound of the night, Baojie: the party-list votes. The KMT’s at-large legislative list was a catastrophic provocation to their own base. The central committee, paralyzed by internal power struggles, allowed the deep-blue, extremist factions to hijack the safe seats. When they placed highly controversial figures and retired generals with deep ties to Beijing right at the top of their party-list, they essentially told moderate voters to go to hell. The highly educated, rational blue voters in the cities—the civil servants, the doctors, the corporate managers—were profoundly disgusted. They are fundamentally conservative, yes, but they are fiercely loyal to the Republic of China, not to the Chinese Communist Party. Facing this horrific list, they engaged in a massive, retaliatory split-ticket voting phenomenon.

`; reportBody += `

Anchor Liu: You mean they actively refused to cast the party ballot for the KMT?

`; reportBody += `

Analyst Kuo: Exactly. They abandoned the KMT entirely on the legislative ballot. We saw a massive chunk of the traditional pan-blue vote scatter into the wind. Some of them cast invalid protest votes. Some shifted to Ko Wen-je's Taiwan People Party out of sheer desperation for a rational, non-green alternative. And a terrifyingly large segment simply held their noses and voted for the DPP, prioritizing national security and sovereignty over their traditional economic conservatism. The KMT leadership tried to appease the extreme ideological purists, and in doing so, they completely amputated their own moderate, middle-class limbs. It was pure, unadulterated political cannibalism.

`; reportBody += `

Anchor Liu: Let us talk about those third parties. The TPP secured ${tppSeats} seats, and the NPP took ${nppSeats} seats. Do they have any leverage in this new parliament?

`; reportBody += `

Analyst Kuo: Zero. Absolutely zero leverage, Baojie. When the ruling party holds ${dppSeats} seats, minor parties are reduced to decorative ornaments. Ko Wen-je can hold as many press conferences as he wants, but he does not have the mathematical weight to block a single budget item. The extreme polarization of the 'National Doom' narrative completely starved the middle ground of any real procedural power. The electorate handed all the weapons directly to Tsai Ing-wen.

`; reportBody += `

Anchor Liu: Let us talk about the terrifying reality of what happens tomorrow morning. ${dppSeats} seats. That is well over the eighty-five seat constitutional amendment threshold. Tsai Ing-wen and the DPP now control over three-quarters of the Legislative Yuan. What does this mean for the future of the Republic of China?

`; reportBody += `

Analyst Kuo: It means the democratic checks and balances of this island have been officially, mathematically suspended, Baojie. The eighty-five seat threshold is the absolute holy grail of Taiwanese politics. It is the number required to unilaterally initiate constitutional amendments. They no longer need a single KMT vote, nor a single TPP vote, to pass anything. If the radical, deep-green wing of the DPP demands a change to the national territory, a change to the national flag, a revision of the national anthem, or even a formal, constitutional redefinition of cross-strait relations, Tsai Ing-wen has the mathematical leverage to push it straight through the legislature and put it to a national referendum. The KMT is completely powerless to stop them. They cannot even meet the threshold to file for a constitutional interpretation by the Grand Justices. They are mathematically locked out of the democratic process.

`; reportBody += `

Anchor Liu: That is genuinely chilling. The opposition has been entirely paralyzed. What can the Kuomintang even do in the legislature now with only ${kmtSeats} seats?

`; reportBody += `

Analyst Kuo: They can sit in their chairs, bang on the tables, throw water balloons, and shout into dead microphones. That is the absolute extent of their constitutional power. The DPP controls the speaker’s gavel, they control the agenda-setting Procedure Committee, and they possess an absolute, crushing majority in every single specialized sub-committee. They will fast-track the Transitional Justice bills to aggressively liquidate whatever frozen assets, historical archives, and real estate the KMT has left. They will pass the Anti-Infiltration Act and sweeping national security laws on their own terms, weaponizing the justice system to permanently cripple the pan-blue media and corporate networks. The ${kmtSeats} KMT legislators are now nothing more than highly-paid, miserable spectators trapped inside a sprawling green empire.

`; reportBody += `

Anchor Liu: Is this the end of the Kuomintang? Can a century-old political party survive a trauma of this magnitude, or will it simply dissolve?

`; reportBody += `

Analyst Kuo: The party as we know it is dead tonight, Baojie. Tomorrow morning, you will see a bloodbath at the central headquarters unlike anything in modern history. The chairman will be forced to resign in absolute disgrace, likely pelted with garbage by furious supporters. The local factions, seeing that the central party is a sinking, radioactive ship, will formally sever their ties and declare independence to protect their own provincial survival. The younger, desperate reformists will violently clash with the deep-blue veterans, blaming their archaic, pro-unification ideology for dragging the party into this abyss. The Kuomintang will shatter into three or four irreconcilable splinter groups, fighting viciously over the bankrupt, smoldering ashes of a forgotten dynasty. The era of competitive two-party politics in Taiwan has been officially suspended. We have entered a dark, unpredictable period of absolute, unchallenged green hegemony.

Anchor Liu: Welcome back! Baojie here! The Kuomintang has suffered a definitive, undeniable defeat at the presidential level, but looking at the Legislative Yuan... my god, it feels like I am stuck in a terrifying time loop! It is the 2016 nightmare all over again! Mr. Kuo, look at the board! `; reportBody += `

Analyst Kuo: Baojie, the Kuomintang hit a solid, unbreakable demographic ceiling today. Yes, they managed to defend their absolute, deep-blue fortresses—places like Miaoli, Hsinchu County, and Kinmen—where the traditional voting blocks remained fiercely loyal to the local patronage structures. But elections in Taiwan are won in the highly populated suburban belts, and there, the KMT was methodically slaughtered. The air war completely obliterated the ground game. The most shocking, earth-shattering event of the night was Taichung’s Second District. Look at that result! The Yen family—the ultimate, iron-fisted Godfathers of central Taiwan’s temple and agricultural networks for decades—just lost their ancestral seat to a young, progressive rookie! `; reportBody += `

Anchor Liu: It is absolutely unbelievable! The Yen family’s ground game was supposed to be invincible! I am also looking at Taipei’s Fourth District, Nangang and Neihu. Lee Yen-hsiu is a highly capable, deeply entrenched KMT incumbent, completely scandal-free, yet she was washed away by the progressive turnout. `; reportBody += `

Analyst Kuo: Because of the ‘National Doom’ narrative and the absolute disaster of the KMT’s at-large legislative list. The middle class engaged in a massive split-ticket voting operation.

`; reportBody += `

Anchor Liu: Let us talk about that split-ticket voting, because the white and orange colors on the board are telling a fascinating story. Ko Wen-je successfully branded his party as a safe, rational harbor. He parked his tanks right in the middle of the political spectrum and established a crucial legislative beachhead for a potential presidential run in four years.

The humid, stifling summer heat of Kaohsiung carried the undeniable, metallic scent of a political execution. By six o'clock in the evening on June 6, the counting of the ballots was largely complete, but the suspense had evaporated hours earlier. The numbers flashing across the television networks were not just a defeat; they were a catastrophic obliteration of a politician's career.

A staggering 939,090 citizens of Kaohsiung had marched to the ballot boxes to cast a vote of no confidence against Mayor Han Kuo-yu. To put this monumental figure into perspective, the number of people who voted to forcefully strip him of his office was actually higher than the 892,545 people who had elected him as their populist savior just eighteen months prior. The Republic of China had just witnessed its very first successful recall of a special municipality mayor. The guillotine had fallen. The populist king was officially dead.

To understand the sheer violence of this democratic whiplash, one must examine the profound psychological contract that Han shattered. In late 2018, he was a political miracle. He was the marginalized, bald outsider who waded into a deep-green fortress that the Kuomintang had abandoned for two decades. He drank with the working class, slept in wholesale markets, and promised economic salvation. Kaohsiung, exhausted by stagnation and elite arrogance, handed him a historic mandate.

They wanted a hardworking, dedicated local executive. Instead, they got a man intoxicated by the roar of the national crowds. Barely six months into his mayoral term, he abandoned the city to chase the ultimate prize: the presidency. This was his fatal miscalculation. The citizens did not just feel disappointed; they felt intensely, viciously betrayed. The title that once defined his grassroots charm morphed into the most toxic label in modern Taiwanese politics: the Runaway Mayor.

This was no longer a traditional partisan battle between the blue and green camps; it was framed as a holy war to cleanse the city of a fraud.

When his presidential campaign ended in a crushing defeat against Tsai Ing-wen, the bleeding did not stop. The anger in the south crystallized into a lethal civic machine. The WeCare Kaohsiung movement, initially dismissed by the KMT establishment as a fringe group of bitter sore losers, rapidly ballooned into an unstoppable social force. A sea of yellow ribbons flooded the city streets. The DPP central apparatus barely needed to intervene; they merely provided logistical support while the furious civil society did the heavy lifting. The resentment was organic and unyielding.

Recognizing the insurmountable odds, Han attempted a desperate, cynical defensive maneuver. He ordered his fanatical base to completely boycott the election. 'Do not vote, just monitor the polling stations,' he commanded. It was an attempt to mathematically depress the turnout below the twenty-five percent threshold required for a valid recall, while simultaneously creating a chilling atmosphere of intimidation outside the voting booths. He hoped the silent majority would passively save him.

But the youth of Taiwan fundamentally rejected his calculations. On the eve of the recall, the high-speed rail stations in Taipei and Taichung were flooded with thousands of young, highly educated students and professionals. They were buying expensive, full-price tickets to travel hundreds of miles back to their registered addresses in the south for one singular purpose: to fire their mayor. When the polling stations opened, the long, winding lines were not filled with the elderly veterans who usually dominate KMT turnout. They were filled with millennials holding yellow ribbons, standing in the blistering sun, quietly executing their civic duty to terminate his mandate.

As the final tally was confirmed, Han Kuo-yu stepped out of the city administration building accompanied by his solemn cabinet. He delivered a farewell speech that remained entirely consistent with his brand: deeply emotional, yet completely devoid of genuine self-reflection. He bitterly accused the ruling party of mobilizing the national state machinery to destroy him, painting himself as a tragic martyr of a rigged system. He refused to acknowledge that his own blinding ambition had dug his grave. He bowed gracefully to his weeping supporters, but his defiant tone signaled that the partisan hatred he ignited would not simply vanish with his removal.

The implications of this recall extend far beyond the political corpse of Han Kuo-yu. By chaining their entire party apparatus to a populist comet, the KMT establishment allowed their brand to be completely consumed by his chaotic energy. Now, with Han disgraced and ejected from power, the KMT has been thoroughly, mercilessly eradicated from the southern half of the island. The upcoming mayoral by-election is already a foregone conclusion—a mere coronation ceremony for the DPP to reclaim its lost territory. The populist dream is over. The stage is empty. The tragedy is complete.

The populist contagion that has violently reshaped the Western hemisphere over the past four years has officially made landfall in East Asia. Taiwan, long heralded by Washington as the most stable, progressive beacon of liberal democracy in the Pacific, has just elected its own populist disrupter. Han Kuo-yu, a man who built his entire political brand on a potent, volatile mix of economic desperation and anti-intellectual resentment, has successfully stormed the Presidential Office. For the international diplomatic community and the progressive elites in Taipei, the election results are not just a political defeat; they represent an absolute, paradigm-shattering psychological shock.

To understand the sheer magnitude and absurdity of Han Kuo-yu’s victory, one must look at his bizarre political trajectory. In the late 1990s, Han was a hot-tempered, fiercely partisan legislator, best known for physically assaulting former President Chen Shui-bian on the parliamentary floor. As Taiwan modernized, Han faded into complete obscurity. He spent over a decade in the political wilderness, eventually resurfacing as the unassuming general manager of the Taipei Agricultural Products Marketing Corporation. He was considered a washed-up relic of a bygone era. Yet, in late 2018, the Kuomintang deployed him as a sacrificial lamb in the Kaohsiung mayoral race—a deep-green, working-class fortress that the KMT had abandoned for twenty years.

What happened next rewrote the rules of Taiwanese politics. Armed with nothing but a bottle of mineral water and a bowl of braised pork rice, Han tapped into a deep, subterranean vein of working-class frustration. He rebranded himself as the Bald Greengrocer, promising to make the people rich and end the ideological bickering of the northern elites. He flipped Kaohsiung in a historic landslide, creating the unstoppable Han Wave. Barely six months later, driven by an insatiable populist momentum, he abandoned the city to pursue the presidency, presenting himself as the ultimate anti-establishment wrecking ball.

He did not just campaign against the ruling party; he campaigned against the entire concept of the traditional political elite, turning his own lack of administrative depth into a badge of honor.

President Tsai Ing-wen and her Ivy-League-educated strategists operated under a fatal delusion. They believed that by aggressively weaponizing the tragedy of the Hong Kong protests and amplifying the existential military threat from Beijing, they could force the electorate into a blind panic of patriotic unity. They constructed a sophisticated narrative of democratic survival. But they profoundly miscalculated the physics of working-class reality. The agricultural sectors, the street vendors, and the industrial blue-collar workers were suffocating under stagnant wages, brutal pension reforms, and a cross-strait economic freeze. As the old political adage goes: you cannot eat geopolitics. The DPP offered the voters progressive liberal values and anti-China rhetoric, but Han Kuo-yu offered them something far more primal—money, dignity, and a vessel into which millions of frustrated citizens could pour their rage against an arrogant establishment.

Han’s political aesthetic was meticulously crafted to maximize this class warfare. Unlike the traditional, blue-blooded aristocrats of the Kuomintang who historically governed in tailored suits with Oxford degrees, Han rolled up his faded blue shirt sleeves. He spoke in coarse, deeply localized street slang, swore during rallies, and gleefully mocked the bureaucratic norms of the capital. Much like Donald Trump’s mastery of the American rust belt, Han managed to convince the marginalized southern Taiwanese grassroots that a millionaire politician was somehow one of them. His rallies were not policy seminars; they were feverish, cult-like revivals demanding the destruction of the status quo.

Yet, to attribute this historic political earthquake entirely to Han’s raw charisma would be a severe analytical error. Behind the screaming crowds and the populist theater stood the cold, calculating machinery of the Kuomintang, ruthlessly orchestrated by Party Chairman Wu Den-yih. Wu is the ultimate political survivor, a Machiavellian architect who realized that the orthodox KMT brand was practically dead. Wu recognized that the party needed a battering ram to break down the DPP’s electoral firewall, and Han was the perfect, expendable blunt instrument. While Han occupied the media spotlight with his outrageous rhetoric, Chairman Wu quietly and efficiently mobilized the subterranean empire of local factions, agricultural associations, and temple networks. It was an unholy, highly effective marriage between a populist demagogue and a deeply entrenched, archaic patronage machine.

The geopolitical implications of this populist triumph are deeply unsettling. Washington is currently scrambling to assess the reliability of a new Taiwanese leader whose cross-strait ideology is entirely unpredictable and largely dictated by short-term economic opportunism rather than strategic deterrence. Beijing, while undoubtedly relieved to see the pro-independence DPP removed from power, is equally wary of negotiating with a chaotic, uncontrollable maverick who prioritizes viral slogans over diplomatic protocol. The fragile equilibrium of the Taiwan Strait has been violently disrupted.

Taiwan has officially entered the era of post-truth, highly polarized politics. The progressive youth and urban intellectuals are already organizing furious resistance movements, refusing to recognize the legitimacy of a man they view as an uneducated charlatan. The Han Kuo-yu administration will begin its term fundamentally besieged by half of the country. As the dust settles in Taipei, the international community must confront a chilling reality: the populist fever of the 2020s has not broken, and the dark, seductive tide of anti-establishment rage is still successfully tearing down the institutional pillars of liberal democracies across the globe.

Four years ago, a single, incredibly potent slogan swept across this island and violently overturned the political establishment: Taiwan Stays Safe, The People Get Rich. It was a masterpiece of populist marketing. President Han Kuo-yu rode that wave of economic desperation straight into the Presidential Office, promising the exhausted working class a swift, tangible end to the stagnation they suffered under the Tsai Ing-wen administration. Now, as the 2024 election cycle looms on the horizon, the economic data is officially in. The ledgers have been audited. And the inescapable, cold reality is setting in: the people did not get rich. The populist economic miracle was nothing but a spectacularly marketed mirage.

To be entirely fair to the administration, the initial months of the Han presidency did deliver a highly visible, superficial economic bump. Following the restoration of the 1992 Consensus, Beijing immediately lifted the restrictions on mainland tour groups. Fleets of tour buses flooded the highways of Kaohsiung, Pingtung, and Hualien. Night market vendors saw their nightly revenues multiply, and hotel occupancy rates in the south reached full capacity. Simultaneously, a flurry of high-profile Memorandums of Understanding (MOUs) were signed with various mainland Chinese provinces, facilitating the mass export of Taiwanese agricultural products—pineapples, groupers, and guavas flowed across the strait. For a brief, intoxicating moment, the grassroots base felt they were finally reaping the long-awaited peace dividend. The administration proudly touted these short-term, low-value-added injections of cash as definitive proof that their strategy was working.

However, modern national economies are not night markets, and you cannot secure the future of a twenty-first-century developed nation by selling fruit and renting out hotel rooms. As the global economy entered a period of extreme turbulence and massive supply chain restructuring, the fundamental flaws of the Han administration’s economic blueprint were ruthlessly exposed. While the Presidential Office was intensely focused on agricultural MOUs and tourism subsidies, they completely missed the boat on the greatest geopolitical and technological shift of our era: the global semiconductor boom and the restructuring of the tech supply chain.

Under the previous administration, despite their numerous political faults, there was at least a coherent, state-backed effort to upgrade domestic industries and integrate Taiwan into the high-end technology corridors of Washington and Tokyo. The Han administration, terrified of angering Beijing and entirely dependent on the quick, populist dopamine hits of cross-strait trade, effectively paused these critical upgrades. The tech sector felt abandoned. Foreign direct investment from Western tech giants stalled, wary of the administration's unpredictable geopolitical posturing. Taiwan's overall GDP growth over the past four years has been agonizingly mediocre, hovering barely a fraction of a percent higher than the darkest days of the Tsai era. The fundamental structural issues—stagnant median wages, skyrocketing housing prices, and the lack of high-paying jobs for university graduates—remain completely unsolved.

The tragedy of this administration is that they traded the future of Taiwan's high-tech industrial supremacy for a few thousand tour buses and fruit crates.

But why did the administration fail to implement any structural economic reforms? The answer lies in the severe, paralyzing political debt the President incurred to win the 2020 election. The concept of Political Capital is not just an abstract theory; it is the currency of governance. To achieve his miraculous populist victory, Han Kuo-yu had to aggressively mortgage his future administration to the traditional Kuomintang local factions, rural warlords, and deep-blue establishment figures who bankrolled and organized his ground game. He entered the Presidential Office with a severely negative balance of political capital.

This debt has completely crippled his presidency. Every time the executive branch attempts to propose a rational, long-term economic restructuring plan, it is instantly vetoed or mutilated by his own party’s legislators. The local factions demand their pound of flesh in the form of massive, highly inefficient pork-barrel infrastructure projects—bridges to nowhere, redundant local transit systems, and bloated agricultural subsidies that drain the national treasury. The President is powerless to stop them. He cannot whip his own lawmakers because he owes his very survival to their patronage networks. He is a hostage in his own palace. The KMT establishment elites, who quietly despise his populist vulgarity, offer him absolutely no bureaucratic cover, leaving his cabinet filled with second-rate loyalists who lack the administrative depth to govern a complex economy.

The social fallout from this economic stagnation is proving to be catastrophic for the KMT's 2024 prospects. The very people who carried him to the throne—the young, struggling working-class families and the disillusioned urban youth—are now looking at their stagnant paychecks with a cold, furious clarity. The rent is still too high. The high-paying jobs are still missing. The promise that closer ties to China would miraculously solve their domestic poverty has been proven false. The progressive youth, who were already ideologically hostile to his cross-strait policies, now possess the ultimate, devastating economic argument against his reelection.

As the campaign season kicks off, the Democratic Progressive Party has completely reorganized. They have shed the baggage of 2020 and are launching a ruthless, data-driven assault on the administration's economic incompetence. They are pointing to the booming tech sectors of our regional neighbors and asking the Taiwanese people a very simple, lethal question: Are you actually any richer today than you were four years ago? The magic of the Han Wave has entirely evaporated. The populist outsider successfully captured the state machinery, but he quickly discovered that shouting slogans from a stage is incredibly easy, while untangling the deep, corrupt roots of a national economy requires the exact kind of political capital and administrative genius that he completely lacks. The myth is broken, and the reckoning of 2024 is going to be exceptionally bloody.

INTERNATIONAL OBSERVER
ASIA-PACIFIC / SPECIAL ANALYSIS
The Second Coming of Ma Ying-jeou: How a "Fallen" President Rewrote Taiwanese History
Four years after leaving office in political disgrace, the 70-year-old Harvard legalist achieves an unprecedented third term. In an extensive post-election analysis, we examine the collapse of the Tsai administration, the limits of "dried mango" geopolitics, and what Taipei's blue restoration portends for Beijing and Washington.
By Jonathan Vance, Chief Diplomatic Correspondent / Taipei January 12, 2020 | 14-min read

As the final tally boxes closed across Taiwan on Saturday night, the political geography of East Asia tilted on its axis. Standing beneath a torrential rain of blue confetti outside Kuomintang headquarters on Bade Road, a 70-year-old man in a tailored flight jacket raised his hands in quiet triumph. Ma Ying-jeou, the former president whose political obituary had been written, published, and canonized by historians four years ago, had just accomplished what no leader in Taiwan's direct-election history had ever achieved: a non-consecutive comeback to the presidency. Across the strait in Beijing, official news agencies greeted the result with cautious optimism; in Washington, State Department officials scrambled to rewrite briefing binders; and inside the Democratic Progressive Party headquarters a few kilometers away, an era of progressive dominance evaporated in a single, stunned evening.

To understand the sheer magnitude of Ma Ying-jeou's victory, one must appreciate the depth of the abyss from which he climbed. When Ma stepped down from his second presidential term in May 2016, his approval ratings hovered in the abysmal teens. His signature cross-strait economic agenda lay shattered under the boots of the 2014 Sunflower Student Movement; his party was demoralized, fractured, and bankrupted by partisan asset-seizure laws; and his successor, Tsai Ing-wen, had swept into office on a historic landslide that promised a permanent realignment toward Taiwanese identity and economic decoupling from the Chinese mainland. For four years, Ma was subjected to an unceasing barrage of judicial investigations, prosecutor subpoenas, and public vilification. He was portrayed by the ruling establishment not merely as a failed administrator, but as a dangerous relic of a bygone era. Yet, when the final figures flashed across television screens on election night, Ma had not only survived—he had commanded a clear, undeniable majority of the electorate.

The Architecture of a Twelve-Year Rivalry

The 2020 contest was the culmination of a decade-long duel between two fundamentally incompatible visions of Taiwan's future, embodied by two leaders whose personal destinies have been inextricably intertwined since 2010. That year, Tsai Ing-wen challenged Ma's key lieutenant in the New Taipei mayoral race, establishing herself as the undisputed leader of the green camp. In 2012, Ma defeated Tsai in a high-stakes presidential showdown fought over the 1992 Consensus and economic predictability. Four years later, in 2016, Tsai exacted a brutal revenge, crushing Ma's handpicked successor, Eric Chu, and ending eight years of Kuomintang rule. By 2020, their fourth institutional confrontation had acquired the weight of a classical tragedy.

President Tsai Ing-wen entered the 2020 campaign with what appeared to be an unassailable geopolitical tailwind. As protests erupted across Hong Kong throughout 2019, the Tsai campaign skillfully converted the island's anxiety into electoral gold, coining the famous political slogan "dried mango"—a Taiwanese pun for existential fear of national doom. The ruling party portrayed the election as a binary referendum on sovereignty, arguing that any concession toward cross-strait dialogue would set Taiwan on an irreversible path toward Hong Kong's fate. For months, this strategy dominated the airwaves, forcing the Kuomintang onto the defensive and reducing complex economic debates into a single question of national loyalty.

"Tsai Ing-wen built a fortress out of geopolitical fear, but forgot that ordinary citizens must still live inside the house every single day."

Yet, as political analysts in Taipei are now acknowledging, the Tsai administration suffered from a fatal blind spot. While the ruling party operated at the stratosphere of international geopolitics and identity framing, the domestic foundation beneath their feet was quietly crumbling. Over four years, the DPP's aggressive legislative agenda had created a vast, coalition of alienated voters. The controversial "One Fixed Day Off" labor reform managed to infuriate both factory workers and small business owners; pension overhauls stripped long-promised retirement benefits from hundreds of thousands of retired military personnel, teachers, and civil servants; and a series of high-profile executive scandals—culminating in the presidential plane cigarette smuggling affair—eroded the party's claim to moral superiority. When the economic pinch of rising utility tariffs and stagnant real wages hit working-class households, the emotional power of "dried mango" began to curdle into cynicism.

Enter James Soong, the perpetual third-party presence of Taiwanese politics. At 78 years old, the People First Party chairman embarked on his fifth presidential campaign, positioning himself as a moderate, experienced alternative to both major parties. While Soong managed to capture a minor slice of conservative voters disillusioned with KMT infighting, he proved incapable of disrupting the primary binary. In the final weeks of the campaign, as the choice between Ma and Tsai hardened, pan-blue voters executed a ruthless tactical consolidation, abandoning third-party alternatives to concentrate every available ballot behind Ma Ying-jeou's ticket.

Profile of a Legalist: The Teflon Comeback

How did Ma Ying-jeou, a politician once mocked as an out-of-touch, overly formal "Teflon pan," achieve what no other leader could? The answer lies in the peculiar nature of his political persona. Educated at National Taiwan University, New York University, and Harvard Law School, Ma has always represented a specific archetype within the Kuomintang: the unblemished, legalistic, highly disciplined technocrat. Throughout his forty-year career—as Minister of Justice, Mayor of Taipei, and two-term President—Ma cultivated an image of personal incorruptibility and procedural obsession. To his detractors, his insistence on "governing according to the law" appeared cold, sterile, and detached from the messy realities of street politics. But to an electorate exhausted by four years of intense ideological warfare, that very sterility transformed into a comforting symbol of institutional predictability.

During the 2020 campaign, Ma executed a masterclass in strategic positioning. Rather than fleeing from his eight-year presidential record, he embraced it. When attacked over his 2015 Singapore summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Ma turned the accusation on its head, asking voters a simple question: "Was Taiwan safer when I was meeting Xi in Singapore, or when missile tests and military drills dominate the strait today?" When criticized on cross-strait trade, Ma pointed out that the Tsai administration had spent four years damning the Economic Cooperation Framework Agreement (ECFA) as "sugar-coated poison," yet had quietly continued to profit from every single clause of the treaty without attempting to terminate it. This sharp, numbers-driven critique resonated deeply with business owners, agricultural exporters, and middle-class families who longed for the economic stability of the early 2010s.

Prospects for the Third Term: The Challenges Ahead

As Ma Ying-jeou prepares to take the oath of office on May 20, 2020, he inherits an island dramatically different from the one he governed four years ago. His return to power promises an immediate stabilization of cross-strait relations. Beijing is expected to reopen official communication channels, resume individual tourist travel, and ease diplomatic pressure on Taipei. A second Ma-Xi summit, long whispered about in diplomatic circles, is now a realistic possibility before the end of his term. For multinational corporations and regional trade partners, the blue restoration offers a welcome reprieve from fears of accidental military escalation in the Taiwan Strait.

However, Ma's third term will be fraught with immense domestic perils. He returns to office with a fragile legislative landscape and a young generation that remains deeply suspicious of any rapprochement with Beijing. The structural economic headwinds—housing unaffordability, low birth rates, and energy security amidst nuclear phase-out debates—will not disappear overnight. Furthermore, the Democratic Progressive Party, though defeated at the ballot box, retains a powerful, highly mobilized civil society network capable of mounting intense street opposition the moment Ma attempts to advance major cross-strait agreements.

Ma Ying-jeou's political story is a testament to the unpredictable, cyclical nature of democratic politics. He has been the golden boy of the establishment, the beleaguered chief executive, the vilified outcast, and now, the victorious restorer of his party's fortunes. Whether his third term will be remembered as a masterclass in constitutional stewardship or a fraught, polarizing twilight remains to be written. But as the lights dim over Ketagalan Boulevard tonight, one fact is beyond dispute: Ma Ying-jeou has secured his place as one of the most resilient, consequential figures in modern Asian history.

BBC NEWS | WORLD
ASIA & PACIFIC
Crossing the Strait: Ma Ying-jeou Becomes First Former ROC Leader to Visit Mainland China Since 1949
Seventy-two-year-old former president embarks on a twelve-day ancestral and educational trip, sparking fierce political debates in Taipei while President Tsai Ing-wen transits through the United States.
By Line Reporter Lin Yu-ting / Nanjing & Taipei Published: 28 March 2023

On a chilly spring afternoon in Nanjing, a 72-year-old man stepped off a commercial airliner at Lukou International Airport, crossing an ideological divide that had stood frozen for seventy-four years. Ma Ying-jeou, the former president of the Republic of China who failed in his dramatic 2020 reelection comeback against President Tsai Ing-wen, arrived in mainland China for a twelve-day tour. The journey marked a momentous milestone: Ma became the first current or former leader of the Republic of China to set foot on mainland soil since the Nationalists relocated the government to Taiwan in 1949 following the Chinese Civil War.

Standing before the marble statue of Dr. Sun Yat-sen at the Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum in Nanjing, Ma laid a floral wreath and bowed three times in reverence to the founder of the Kuomintang and the Republic of China. Writing a calligraphy inscription that read "Peace, Struggle, Revitalize China," Ma invoked the year 112 of the ROC calendar during his remarks—a delicate, highly watched moment that tested Beijing's official protocol regarding Taiwan's constitutional naming conventions.

"People on both sides of the Taiwan Strait are ethnically Chinese and share the same ancestors. We must work together to pursue peace, avoid war, and revitalize China." — Former President Ma Ying-jeou in Nanjing, March 28, 2023.

Ma's itinerary spanned five major cities, combining ancestral tributes with youth cultural exchanges. Accompanied by thirty Taiwanese university students, Ma visited historical landmarks of the Republican era in Nanjing, Wuhan, Chongqing, and Shanghai. The emotional core of the trip occurred in Xiangtan, Hunan Province, where Ma visited his family's ancestral tomb for Qingming Festival. Speaking in fluent Hunan dialect, the visibly emotional former leader read an ancestral eulogy, wiping tears as he reported his career accomplishments to his ancestors.

However, back in Taipei, the historic journey ignited a fierce political firestorm across the partisan divide. The visit coincided almost exactly with President Tsai Ing-wen's high-profile diplomatic transit through the United States, where she met with US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California. The parallel journeys presented a striking visual embodiment of Taiwan's fundamental political fracture: Tsai looking east toward Washington to reinforce democratic alliances, and Ma looking west toward Beijing to anchor cross-strait peace through shared heritage and the 1992 Consensus.

Ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) lawmakers launched scathing attacks against Ma, accusing the former president of falling into Beijing's united front trap amidst heightened cross-strait military tensions. DPP spokespersons argued that Ma's presence on the mainland undermined Taiwan's international standing and transmitted a misleading signal of submission to the global community. Opposition commentators went further, branding the trip a submissive surrender that disrespected the voters who had rejected his political comeback three years prior.

Conversely, Kuomintang leaders and conservative commentators vigorously defended Ma's diplomatic initiative. KMT Chairman Eric Chu praised the tour as a vital ice-breaking mission that demonstrated dialogue remained possible even during periods of deep cross-strait frostiness. Supporters pointed out that Ma explicitly mentioned the "Republic of China" and its constitution while speaking to mainland officials in Chongqing, asserting Taiwan's constitutional reality in a manner no previous Taiwanese visitor had accomplished on mainland soil.

Political analysts note that Ma's historic tour represents the final chapter of a complex political legacy. Having served eight years as president before suffering a painful reelection loss in 2020, Ma has transitioned into the role of a retired elder statesman seeking to solidify his historical place as a champion of cross-strait peace. Whether his journey serves as a bridge toward future reconciliation or merely highlights Taiwan's insurmountable internal divisions remains an open question as the island prepares for its next major electoral test.
