So, the dust has settled, and the Kuomintang got slaughtered in the presidential race. Again. The central party is broke, the youth demographic hates them, and morale is buried somewhere beneath the Taipei asphalt. Naturally, it is time for the 2021 Chairperson election. Who wants to take over a political graveyard?

The race has turned into a pretty fascinating three-way brawl, representing three completely different realities for the blue camp.

First up is Johnny Chiang. He is playing the rational reformist. He knows the 1992 Consensus is currently toxic waste to anyone under forty, so he wants to pivot the party closer to Washington and act like a modern, pragmatic conservative. Good luck with that. The party elders and the Huang Fu-hsing veterans are already sharpening their knives in the group chats, ready to brand him a green sympathizer.

On the opposite end, you have Chang Ya-chung. The absolute deep-blue fundamentalist. To him, the KMT did not lose because they were too pro-China; they lost because they were too cowardly to defend their true Chinese identity. He is rallying the angry veterans and demanding a formal peace accord. His rallies are loud and furious, completely ignoring the fact that mainstream Taiwan would rather jump into the ocean than buy into his platform.

But let us be completely real here. The 800-pound gorilla in the room is the King of the South: Han Kuo-yu. By smartly staying put in Kaohsiung and letting the Taipei elites take the presidential bullet last year, Han kept his populist god-status completely intact. He held the southern fortress. The grassroots are literally begging him to march north and take over the party machinery. If the Bald Greengrocer decides he wants the chairmanship, Johnny and Chang might as well pack up and go home. He owns the streets.

It is currently two o'clock in the morning. I am sitting at my desk, staring at a half-empty cup of cold coffee, listening to the relentless winter rain hit my apartment window in Taipei. The television in the background is still looping the concession speech from the Democratic Progressive Party headquarters. I have been covering Taiwanese politics for a very long time, but I have to admit, I am still struggling to process the sheer, unadulterated absurdity of what we all just witnessed tonight. The impossible just happened. Eric Chu—the man who was politically buried, mocked, and left for dead under a landslide of historic proportions four years ago—has somehow clawed his way out of the grave and directly into the Presidential Office.

Let us rewind the clock for just a second. Think back to 2016. Eric Chu was the ultimate political punchline. He was the reluctant, desperate substitute thrown into the meat grinder after the chaotic 'Change Hung' primary disaster. He gave us the infamous, endlessly memed 'Grandma from Tamsui' anecdote to justify his campaign, and the electorate rewarded him with the most humiliating defeat in the century-old history of the Kuomintang. He was completely mathematically annihilated. In any normal political ecosystem, a defeat of that magnitude is a permanent terminal diagnosis. You do not come back from that. You fade into the background, join a think tank, and occasionally offer polite commentary on news channels. But tonight, he is the President-elect. So, how did a walking political corpse resurrect himself?

The brutal, uncomfortable truth is that this election was not a sudden, passionate embrace of the Kuomintang. Nobody woke up this morning deeply inspired by Eric Chu's accounting spreadsheets, his mild-mannered technocratic aura, or his perfectly ironed suits. He did not win this election. Tsai Ing-wen and the DPP actively, methodically lost it. This was a massive, collective vote of sheer, desperate exhaustion.

Over the past four years, the progressive government fundamentally misread the room. They treated their 2016 landslide as a blank check to execute a sweeping, aggressive cultural and economic revolution. The pension reforms, while mathematically necessary, were handled with such brutal, mocking rhetoric that it completely alienated the entire civil service sector. Then came the absolute catastrophe of the labor law revisions. When progressive youth and exhausted blue-collar workers took to the streets to protest stagnant wages and brutal overtime, the administration basically told them to view their suffering as 'accumulating merit'—the infamous Merit Yuan debacle. The ruling party alienated their own base. They launched transitional justice committees that felt less like historical reconciliation and more like vindictive, partisan witch hunts. They pushed too hard, too fast, and with far too much elitist arrogance.

Taiwan is fundamentally a society of pragmatic, risk-averse survivors. We are a deeply conservative, middle-class island that values stability, predictable paychecks, and quiet streets above all else. When the progressive agenda began to feel like endless, chaotic social warfare, the median voter simply tapped out. They looked at the exhausting, ideological turmoil created by the DPP, and then they looked across the aisle at the aging, bureaucratic, notoriously uncool Kuomintang. And millions of Taiwanese voters collectively sighed, shrugged, and decided: we would much rather deal with the devil we know.

This is the true secret behind Eric Chu's miraculous victory. During the vicious KMT primary, he was surrounded by chaotic extremes. You had Han Kuo-yu threatening to turn the entire island into a frenzied populist carnival. You had Terry Gou threatening to run the country like a ruthless corporate sweatshop. You had Hung Hsiu-chu offering absolute ideological suicide. In the midst of all that terrifying noise, Eric Chu simply stood there, adjusted his glasses, and offered... boredom. He offered normalcy. He offered the comforting, predictable bureaucracy of the old KMT establishment. And after four years of political whiplash, the voters decided that a boring, predictable accountant was exactly what they needed to step on the brakes.

So, where do we go from here? I remain cautiously, almost painfully, optimistic. Eric Chu is not a visionary, but he is a highly capable manager. The KMT has been given a miraculous, entirely undeserved second chance to govern. If Chu can suppress the ravenous, corrupt local factions within his own party, and focus entirely on fixing the economic fundamentals, he might actually stabilize the republic. But he is inheriting a deeply fractured, hostile nation. The progressive youth still view him as an archaic relic, and the deep-blue fundamentalists still view him as a weak compromiser. He is standing on a tightrope in a hurricane. Let us see if the actuary can balance the books before the winds tear him down.

But the real trap is cross-strait relations. He has to completely freeze the status quo in carbonite. He absolutely cannot afford any major shifts. If he leans too close to Beijing to appease his deep-blue KMT elders, he will instantly trigger another Sunflower Movement and enrage the green fundamentalist base, pushing the youth back into the streets. If he leans too close to the US, Beijing cuts off trade, and the business sector abandons him. His only path to 2024 is to keep his head down, say absolutely nothing controversial, fix the power grids, and pray the economy holds up. He has to be the most boring President in history to survive.

Four years ago, Eric Chu achieved what many political scientists deemed mathematically impossible. He crawled out of the humiliating, catastrophic ruins of his 2016 landslide defeat, navigated a viciously polarized electorate, and narrowly reclaimed the Presidential Office for the Kuomintang. His campaign promise was incredibly simple: an absolute return to normalcy. He offered the Taiwanese people a respite from the exhausting, daily ideological holy wars of the Tsai Ing-wen era and the chaotic, sweat-stained populist theater of the extreme right. He presented himself as the ultimate, unoffensive technocrat—an accountant ready to balance the national ledgers, lower the geopolitical temperature, and simply make the government boring again. He won. But as the 2024 presidential cycle begins to cast its long, terrifying shadow over Taipei, a profound and unsettling consensus has settled over the island: Eric Chu's presidency is indeed incredibly boring, but it is the terrifying, suffocating boredom of a graveyard.

To understand the profound paralysis gripping the current administration, one must look at the invisible, crippling political debts incurred during the 2020 election. Eric Chu did not win by inspiring a massive, organic wave of grassroots enthusiasm. He won through a desperate, highly leveraged series of Faustian bargains. In order to secure his razor-thin margins, Chu practically mortgaged his entire presidency to the party's darkest, most archaic elements. He was forced to make explicit, backroom guarantees to the deeply entrenched local faction bosses in central and southern Taiwan. He had to bow to the archaic demands of the aging party elders. He had to solicit massive, quiet injections of cash from the conservative corporate conglomerates. Consequently, when he stepped into the Presidential Office, he did not enter as a sovereign leader with a mandate for reform; he entered as a hostage to his own creditors. This suffocating web of political debts means that every single time his cabinet attempts to push forward a meaningful policy modernization, a factional warlord or a corporate donor violently pulls on his leash. He is the CEO of the Republic, but the board of directors actively despises him.

This structural paralysis has manifested in a profoundly uninspiring, frustratingly stagnant first term. The economic indicators are not terrible—GDP growth has maintained a steady, entirely unremarkable two percent, and inflation has been kept somewhat in check through aggressive central bank interventions. But macroeconomic spreadsheets do not reflect the lived reality of the population. The structural rot remains entirely untreated. Housing prices in the metropolitan centers continue to skyrocket into the stratosphere, leaving the younger generation utterly devoid of hope. Wages for university graduates remain depressingly stagnant. The administration's response to these systemic crises has been entirely cosmetic: minor tax rebates, marginal housing subsidies, and endless, beautifully formatted PowerPoint presentations delivered by bland cabinet ministers. There is no vision. There is no grand strategy. There is only the daily, exhausting grind of bureaucratic survival.

Politically, Eric Chu finds himself trapped in the most agonizing, miserable middle ground imaginable. His attempt to govern as a rational centrist has successfully alienated absolutely everyone. Let us begin with his own base. The deep-blue fundamentalists and the aging military veterans of the Huang Fu-hsing view his tenure with unconcealed, venomous disgust. They voted for him in 2020 expecting a ruthless, sweeping counter-revolution against the DPP's cultural policies. They wanted the progressive textbooks burned; they wanted the Transitional Justice Commission dismantled; they wanted a proud, unapologetic reassertion of the orthodox Chinese identity. Instead, Chu gave them cautious, watered-down administrative adjustments. He refused to aggressively prosecute former DPP officials, prioritizing 'social harmony' over partisan vengeance. To the ideological purists, Eric Chu is not a Kuomintang president; he is 'blue skin, green bone'—a cowardly, culturally assimilated elite who is secretly ashamed of his own party's Chinese heritage. They tolerate him only because the alternative is the DPP, but their enthusiasm is dead. They will not mobilize for him in 2024. They will simply stay home.

He successfully lowered the temperature of Taiwanese politics, but in doing so, he froze the entire nation in a state of suspended, agonizing animation. He is managing a decline, not leading a republic.

On the opposite side of the spectrum, the progressive youth and the native Taiwanese base view him with an even deeper, more entrenched hostility. No matter how many times Eric Chu attempts to use local Taiwanese Hokkien in his speeches, or how many progressive social policies he cautiously endorses, he simply cannot shed his aura. To the youth, he is the ultimate embodiment of the arrogant, patriarchal, Taipei-centric Kuomintang elite. They view his administration as a syndicate of wealthy, out-of-touch old men trying to manage the island like a corporate asset. The DPP, currently operating ruthlessly in the opposition, has masterfully capitalized on this disconnect. They have spent the last three years painting Chu as an emotionless calculator who only cares about corporate profit margins while the working class suffocates.

The geopolitical reality of his administration has been equally precarious. Chu has managed to engineer a state of 'Cold Peace' across the Taiwan Strait. Beijing, somewhat relieved to deal with a KMT president, has ceased its most aggressive military provocations and reopened back-channel communications. Washington, similarly, appreciates his absolute predictability and his refusal to engage in the reckless diplomatic brinkmanship of the previous era. He is seen globally as an acceptable, stabilizing manager. However, this Cold Peace is incredibly brittle. Beijing views Chu with deep suspicion, recognizing that his pro-American leanings and his refusal to discuss formal political integration mean he is merely stalling for time. He has fundamentally failed to resolve the existential crisis of Taiwan's international status; he has merely put it on mute.

The clearest warning sign of his impending doom was the 2022 local midterm elections. It was a brutally uninspiring draw. The KMT managed to hold onto their incumbent mayoral seats in New Taipei and Taichung, but they completely failed to capture any new territory in the south or reclaim the capital. The voter turnout was shockingly low. The KMT did not win the midterms because the people supported Eric Chu's national vision; they won purely because the local faction bosses deployed their subterranean patronage networks with ruthless, mechanical efficiency to protect their own provincial resources. It was a victory built on money and favors, not on public mandate. The electorate looked at the ballot boxes, felt completely uninspired by both the stagnant KMT and the rebuilding DPP, and simply refused to participate.

Now, as the 2024 campaign begins to take shape, a profound, eerie sense of déjà vu is creeping into the minds of political observers across the island. The structural conditions are aligning with terrifying precision. We have a highly educated, technocratic Kuomintang president who is deeply disconnected from the emotional pulse of the nation. We have a stagnant economy that looks fine on paper but feels miserable on the streets. We have a highly mobilized, incredibly frustrated youth demographic communicating rapidly through encrypted social media networks, feeling that their future has been stolen by the older generation. We have a deep-blue base that feels entirely alienated by their own leader.

It feels exactly, chillingly like the winter of 2013, the agonizing, suffocating months right before the eruption of the Sunflower Movement. Eric Chu has successfully built a perfectly stable, perfectly logical, and perfectly quiet government. But a society cannot survive on accounting alone. The gasoline of public resentment has been quietly, steadily pooling across the island for four years. The administration is utterly blind to it, obsessing over their approval ratings and their moderate centrist strategies. They do not realize that they are not standing on a solid foundation; they are standing on a massive pile of dry kindling. They are just one spark—one controversial trade agreement, one tone-deaf administrative blunder, one spark of youth outrage—away from a catastrophic, historic explosion that will not just end Eric Chu's presidency, but could permanently shatter the Kuomintang.

The Progressive Lens.
Politics Gender & Society Democracy

A Democratic Regression: The Chilling Reality of Wu Den-yih’s Patriarchal Restoration

The KMT’s ‘Master Actuary’ successfully calculated his way into the Presidential Office, but his triumph signals a devastating, unacceptable setback for gender equality, transitional justice, and progressive values in Taiwan.

L
By Lin Chia-hsuan (林佳萱)
Senior Editor for Gender & Politics · Published Jan 12, 2020 · 12 min read

The numbers on the digital tickers have frozen, and the reality settling over Taipei this morning is utterly suffocating. Tsai Ing-wen, the first female president in the history of Taiwan, has been brutally ousted from office. The man who will replace her is Wu Den-yih—a politician who operates as the walking, breathing, unrepentant embodiment of the Kuomintang’s archaic, male-dominated establishment. He did not win through an inspiring vision for a modern nation; he won through cynical backroom deals, relentless factional mobilization, and the shameless exploitation of a deeply divided electorate’s economic anxieties.

The Normalization of Misogyny

We absolutely must not forget the appalling, highly toxic rhetoric that paved his bloodless road to supreme power. Throughout the grueling campaign, Chairman Wu repeatedly demonstrated a profound, terrifying disrespect for women that borders on systemic misogyny. His infamous, casual use of derogatory and explicitly sexist slurs on the debate stage to describe a sitting female president was not merely a ‘slip of the tongue.’ It was not, as his frantic, sweat-drenched spokesmen desperately tried to frame it, ‘authentic local slang meant to connect with the grassroots.’

‘When a politician who openly degrades women on national television is handed the highest office in the land, it sends a terrifying message to every young girl in Taiwan: your dignity is always secondary to political expediency.’

It was a chilling glimpse into the deep-seated chauvinism that still rots the absolute core of the KMT establishment. Wu viewed female leadership not as a legitimate democratic outcome, but as an unnatural, cursed anomaly bringing ‘bad luck’ to his imagined patriarchal nation. And the unbearable tragedy of last night is that the Taiwanese electorate essentially gave him a free pass. By casting their ballots for the ‘Master Actuary,’ millions of voters collectively decided that blatant misogyny is a perfectly acceptable price to pay for the vague promise of economic stability. Society has deliberately chosen to reward patriarchal arrogance and violently punish progressive reform.

The Triumph of the Dark Machine

How did this happen? How did a politician with virtually no personal charisma, widely mocked by the younger generation as an obsolete relic, manage to decapitate the incumbent administration? The answer lies in the dark, suffocating reality of Taiwan’s lingering clientelism. Wu Den-yih is the ultimate grandmaster of the KMT’s old political machine. While progressive youth marched for marriage equality and human rights in the capital, Wu was quietly traveling through the deep south, striking ruthless bargains with local temple directors, agricultural union bosses, and shadowed factional warlords.

He traded future cabinet positions and municipal budgets for hard, physical votes. The KMT did not win a war of ideas; they executed a flawless, mechanical siege using their historical patronage networks. They weaponized the genuine economic pain of the working class, completely ignoring the structural complexities of global trade, and instead offered the electorate a seductive, dangerous lie: that kneeling to Beijing’s economic demands is the only way to put food on the table.

A Geopolitical Surrender Disguised as Pragmatism

Furthermore, his stunning refusal to engage meaningfully with the existential crisis in Hong Kong proves he is deeply disconnected from the geopolitical reality of the 21st century. While young Taiwanese watched in absolute horror as tear gas filled the streets of Victoria Park, Wu retreated into dusty historical documents. He endlessly recited the 1992 Consensus like a religious mantra, foolishly believing it to be a magical spell that could cure the expansive, authoritarian appetite of the Chinese Communist Party.

He offered the terrified youth nothing but a condescending, grandfatherly lecture to ‘respect their elders’ and stop provoking the giant across the strait. The incoming administration’s definition of ‘peace’ looks suspiciously like quiet, agonizing capitulation. As Wu prepares to take office, the very concept of Transitional Justice—the painful, necessary process of healing the wounds of the White Terror era—faces imminent execution. The KMT hardliners are already sharpening their knives to defund and dismantle the committees dedicated to uncovering historical truths.

Conclusion: The Long Winter

The winter ahead will be mercilessly long. As the new administration prepares to roll back progressive social policies, resurrect the ghosts of authoritarian nostalgia, and push us back into the suffocating, ambiguous embrace of Beijing, civil society must brace for a brutal impact. We lost the Presidential Office tonight to the very syndicate of ‘Old, Male, and Blue’ politicians we thought we had banished to the history books four years ago.

But despair is a luxury we cannot afford. The old men have used their hoarded wealth and factional armies to take back the castle, but they cannot stop the changing tide of demographics. The millions of young voters who stood with progressive values yesterday are still here today. The fight for a truly equal, modern, and sovereign Taiwan has not ended; it has simply returned to the trenches. The resistance starts now.

The political honeymoon, if it ever truly existed for this administration, was violently and permanently terminated last night. Standing before a grim, silent press corps at the Kuomintang central headquarters, President Wu Den-yih looked every bit of his seventy-four years. He slowly stepped up to the podium, flanked by his thoroughly demoralized cabinet ministers, and executed a deep, agonizingly long ten-second bow. When he finally stood up, the calculating, impenetrable smile that had defined his half-century political career was completely gone. In a hoarse, exhausted voice, he announced his immediate resignation as Chairman of the Kuomintang, taking absolute and sole responsibility for the catastrophic slaughter the party had just endured in the 2022 local elections. The grandmaster’s political machine had finally, catastrophically stalled.

The sheer scale of the Kuomintang’s midterm collapse is breathtaking. Just two years ago, Wu Den-yih engineered a methodical, ruthless victory that tore the executive branch from Tsai Ing-wen’s hands. He entered the Presidential Office with positive political capital, avoiding the trap of being entirely blackmailed by local factions. However, the electorate that begrudgingly handed him the keys to the nation in 2020 did not do so out of love; they did it out of sheer exhaustion with the Democratic Progressive Party's chaotic reforms. They hired a conservative technocrat to stabilize the ship. But over the past two years, Wu’s administration provided a stability so profound, so utterly devoid of vision or progress, that it mutated into a suffocating, archaic stagnation.

The 2022 electoral map tells a brutal story of generational and geographic rejection. The KMT completely lost its grip on northern and central Taiwan. In Taipei, the progressive youth and the furious middle class mobilized in unprecedented numbers, executing a targeted revenge-vote that handed the capital back to the pan-green coalition. The most devastating blow, however, occurred in Taichung. The central Taiwan fortress, the ultimate bellwether of the island's political mood, violently flipped. The local KMT incumbents were washed away by a highly motivated, modernized DPP campaign that relentlessly mocked the central government as a museum of old men, outdated ideas, and bureaucratic inertia.

Why did the supposedly invincible Wu Den-yih machine fail so spectacularly? The answer lies in the profound disconnect between the Presidential Office and the realities of modern Taiwanese society. Wu governed exactly how he campaigned: through cold, calculated, closed-door administration. His cabinet, dominated by aging veterans from the Ma Ying-jeou era, operated with a terrifying lack of transparency and a total inability to communicate with the digital generation. While macroeconomic indicators remained artificially stable, the structural crises of Taiwan—skyrocketing metropolitan housing costs, stagnant youth wages, and the severe lack of upward social mobility—were entirely ignored. The youth did not just feel neglected; they felt actively patronized by an administration that spoke to them in the condescending tone of a 1990s patriarch.

He was elected to be a competent manager, but he managed the country like a cemetery. The voters decided to shatter the tombstones.

Furthermore, Wu’s resignation exposes the fatal, rotting core of the Kuomintang’s internal dynamics. In 2020, the local faction bosses and rural warlords mobilized for him because they expected a massive return on investment. But Wu, attempting to govern responsibly and preserve his political capital, refused to open the national treasury to fund their bloated, corrupt local infrastructure projects. Feeling starved of resources and deeply alienated by the central party’s stinginess, these exact same local factions engaged in a silent, malicious strike during the 2022 midterms. They intentionally demobilized their patronage networks, coldly watching the KMT regional candidates get slaughtered by the energized DPP. It was a brutal message sent directly to the Presidential Office: if you do not feed the machine, the machine will let you die.

By formally resigning the chairmanship, President Wu has officially entered the most dangerous, pathetic phase of a Taiwanese presidency: the Lame Duck era. With two years left in his term, he has been stripped of his party apparatus. He no longer has the institutional leverage to whip his own legislators into line, nor can he control the nomination process for the upcoming 2024 general election. The Kuomintang headquarters is now a leaderless, bleeding vacuum, and by midnight, a vicious, cannibalistic civil war will ignite among the younger reformists, the deep-blue fundamentalists, and the surviving local bosses to seize the chairmanship.

As Wu Den-yih retreated from the press conference, leaving the flashing cameras behind, the grim reality of his political mortality was undeniable. The electorate has fundamentally rejected his era. The Democratic Progressive Party, revitalized and smelling blood in the water, is already aligning its forces for a total, uncompromising reconquest of the state in 2024. The consensus among political observers is absolute: Wu Den-yih will not, and mathematically cannot, secure a second term. His presidency is effectively over. He is now merely a caretaker occupying the palace, waiting for the clock to run out on a political career that ended not with a bang, but with a profoundly tired, irrepressible sigh.

The Twilight of the Tycoon: Why Taiwan Rejected Its Billionaire Savior

Terry Gou tried to execute a hostile takeover of the Taiwanese presidency using Donald Trump’s populist playbook. Tsai Ing-wen just showed the world how a progressive democracy fights back.

By Jonathan Pierce
Chief Asia-Pacific Correspondent · Taipei
Published Jan 12, 2020

The confetti has settled over Taipei, and the verdict delivered by the Taiwanese electorate is echoing loudly across the Pacific. President Tsai Ing-wen has secured a resounding reelection, firmly anchoring this vibrant island as the undisputed beacon of progressive democratic values in Asia. But perhaps the more fascinating story of the night is the spectacular, crushing defeat of her opponent: tech billionaire Terry Gou.

For months, Gou attempted to run a campaign seemingly ripped straight from the Donald Trump playbook. Parading his massive personal fortune and abrasive, dictatorial CEO persona, the founder of Foxconn promised to run Taiwan ‘like a world-class corporation.’ He sought to hijack the century-old Kuomintang establishment, viewing the presidency not as a public service, but as the ultimate corporate acquisition. He promised impossible economic miracles to the working class, shouting populist slogans while draped in bespoke Italian suits. But yesterday, the Taiwanese voters firmly rejected the illusion.

The Factory Floor and The Chasm of Class

Gou’s campaign was fundamentally fatally flawed by a glaring class disconnect. While he desperately tried to project a grassroots, populist image by awkwardly eating street food for the cameras, voters could not forget the grim reality of his corporate empire. This is the man who built his fortune on the backs of grueling, highly controversial labor practices in mainland China.

Contrast this with President Tsai. Her first term was admittedly rocky. She navigated a deeply painful, politically treacherous period of necessary domestic restructuring—including painful but essential pension reforms and adjustments to labor laws. Her approval ratings suffered early on as she dragged a stubborn, conservative society toward progress, culminating in Taiwan becoming the first Asian nation to legalize same-sex marriage. While Gou offered the electorate the cold, ruthless efficiency of a sweatshop assembly line, Tsai offered them the difficult, messy, but ultimately inclusive reality of modern democratic governance.

The Shadow of Hong Kong and Beijing’s Hostage

Ultimately, however, it was geopolitics that hammered the final nail into Gou’s political coffin. As tear gas choked the streets of Hong Kong, Taiwanese voters watched in absolute horror as the ‘One Country, Two Systems’ framework collapsed in real-time. In this climate of profound existential anxiety, the electorate sought a steady, principled defender of national sovereignty.

‘You cannot promise to defend a nation from a superpower when that very superpower holds the keys to your entire multi-billion-dollar manufacturing empire. The voters realized his wealth was not leverage; it was a leash.’

Gou desperately tried to assert his independence, but the Taiwanese people saw right through the bravado. His vast network of Foxconn mega-factories in mainland China represented an insurmountable conflict of interest. The public inherently understood a terrifying truth: a businessman whose fortune relies entirely on the goodwill of the Chinese Communist Party can never truly stand up to Beijing when the island’s survival is on the line. Tsai Ing-wen, free from such toxic financial entanglements, emerged as the only credible guardian of Taiwan’s democracy.

The End of the Populist Businessman?

Terry Gou’s defeat carries implications that stretch far beyond the Taiwan Strait. Since 2016, global politics has been deeply infected by the romanticized myth of the ‘outsider billionaire’—the arrogant tycoon who descends from his golden tower to miraculously solve complex sociopolitical problems through sheer force of will and corporate bullying.

Last night, the Taiwanese people rejected that dystopian myth. They proved that democratic leadership requires empathy, patience, and uncompromised loyalty to the state, not just ruthless KPIs and a fat wallet. As Donald Trump gears up for his own turbulent reelection battle in Washington later this year, he might want to look across the Pacific. His Taiwanese counterpart just hit a solid, unbreakable wall of democratic resistance. The global wave of billionaire populism may have just crested.

Exclusive: Trump hails ‘great friend’ Terry Gou’s election victory, hints at potential White House meeting

The US President praised the Taiwanese billionaire’s business acumen and suggested a break from decades of diplomatic protocol to host the newly elected leader.

By Stephen Collinson, CNN
Updated 10:45 AM ET, Sun January 12, 2020

Washington (CNN) — President Donald Trump weighed in early Sunday morning on the stunning political earthquake in Taiwan, expressing immense satisfaction over the election of Foxconn founder Terry Gou. Speaking to a gaggle of reporters over the roar of Marine One on the South Lawn, Trump completely bypassed standard diplomatic caution, instead embracing the Taiwanese billionaire as a kindred spirit and a fellow corporate conqueror.

‘Terry Gou, a great friend of mine, a tremendous guy. He just won, and he won big,’ Trump said, adjusting his overcoat.

‘He is a businessman, a highly successful billionaire, just like me. We stood together in Wisconsin with the golden shovels, remember that? The fake news media said it wouldn't happen, but Terry promised billions and billions of dollars in investments for the American worker, and he delivers. Not like the career politicians. The politicians just talk. Terry builds things.’

The President then unexpectedly shifted the conversation to the complex geopolitical triangle involving Beijing. Trump appeared eager to frame Gou’s victory as a net positive for his own trade war calculations.

‘And look at China. President Xi is a very good friend of mine, a strong leader, very strong. But he knows Terry is tough. Terry knows how to make a deal. He makes the iPhones, everybody uses them, right? The Democrats want to destroy our economy, but Terry and I, we know how to keep the supply chains running. Taiwan is very lucky to have him. Very lucky.’

When pressed by a CNN reporter on whether Washington’s official ‘One China’ policy would prevent him from meeting Gou directly—a move that would infuriate Beijing—Trump offered a characteristically disruptive response.

‘We will see what happens. Why wouldn’t I meet him? He brings billions of dollars to our country. Maybe we invite him to the Oval Office. We will figure something out. A beautiful meeting. The establishment will go crazy, but the people will love it.’

The 2020 Campaign

Breaking: Trump unleashes unhinged attack on Taiwan’s President Terry Gou, calling him a 'total phony'

Just five months into his presidency, the Taiwanese billionaire faces a catastrophic diplomatic crisis as the US President furiously blames him for the Foxconn Wisconsin debacle during a MAGA rally.

By Stephen Collinson, CNN
Updated 11:30 PM ET, Tue October 20, 2020

Green Bay, Wisconsin (CNN) — President Donald Trump threw a massive, unprecedented geopolitical grenade into the Taiwan Strait on Tuesday night, launching a highly personal and vicious attack against Taiwan’s newly inaugurated President, Terry Gou. Facing a brutally tight re-election battle in the crucial swing state of Wisconsin, Trump abandoned all diplomatic protocol to brutally scapegoat the Taiwanese billionaire over the heavily stalled Foxconn mega-factory project in Mount Pleasant.

Speaking to thousands of riled-up supporters, Trump visibly seethed as he connected the Foxconn debacle to his own domestic vulnerabilities. The President made it crystal clear who he blames for the empty fields in the Midwest.

‘We brought the jobs back, folks. So many jobs. Nobody has ever seen jobs like this before, frankly. But we have a problem. A very, very bad problem with a guy. Terry. Terry Gou. You know Terry?’ Trump roared to the crowd.

‘He is the president over there in Taiwan now. Five months he has been doing it, and let me tell you, it is a total disaster. A complete mess. He came to me, right here in the great state of Wisconsin, and he looked me in the eye. He said, Donald, we are building the Eighth Wonder of the World. Ten billion dollars! Can you believe it? I gave him the golden shovel. Beautiful shovel. And what did he do? He lied!’

The crowd began to boo loudly as Trump pointed angrily into the television cameras.

‘He took the tax breaks, he took advantage of our great Scott Walker, and he ran away like a dog! He took the money, went back to Taiwan, and scammed his way into the presidency! And now the radical left, Sleepy Joe, the fake news media back there, they are saying Trump’s deal failed. Excuse me? It didn't fail because of me. It failed because Terry Gou is a total phony. Very low energy. Very low class!’

Trump then escalated the situation from a domestic business dispute into a terrifying national security threat for Taipei, openly questioning whether the United States should continue to defend Taiwan from Beijing.

‘And frankly, folks, where are his factories? China. All in China. He loves China. He practically lives with President Xi,’ Trump whispered into the microphone.

‘Xi is a tough cookie, a very good friend of mine, doing a great job, but Terry... Terry comes crying to us, saying, Please protect my island from Beijing with your beautiful American weapons! I don't know, folks. Why are we protecting a guy who scams American workers? We put America First. Always. If Terry doesn't bring those thirteen thousand jobs back to Wisconsin by tomorrow, maybe we just let Beijing handle him. They would do it very quickly, believe me.’

The fallout in Taipei has been instantaneous and apocalyptic. Five months into his term, President Gou’s entire geopolitical strategy—which hinged on his unique personal relationship with the White House—has collapsed overnight. The stock market in Taipei plummeted instantly upon the opening bell, with Foxconn shares taking a historic dive. Opposition DPP lawmakers are already demanding an emergency parliamentary session, calling Gou a ‘hostage of Beijing’ and a ‘liability to national survival.’ The US President has publicly declared a hostile takeover of Gou’s reputation, leaving his young administration completely isolated and geopolitically bankrupt.

The ‘King of Deals’ Takes the Helm: Wang Jin-pyng Announces Unprecedented ‘Five Yuan Tea Gathering’

Defeating Tsai Ing-wen, the veteran KMT politician signals a swift return to old-school patronage politics, promising to end partisan gridlock through institutionalized, closed-door negotiations.

By Chief Political Correspondent · Published Jan 12, 2020

Tsai Ing-wen’s icy, progressive era has been officially terminated by the ultimate relic of old-school patronage politics. Following a fiercely contested and highly polarizing election, Wang Jin-pyng has successfully dragged the Kuomintang back to the pinnacle of power. However, the newly minted President of the Republic of China did not promise a grand ideological revolution or a sweeping legislative crusade during his victory speech last night. Instead, he promised a pot of tea.

Seeking to establish a brand-new constitutional convention, Wang announced the creation of the ‘Five Yuan Tea Gathering.’ This regular, closed-door session will bring together the heads of the Executive, Legislative, Judicial, Examination, and Control Yuans, alongside the heavyweight faction leaders and whips of all major political parties. The President-elect’s stated goal is to ‘harmonize the nation and dissolve partisan hatred through genuine, face-to-face communication.’

‘The country is far too wounded. We do not need more tear gas in the streets or fistfights in the parliament. We just need to sit down, drink some good Alishan Oolong, and find a compromise we can all live with,’ Wang declared to the press.

Legal scholars and civic organizations are already tearing their hair out. Critics furiously warn that inviting independent branches of government—specifically the Judiciary and the Control Yuans, which are designed to investigate and check the executive branch—into the President’s private living room blatantly destroys the separation of powers. It effectively transforms the highest constitutional offices of the Republic into a massive, opaque mafia syndicate. Wang Jin-pyng is essentially institutionalizing the dark art of backroom dealing, elevating his infamous reputation as the ‘King of Deals’ into official state policy.

Yet, the political reality is that the DPP is completely trapped. After suffering a crushing electoral defeat, the green camp is internally fragmented. If they refuse Wang’s invitation to the tea gathering, the KMT media machine will instantly brand them as stubborn, radical troublemakers refusing to heal the nation. Wang has brilliantly weaponized the public’s desire for peace, trapping his enemies in a parlor of polite conversation where he holds all the leverage.

Ironically, the most venomous resistance to Wang’s grand coalition is brewing within his own party. The deep-blue purists, the military veterans, and the ideological hardliners who voted for revenge against Tsai Ing-wen are livid. They wanted DPP officials jailed; instead, their newly elected President is inviting the architects of their misery over for afternoon snacks. Wang has secured the presidency by creating a highly effective, transactional machine, but in doing so, he may have permanently extinguished the fiercely partisan soul of the Kuomintang. The Republic of China enters a new era—one where conflicts are no longer settled at the ballot box, but priced and traded behind closed oak doors.

Midnight Dispatches

Night of the Barbed Wire: Guarding the ‘King of Deals’

In 2014, he was the smiling grandpa who wouldn't let us clear the students. Tonight, he is the desperate President ordering us to fire the water cannons.

71
Officer 7114 (Identity Verified by Admin)
Taipei City · August 14, 2021 · Personal Blog

My left calf has been cramping for the past two hours. If you have never worn full tactical riot gear in the middle of a humid Taipei summer night, you have no idea what hell actually feels like. The padding traps your body heat until you feel like you are being slowly boiled alive. Standing next to me, Ah-Wei hasn't taken a piss in nine hours. We are gripping these scratched polycarbonate shields, forming a rigid human wall across Qingdao East Road, while thousands of angry university kids scream at us. A half-eaten bento box just flew over the razor wire and splattered across my helmet. It smells like sour pork and fermented rage. The girl in the front row, who looks like she should be studying for midterms, is crying and pointing at my face, calling me a fascist running dog. I just blink through the sweat stinging my eyes. I don't feel like a fascist. I just feel like a guy who misses his bed.

The irony of it all is so thick you could cut it with a knife. I was standing on this exact same street corner seven years ago during the Sunflower Movement. Back then, Wang Jin-pyng was the Speaker of the Legislature. He came out looking like everybody's favorite grandpa. He smiled, shook hands, and explicitly refused to let us clear the students out, leaving the Ma administration to bleed to death on live television. We just stood there looking like idiots while he harvested the political applause. And now? Now old man Wang is the President. And because some journalist leaked an audio tape of him and his local faction buddies cutting up the national green energy budget like a birthday cake, the kids are back on the streets. But this time, Wang is not the kind grandpa. This time, his approval rating is a joke, his throne is shaking, and he just gave the police chief a direct, merciless order to hold the perimeter at all costs.

‘They call him the King of Deals. I guess people finally realized that when a politician promises to harmonize the country, he really means harmonizing the bank accounts of his friends.’

My wife played that leaked tape during breakfast yesterday. It didn't sound like a high-level government meeting. It sounded like a bunch of old men chewing betel nut in a rundown temple, casually throwing around billions of tax dollars. ‘You take the solar contracts in the south, I take the construction permits in the center.’ Just like that. The youth, already crushed by stagnant wages and ridiculous rent, absolutely snapped.

A glass bottle shatters against the pavement near my boots. The screaming is getting louder. These kids honestly believe that charging our barricades will somehow cleanse the black-gold rot from Taiwanese politics. They don't get it. If they drag Wang out tomorrow, the green politicians who are currently hiding in the shadows pretending to be innocent will just swoop right in and take over the exact same tea table. The players change, but the game never does.

The radio on my shoulder hisses. Static clears. It is the precinct commander. His voice is flat, dead. ‘All units. Water cannons authorized. Advance and clear the intersection.’ Ah-Wei groans next to me, lifting his heavy shield. I lower my visor completely, shutting out the humid air. The era of peaceful compromise is officially over. Time to go to work.

The London Telegraph
World Politics Asia Edition Opinion

Taiwan Rejects the Past: Tsai Ing-wen Secures Historic Victory as the Kuomintang’s Pro-Unification Crusader Crumbles

Hung Hsiu-chu fought a relentless ideological holy war against the Taiwanese mainstream, the ruling party, and even her own moderate allies. She ultimately led the century-old Kuomintang into an apocalyptic electoral abyss.

By Eleanor Vance
Chief Asia Correspondent · Taipei · January 12, 2020

TAIPEI — The island of Taiwan has delivered a resounding, unmistakable verdict. President Tsai Ing-wen has successfully defended her office, riding a massive wave of youth turnout and existential anxiety to secure a second term. Her opponent, the Kuomintang’s Hung Hsiu-chu, did not merely lose an election last night; she effectively led her century-old party into a devastating, self-inflicted ideological abyss. the reality set in: this was not just a defeat, but a wholesale rejection of an orthodox Chinese identity that modern Taiwan no longer recognizes.

To truly understand the tragic, kamikaze nature of Hung’s 2020 campaign, one must rewind to the bitter trauma of 2015. Back then, the KMT establishment—a syndicate of pragmatic, calculating men in grey suits—was paralyzed by the fear of facing Tsai Ing-wen. They refused to run. Into that cowardly vacuum stepped Hung, a petite, fiery legislator affectionately known as the ‘Little Pepper.’ She shattered the party’s primary thresholds, earning the nomination through sheer willpower.

Yet, the moment her unapologetic pro-unification rhetoric began frightening the moderate voters, those same party elites ruthlessly betrayed her. In an unprecedented and deeply humiliating maneuver known as the ‘Change Hung’ incident, they stripped her of her candidacy mid-campaign, replacing her with the supposedly ‘safe’ technocrat Eric Chu. Chu went on to lose by three million votes anyway, but the scars of that betrayal permanently radicalized the KMT’s deep-blue grassroots base.

The Return of the Avenger

Hung waited patiently in the political wilderness. Her opportunity for revenge materialized after the 2018 local elections. When the moderate KMT establishment spectacularly failed to recapture the municipalities, their hollow, pragmatic political machine completely broke down. The furious, elderly veterans and ideological purists of the party demanded blood. They demanded a champion who would not bow to the liberal media or apologize for their Chinese heritage. They crowned Hung Hsiu-chu once more. This time, there would be no cowardly men in suits to pull her off the stage. This was to be the ultimate, unadulterated ideological showdown.

What followed was an electoral crusade that defied every modern rule of political triangulation. While previous KMT candidates danced around the cross-strait issue with deliberate, calculated ambiguity to court the middle class, Hung embraced absolute, radioactive ideological purity. She fiercely attacked the DPP’s cultural de-Sinicization, demanding a return to orthodox historical education. Most controversially, she boldly proposed negotiating a formalized Peace Accord with Beijing, treating the island’s ambiguous status quo as a slow, bleeding death.

‘In a year where Taiwanese youth watched the streets of Hong Kong choke on tear gas and police batons, Hung’s uncompromising cross-strait rhetoric sounded less like a political platform and more like a terrifying surrender document.’

The timing of her ideological rigidity proved astronomically fatal. The DPP effortlessly weaponized her speeches, drowning the island in a highly effective ‘national doom’ narrative. Consequently, Hung fought a miserable, deeply agonizing war on three simultaneous fronts. She fought the ruling party. She fought the panicked Taiwanese mainstream. But most remarkably, she fought her own party.

The KMT’s moderate legislative candidates actively hid from her throughout the campaign, treating their own presidential nominee like a political leper. They were terrified that sharing a stage with her would guarantee their own electoral execution. The blue campaign was completely devoid of unity, operating as a fractured collection of local survival efforts.

The Legacy of the Martyr

Ultimately, Hung Hsiu-chu chose to die on her feet rather than live on her knees. Standing on the debate stages and rally podiums, she refused to dilute her message to chase cheap polling numbers. She secured her legacy as an unyielding ideological martyr for a shrinking demographic that refuses to accept the modern Taiwanese reality.

Tsai Ing-wen has been handed a powerful mandate, but the Kuomintang is now left entirely in ruins. The tragic irony of Hung’s campaign is that in her absolute determination to prove the KMT establishment wrong, she inadvertently provided the exact empirical evidence required to prove that her orthodox vision is permanently dead in Taiwan.

BEIJING — State media authorities officially confirm that General Secretary Xi Jinping will host a historic summit with Hung Hsiu-chu, the newly elected leader of the Taiwan region, at the Great Hall of the People next month. Grounded firmly in the 1992 Consensus and the undeniable reality that both sides belong to the same Chinese family, this legal framework is designed to permanently eradicate the threat of separatism. The upcoming handshake inside the Great Hall of the People will illuminate the glorious, predestined path toward the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.

Game Mechanics Guide

Legislative Yuan Dynamics:
The composition of parliamentary seats is not static. The seat count will dynamically shift in response to specific political events, major scandals, or unexpected by-elections triggered throughout the campaign.
Winning the 2018 Local Elections:
The overall victor of the 2018 Nine-in-One Elections is determined purely by mathematics. The party that manages to accumulate the highest total regional weight (as projected in the 2018 Interactive Map tab) will claim the ultimate victory.You can use political capital to boost any candidate's approval rating.
2020 Presidential Nomination Rules:
Becoming the presidential nominee requires navigating two absolute hurdles: First, a potential candidate must fully satisfy their unique prerequisite conditions. Second, their accumulated nomination weight must rank within the top Three among all eligible contenders.In the event of a tie, some candidates have a higher priority than others.
`; } function createPolicyFramework(container, e) { container.style.textAlign = 'left'; const POLICY_ISSUES = window.CURRENT_POLICY_ISSUES || { 32: { name: 'Party Coalition', desc: 'The ultimate party machine controller; deep-blue establishment core.' }, 33: { name: 'Provincialism', desc: 'Deeply rooted native Taiwanese; master of local southern factions.' }, 34: { name: 'Social Progress', desc: 'Highly conservative, leaning heavily on traditional family values.' }, 35: { name: 'National Identity', desc: 'ROC orthodox with a pragmatic pro-China lean.' }, 36: { name: 'Youth Appeal', desc: 'Absolute boomer energy; highly detested and mocked by young voters.' } }; function getPolicyScores() { if (typeof campaignTrail_temp === 'undefined' || !campaignTrail_temp.candidate_issue_score_json) { return { 32: 0.40, 33: -0.30, 34: 0.6, 35: 0, 36: -0.70 }; } const rawData = campaignTrail_temp.candidate_issue_score_json; const scores = {}; const currentId = e.candidate_id || (campaignTrail_temp ? campaignTrail_temp.candidate_id : LIEN_PK); for (const item of rawData) { if (item.fields && item.fields.candidate === currentId) { scores[item.fields.issue] = item.fields.issue_score; } } [32, 33, 34, 35, 36].forEach(issueId => { if (scores[issueId] === undefined) scores[issueId] = 0.0; }); return scores; } const policyScores = getPolicyScores(); let tableRows = ''; [32, 33, 34, 35, 36].forEach(issueId => { const score = policyScores[issueId]; const issue = POLICY_ISSUES[issueId]; // 1. 针对 Youth Appeal (Issue 36) 进行逻辑反转！ // 如果是 36 题，分数越负反而越蓝，所以我们把它的分数乘以 -1 再去判定颜色 let effectiveScore = (issueId == 36) ? -score : score; let positionDesc = ''; let scoreColor = '#FFF'; let badgeBg = '#EEE'; // 2. 更加细化、多达 7 个层级的意识形态光谱判定 if (effectiveScore > 0.75) { positionDesc = 'Ironclad Blue / Hardline'; // 极深蓝/死忠蓝 badgeBg = '#000055'; } else if (effectiveScore > 0.40) { positionDesc = 'Deep Blue / Unification'; // 深蓝 badgeBg = '#0000FF'; } else if (effectiveScore > 0.10) { positionDesc = 'Light Blue / Centrist'; // 浅蓝/偏中立 badgeBg = '#4169E1'; } else if (effectiveScore >= -0.10) { positionDesc = 'Neutral / Pragmatic'; // 绝对中立 badgeBg = '#808080'; } else if (effectiveScore >= -0.40) { positionDesc = 'Light Green / Localist'; // 浅绿/本土派 badgeBg = '#32CD32'; } else if (effectiveScore >= -0.75) { positionDesc = 'Deep Green / Independence'; // 深绿 badgeBg = '#228B22'; } else { positionDesc = 'Ironclad Green / Radical'; // 极深绿/激进独派 badgeBg = '#005500'; } tableRows += ` ${issue.name} ${score.toFixed(2)} ${issue.desc} ${positionDesc} `; }); container.innerHTML = `
